The 175th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in July 1940 and was assigned to the 64th Rifle Corps, North Caucasus Military District, near Nalchik. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at peacetime strength, about 50%. It was held back to finish mobilizing and in July 1941 was assigned to the Southwestern Front Reserves where it remained till August. It was then assigned to the 37th Army for the defense of Kiev and was wiped out in the Kiev pocket in September 1941. In March 1942 the Division was recreated for a second time at Tyumen , fought at Stalingrad, assigned to the 64th Army, and suffered heavy causalities, It was deactivated in September 1942. Recreated again for the third time at Sverdlovsk in late 1942, the Division fought at Demyansk and in Belorussia. It finished the war assigned to 47th Army of the 1st Belorussian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#171%E2%80%93180 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of J Tomlinson

The 176th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in July 1940 and was assigned to the 35th Rifle Corps, 9th Army, Southern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at peacetime strength, about 50%. Located on the Rumanian border at the start of hostilities, the Division was able to make an orderly retreat, and despite suffering heavy causalities, survived 1941 intact, in reserve to the Southern Front. In October 1943 the Division was renamed the 129th Guards Rifle Division. The Division was formed for a second time at Maselkaya, from the 65th and 80th Naval Rifle Brigades, and finished the war assigned to 31st Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#171%E2%80%93180 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of J Tomlinson

The 178th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in 1939 at Omsk in the Siberian Mlitary District. At the start of the war, the Division was close to full strength, and was assigned to the 53rd Rifle Corps, 24th Army, Stavka Reserve (RVGK). In early July 1941 the Division was moved forward to take up defensive positions near Vyazma, and then east of Smolensk where it saw little action. The division was assigned to the 22nd Army, Kalinin Front in September 1941 and ended the year intact. The Division finished the war with the 23rd Army of the Leningrad Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#171%E2%80%93180 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 179th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in August 1940 from the 1st Lithuanian Infantry Division and was assigned to the 29th Rifle Corps, 11th Army, Northwestern Front. At the start of the war the Division had non standard equipment and was still forming. Many of the soldiers were not sympathetic to the Soviet cause and the Division was classed as unreliable. Despite this the Division kept its cohesion in combat though by August 1941 it was down to 300 men. It finished the year assigned to the 22nd Army of the Kalinin Front. At the end of the war it was assigned to the 4th Shock Army, Leningrad Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/179th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 17th Air Army was formed in October 1942 on the basis of the Air Forces of the Southwestern Front. It included a mixed air corps, two fighter, one ground-attack, one bomber, and one night bomber division. It immediately took part in the Battle of Stalingrad. On 19 November 1942 during the Battle of Stalingrad it was under the command of General Major Stepan Krasovsky. On 1 April 1943, as part of the Southwestern Front, it comprised the 3rd Mixed Aviation Corps (207th Fighter Aviation Division, 290th Assault Aviation Division), 7th Mixed Aviation Corps (202nd Bomber Aviation Division, 235th Fighter Aviation Division), 9th Mixed Aviation Corps (305th, 306th Assault Aviation Division, 295th Fighter Aviation Division), 244th Bombardment Aviation Division, 262nd Night Bomber Aviation Division, 39th, 132nd Bomber Aviation Regiments, 208th, 637th Attack Aviation Regiments, 282nd Mixed Aviation Regiment, 371st Transport Aviation Regiment, 10th, 50th Reconnaissance Aviation Squadrons, 34th Fire Correction Squadron. From March 1943 until the end of the war Vladimir Sudets commanded the 17th Air Army. From 1943-45 it participated in the Ostrogozhsk-Rossoh, Left and Right Bank Ukraine operations, and the capture of Romania, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Hungary, and Austria. Over 200,000 sorties were flown.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Air_Army

On 22 June 1941, the 17th Army was part of Army Group South (Heeresgruppe Süd) when Nazi Germany launched Operation Barbarossa (Case Barbarossa) and invaded the Soviet Union. From 1 July, the Hungarian 'Fast Moving Army Corps' (Gyorshadtest) was subordinated to the 17th Army.The 17th Army was engaged in some very heavy fighting with Soviet forces in southern Russia. Along with 1st Panzer Army, the 17th Army encircled Soviet forces near Uman in central Ukraine during the Battle of Uman. Approximately 100,000 Soviet troops were captured.Afterwards, the 17th Army and other German formations encircled even more Soviet troops during the Battle of Kiev. Approximately 450,000 were captured and, afterwards, Marshal of the Soviet Union (Marshal Sovietskovo Soyuza) Semyon Budyonny was dismissed from duty.After Kiev, the German focus shifted towards Moscow and the Battle of Moscow. Army Group South was ordered to resume the offensive, with the objective of capturing Rostov-on-Don, the gateway to the Caucasus oil fields, and Kharkov a major center of heavy industry for the Soviet Union.In 1942, Army Group South was to spearhead the German summer offensive in Russia known as Fall Blau. The 17th Army was to give flank protection to 1st Panzer Army as it struck towards the Don River. From June to July, the German 17th Army, the Italian Expeditionary Corps in Russia, and the Romanian 3rd Army were organized as 'Army Group Ruoff' (Heeresgruppen Ruoff).In August 1942, what he considered slow progress, caused German dictator Adolf Hitler to re-organize his forces. Hitler sub-divided Army Group South into two new army groups: Army Group A (Heeresgruppe A) and Army Group B (Heeresgruppe B). Army Group A included the 17th Army, the 1st Panzer Army, and the 4th Panzer Army. Army Group B included the 2nd Army, the Sixth Army, theItalian 8th Army, and the Hungarian 2nd Army. By October 1942, the Romanian 3rd Army and the Romanian 4th Army were added to further bolster Army Group B.While Army Group B struck towards Stalingrad, Army Group A and the 17th Army attacked towards the Caucasus oilfields in what was to be known as the Battle of the Caucasus. However, by December with Soviet forces en-circled the 6th Army at Stalingrad, Army Group B withdrew from Southern Russia but 17th Army was ordered to hold the Kuban bridgehead. Hitler demanded a three-mile road and rail bridge across the Strait of Kerch in spring 1943 to support a push through the Caucasus to Persia, although the Cable Railway (Aerial tramway) which went into operation on July 14 with a daily capacity of one thousand tons was adequate for the defensive needs of the 17th Army in the Kuban bridgehead. Because of frequent earth tremors, vast quantities of extra-strength girders would be required, and their transport would curtail shipments of military material to the Crimea.By October 1943, the 17th Army was forced to retreat from the Kuban Bridgehead across the Kerch Strait to Crimea. During the following months, the Red Army pushed back the German Army (Heer) in the southern Ukraine. In November 1943, they eventually cut off the land-based connection of 17th Army through the Perekop Isthmus.Hitler forbade a sea evacuation of 17th Army because he thought the Soviets could use the Crimea to launch air attacks against Romanian oil refineries. However, by the end of 1943, the Soviet began landing troops in Kerch Strait and, by 10 April 1944, moving troops near the Sivash and together with an attack at the Perekop Isthmus forced 17th Army to fall back to Sevastopol. The German Supreme Command of the Armed Forces (Oberkommando der Wehrmacht, or (OKW)) intended to hold Sevastopol as a fortress, much as the Red Army had done during the first battle for the Crimea from 1941 to 1942. Inadequate repair to the defenses of Sevastopol made this impossible and, on 9 May 1944, Sevastopol fell in less than one month after the start of the battle.The Army lost much of its heavy equipment in the Crimea. Considerable losses were suffered in terms of men lost in battle and losses associated with the sea evacuation.he Army was subsequently reorganized and continued to fight on the Eastern Front, including in the Battle of Bautzen.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Army_(Wehrmacht)

Formed 9/8/43 from 20th Mountain Cavalry Division, it was part of II Guards Cavalry Corps. It fought in the Lublin-Brest Offensive in June 1944.The Organization and Order of Battle of Militaries in World War II: volume V - Book B Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Trafford, 2009 Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert,The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 17th Guards was one of four Guards rifle divisions created in Kalinin Front on the same date, March 17, 1942, (along with 20th, 21st and 22nd Guards) in recognition of their role in driving in the left flank of Army Group Center during the winter of 1941-42. When formed, its order of battle was as follows: 45th Guards Rifle Regiment from 365th Rifle Regiment 48th Guards Rifle Regiment from 421st Rifle Regiment 52nd Guards Rifle Regiment from 634th Rifle Regiment 26th Guards Artillery Regiment from 349th Artillery Regiment 22nd Guards Antitank Battalion from 230th Antitank Battalion 16th Guards Sapper Battalion from 224th Sapper Battalion The division was part of 22nd Army when it was formed, and remained in Kalinin Front, in either that army or the 41st Army for the next year. In early 1943 it was transferred to 5th Guards Rifle Corps in 39th Army, and remained under those commands for the duration. In late 1943 the division, along with the rest of 39th Army, was transferred to Western Front, and took part in the campaign to liberate Smolensk. The division was the first Soviet unit to enter the city of Dukhovshchina after it was abandoned by German XXVII Army Corps on the night of September 16/17 and received its name as an honorific. During Operation Bagration the 17th Guards, now under 3rd Belorussian Front, advanced into the southern Baltic States. At the time of the German surrender the division was in East Prussia, near Königsberg. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Guards_Rifle_Division

The 17th Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 17th Light Division. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 17th Light Division was merged with other units and disbanded.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 17th Infantry Division was in the forefront of Army Group Center’s last thrusts toward Moscow in the winter of 1941–42. (Earlier it had fought at Brest-Litovsk, Bialstok and Gomel, among other places.) The 17th was exhausted after the Soviet winter offensive and was sent to France to rest and rebuild in the summer of 1942. It returned to Russia in February 1943, after the fall of Stalingrad brought the German southern sector to the verge of collapse. In the spring of 1943 it took part in the battles around Juchnov and Gshatsk. After the German defeat at Battle of Kursk in July, the 17th Infantry fought on the Mius, the lower Dnieper, at the Nikopol Bridgehead and in the southern Ukraine, where it again suffered heavy casualties. It was reorganized as a Type 44 division (with six grenadier battalions) in October 1943. It was defending in southern Poland in late 1944 and was smashed on the Vistula in January 1945. In March, it was defending the Hirschberg-Bad Warmbrunn zone of Silesia and consisted of the 95th Grenadier Regiment (two battalions), the 1246th Grenadier Regiment, the 17th Division Fusilier Regiment and assorted divisional troops. (The 1246th Grenadier Regiment consisted of the Staff and students of the Army NCO School at Bruenn [Brno], which the division had absorbed.) The division absorbed elements of the defunct 88th and 291st Infantry Divisions that same month. Remnants of this veteran division were surrounded in Czechoslovakia in late April 1945 and surrendered there.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 17th Mechanized Corps was formed in March 1941 at Baranovichi under the command of Mikhail Petrovich Petrov. It was part of the Western Special Military District's reserve at Slonim. The corps included the 27th and 36th Tank Divisions, and the 209th Motorized Division. The 17th Mechanized Corps was a cadre-strength formation equipped with only 36 tanks, which included 24 BT tanks, a T-26 tank, and eleven T-37, T-38, and T-40 amphibious tanks.<cr>Following the German invasion of the Soviet Union, the 17th Mechanized corps fought in the Battle of Bia?ystok-Minsk. The corps was initially stationed in the rear but was moved forward to Baranovichi to stop the German advance. On 26 June it fought in defensive battles around Baranovichi, Stowbtsy, and Minsk. Its positions were broken through by the German XLVII Army Corps (Motorized). The outnumbered 17th Mechanized Corps was unable to offer much resistance to the attack and its remnants retreated eastwards to the Berezina, where they linked up with other Soviet units. By 3 July it was still mostly fighting on the western bank of the Dnieper. It suffered heavy losses in the fighting and on 5 July was allocated to the 21st Army after being ordered to Babruysk on the previous day.<cr>On 7 July the corps' strength returns (lists of equipment) showed no armored vehicles. On 14 July the 16th Army was ordered to attack south towards Gorki alongside the 17th Mechanized Corps to destroy the German advance troops. The corps increased its resistance as it retreated, fighting against the German 10th Panzer Division as it advanced towards Pochinok on 16 July. On 18 July, the 16th Army was again ordered to attack south towards Gorki with the corps. On 21 July the corps ordered to withdraw to the Sukhinichi area with 4th Army. On 24 July it was regrouping from Yartsevo to support the 16th Army with a strength of 1,600, according to Western Front commander Semyon Timoshenko's situation report on that day. The corps became the 147th Tank Brigade on 1 August. Its 27th and 36th Tank Divisions were disbanded on the same date.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Mechanized_Corps_(Soviet_Union)</url>

In June 1941, the 17th Panzer Division struck into Russia with Army Group Centre, fighting at Brest-Litovsk, the Minsk encirlement, in the Dniepr crossings, at Smolensk, and in the Battle of Moscow. It destroyed 100 Russian tanks in a single day-July 9, 1941-at Orsha, during the Dnieper crossing operations. That winter it was pushed back to Orel and remained there until December 1942, when it was transferred to the southern sector of the front. Although it was poor shape (it only had thirty tanks left and all of its armored cars had been destroyed), it took part in the attempt to relieve Stalingrad, but was itself encircled and had to fight its way out. It nevertheless acquitted itself very well, destroying twenty-one Soviet tanks in a single day in temperatures of minus 22 degrees Fahrenheit. By Christmas Eve 1942, the 17th was down to a strength of eight tanks and one anti-tank gun, and one of its regiments was commanded by the lieutenant.It was taken out of the line shortly thereafter and was partially rebuilt. It received fifty new tanks and the 297th Army Motorized Anti-Aircraft Battalion, which later became the 27th (Flak) Tank Destroyer Battalion, which was added to its table of organization on January 12, 1943. Sent back to the front almost immediately, it took part in Manstein's Kharkov counteroffensive in March, it fought at Kursk (July), and in the subsequent retreats from the Donets, the Dniepr bend, and the northern Ukraine. In March 1944, it was encircled with the 1st Panzer Army, but again broke out. It took part in the retreat across eastern Poland and, in September 1944, was still resisting west of the Vistula. In late 1944, the 17th Panzer Division was reorganized again-this time as a regimental-sized Kampfgruppe. The Staff, 39th Panzer Regiment, was used to form the 108th Panzer Brigade, and the division was left with a single tank battalion. The seriously depleted and understrength 63rd Panzer Grenadier Regiment was dissolved and used to form the III/40th Panzer Grenadier Regiment-a bicycle unit. All of the division support units were reduced to companies, and the 27th Panzer Artillery Regiment became the 27th Panzer Artillery Battalion. The 17th Panzer Division nevertheless opposed the Russian drive west of the Vistula River in the winter of 1944-45, fought in the disastrous Battle of the Baranov Bridgehead and at Goerlitz, and ended the war in the Deutsch-Brod pocket east of Prague. It surrendered to the Russians near Olmuetz on May 11, 1945.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

Hero of the Soviet Union and future marshal Ivan Stepanovich Konev commanded this corps in 1932-33. The corps was at Chernovtsy in June 1941 as part of 12th Army and consisted of 60th and 96th Mountain Rifle and 164th Rifle Divisions. It was part of the Uman Pocket in August and was destroyed. It was reformed in North Caucasus Front in May 1943 and fought in the Proskurov-Chernovtsy Operation as part of 1st Guards Army. Wikipedia says 17th Rifle Corps was part of 25th Army in the Khabarovsk region of the Far East Military District from 1943-1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Rifle_Corps Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 17th Rifle division was formed in October 1918 from the 1st Vitebsk Rifle Division and 2nd Smolensk Rifle Division by order of the Military council of the Smolensk Defensive Region. The division participated in the Russian Civil War in Lithuania, Ukraine and Belorussia. After that the division participated in the Polish–Soviet War. The division was disbanded in 1930 and its elements used to form the 17th, 136th and 137th Rifle Divisions. It was reformed in 1939 from the 49th Rifle Regiment. By December 1940 the division was brought to full strength and participated in the Winter War.At the start of Operation Barbarossa the division was part of the 10th Army in the area of Vitebsk and Polotsk. It consisted of the 55th, 271st and 278th Rifle Regiments, 20th Artillery Regiment, 390th Howitzer Regiment and various support units. By the end of June 1941 the division was surrounded in the area east of Minsk. Though the division was destroyed in late June 1941 it was not officially disbanded until September 1941.In October 1941 the division was reformed from the 17th Moscow People's Militia Rifle Division. It participated in the Moscow. In July 1943 it was part of the Orel Counter-offensive and in June 1944 Operation Bagration. From February to April 1945 the division participated in the East Prussian Offensive ending the war there as part of the occupation forces.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Rifle_DivisionEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 17th Tank Corps was officially formed on 19 June 1942 in the Moscow Military District with:
66th Tank Brigade
215th, 216th Tank Battalions - total 23 KVs, 27 T-60s
66th Motorized Rifle Battalion
67th Tank Brigade
217th, 218th Tank Battalions - total 45 T-34s, 20 T-60s
67th Motorized Rifle Battalion
174th Tank Brigade
380th, 381st Tank Battalions - total 45 T-34s, 20 T-60s
174th Motorized Rifle Battalion
3lst Motorized Rifle Brigade
39th Mine-Engineer Company
85th (Tank) Repair Base
92nd (Motorized Vehicle) Repair Base<cr>Just a week after it officially formed up, 17th Tank Corps was moved to Voronezh and assigned to Bryansk Front reserves. It was committed in attacks with 40th and 60th Armies against German forces around Voronezh July to September 1942. As usual for Soviet tank corps in the summer of 1942, these attacks resulted in severe tank losses to little effect. On 6 October the corps went back to Volga Military District for complete refitting. It remained there until December, and during this time all the tank brigades were re-equipped to the July 1942 standard with 32 T-34 and 21 T-70 tanks each. On 15 December 17th Tank Corps went into the attack with 1st Guards Army in the 'Malyy Saturn' ('Little Saturn') Offensive. At that time the corps had 98 T-34s and 70 T-70s. As a result of this offensive the Italian 8th Army was annihilated and the Germans pushed away from Stalingrad so that Don Front could finish the destruction of the isolated German 6th Army. In recognition of its contributions
to the Soviet successes, on 3 January 1943 17th Tank Corps became 4th Guards Tank Corps.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 17th Tank Division was formed in July 1940 at Crossing 77 with the 5th Mechanized Corps from the 37th Light Tank Brigade. It also included the 199th Flamethrower and 526th Transport Battalions. The 17th Tank Division's structure in 1941 included the 33rd and 34th Tank Regiments, the 17th Motor Rifle Regiment, the 17th Howitzer Artillery Regiment, the 17th Reconnaissance Battalion, the 17th Transport Battalion and the 17th Maintenance Battalion. The division was commanded by Major General Ilya Alekseyenko. On 1 March 1941 Colonel Ivan Korchagin took command. Beginning on 12 June 1941 the division was relocated to Izyaslav. After the German invasion of the Soviet Union, the division moved with the corps to Smolensk. The division was 60% Ukrainian in early July, and German troops attributed its reportedly poor performance to its ethnic composition. On 6 July, the division had 413 tanks, including 237 BT tanks and 130 T-26 tanks. The remainder were flamethrower or amphibious tanks. The division fought in the 5th Mechanized Corps' counterattack towards Senno and Lepel. The division was placed in the corps' first echelon during the counterattack. When it reached the region south of Senno, the division, reinforced by 6 KV-1 and 10 T-34 tanks, ran into the 17th Panzer Division. The counterattack failed with heavy losses. The division was encircled in the Smolensk Pocket, in which it defended the Dnieper line to the west of the city. The division fought against the 17th and 18th Panzer Divisions, which were attempting to establish positions on the southern bank of the river. On 25 July, the division had three KV tanks, four T-34s, 73 BT tanks, 28 T-26s, 16 KhT-26 flamethrower tanks, for a total of 124 tanks. On the night of 31 July to 1 August, the division and the rest of the corps escaped the Smolensk Pocket through the gap in the German encirclement line. On 28 August, it was converted into the 126th Tank Brigade. The brigade was destroyed in the Vyazma Pocket in October. It was not officially disbanded until 22 August 1942. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Tank_Division_(Soviet_Union) Entry courtesy of NotOneStepBack

The 180th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in September 1940 from elements of 2 Estonian Peoples Army Divisions and was assigned to the 22nd Rifle Corps, 27th Army, Northwestern Front. At the start of the war the Division was at about 50% strength, and some of the equipment was non standard eg of British or Swedish manufacture, with ammunition limited. By July 1941 the Division was assigned to the 11th Army where it fought at Staraya Russa and Demyansk. In May 1942 the Division was renamed as the 28th Guards Rifle Division. The Division was formed for a second time at Cherepovets in June 1942 from the 41st Rifle Brigade. It fought at Kiev, Târgu Frumos, and Budapest. The division was part of the 53rd Army of the 2nd Ukrainian Front in May 1945. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, the Order of Suvorov 2nd class and the Order of Kutuzov 2nd class. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/180th_Rifle_Division Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of J Tomlinson

The 181st Soviet Rifle Division was formed in September 1940 from elements of 2 Latvian Peoples Army Divisions and was assigned to the 24th Rifle Corps, 27th Army, Northwestern Front. At the start of the war the Division was at about 50% strength, and much of the equipment was non standard. Reinforcements were naturally hard to mobilise. The Division suffered heavy losses and by the end of September had been officially disbanded. The Division was reformed at Stalingrad in 1942 and by August had been wiped out at Kalach. The Division was reformed for the 3rd time at Chelyabinsk in February 1942, with the renaming of the depleted 10th NKVD Rifle Division to 181st 'Stalingrad' of the Order of Lenin Rifle Division. The Division fought at Demyansk, and at Korosten, and ended the war assigned to the 6th Army, 1st Ukrainian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/181st_Rifle_Division Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

Editor Name: 182nd Infantry Division;182nd Reserve Division;282nd Infantry Division
text: The 182nd Infantry Division has a complicated lineage. The division was originally formed in late 1939 as the 182nd Replacement and Training Division which was part of the Replacement Army. In December 1939 the division was in Lodz Poland but by July 1941 the division was in Nancy France. In July 1942 the division was designated the 182nd Infantry Division. Around this time some of the division was removed and used to form the 182nd Reserve Division and the remaining units of the 182nd Infantry Division were designated the Gumbel Division. In August 1942 the Gumbel Division was renamed again and designated the Karl Division. In September 1942 the 182nd Reserve Division was designated the Nanzig Division. In March 1943 the Karl division became the 282nd Infantry Division. In October 1942 the Nanzig Division was designated the 462nd Infantry Division but in November 1942 part of this division was removed and a new 182nd Reserve Division was formed. In November 1944 the division was reformed in Slovakia and designated the 182nd Training Division.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIhttp://www.axishistory.com/axis-nations/145-germany-heer/heer-unsorted/4338-the-german-replacement-army-1939-to-1945Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 182nd Soviet Rifle Division was formed in September 1940 from elements of 2 Estonian Peoples Army Divisions and was assigned to the 22nd Rifle Corps, 27th Army, Northwestern Front. At the start of the war the Division was at about 50% strength, and much of the equipment was non standard. By July 1941 the Division was assigned to the 11th Army where it remained for the rest of the year. The Division showed some natural reluctance to fight for the Soviet cause but under the circumstances performed reasonably well in 1941. The Division ended the war assigned to the 43rd Army, 2nd Belorussian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#181%E2%80%93190 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of J Tomlinson

The 183rd Infantry Division was not involved in heavy fighting on the Eastern Front until October 1941, when it took part in the Battle of Vyazma. The 183rd was also engaged in fierce combat in the latter stages of the advance on Moscow. It remained on the central sector until after the Rzhev withdrawal, fighting in the defensive battles of 1942 and the first eight months of 1943. It suffered so many casualties that its 343rd Grenadier Regiment had to be disbanded.Transferred to the southern zone of operations in September 1943, the division suffered heavy losses in the Kiev fighting that autumn and on November 2, 1943, its Staff was redesignated Corps Detachment C (Korps-Abteilung C). It controlled the former 183rd, 217th, and 339th Infantry Divisions (now Division Groups 183, 217, and 339), as well as the 219th Artillery Regiment, 219th Tank Destroyer Battalion, 219th Engineer Battalion, 219th Signal Battalion, and 219th Field Replacement Battalion. The new command fought at Zhitomir, Tarnopol, and the Brody Pocket in Belorussia (July 1944). Here it broke out of the pocket and most of its survivors escaped. Withdrawn from the combat zone after Brody, the 183rd was rebuilt at the Döllersheim Maneuver Area (Wehrkreis XVII, formerly Austria) as a Volksgrenadier unit. Most of its personnel were inexperienced, poorly trained Austrians from the 564th Grenadier Division. It absorbed Shadow Division Doellersheim on August 3 and was officially activated on September 15, 1944. The fighting caliber of the 183rd declined considerably after that, although it continued to achieve creditable results. (Its subordinate units retained their old numbers, although the grenadier regiments were reduced from three to two battalions.)German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 183rd Soviet Rifle Division was formed in September 1940 from elements of 2 Latvian Peoples Army Divisions and was assigned to the 24th Rifle Corps, 27th Army, Northwestern Front. At the start of the war the Division was at about 50% strength, and much of the equipment was non standard. Reinforcements were hard to mobilise. The Division suffered heavy losses and by mid August 1941 had practically ceased to exist. The division was withdrawn to be re-built and by the end of 1941 was assigned to the 29th Army, Kalinin Front. The Division fought at Rzhev, Kursk and Lvov and by 1944 it was assigned to the 101st Rifle Corps, 38th Army, 4th Ukrainian Front. It ended the war in the Carpathians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#181%E2%80%93190 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/38th_Army_(Soviet_Union) Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 184th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in September 1940 from the 2nd Lithuanian Infantry Division and was assigned to the 29th Rifle Corps, 11th Army, Northwestern Front. Most of the soldiers were not sympathetic to the Soviet cause and the Division was classed as very unreliable. The Division was disbanded by mid August 1941 without having seen any significant combat. The Division was reformed in the Crimea in October 1941, based on the 4th Crimea Militia Division, assigned to the 51st Army, and was destroyed there in November, 1941. The Division was reformed for the third time and by 1944 it was assigned to the 45th Rifle Corps, 5th Army. Units of 184th Rifle Division were the first Soviet soldiers to reach the prewar frontier on 17 August 1944. The Division ended the war fighting in Manchuria. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Machine_Gun_Artillery_Division https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51st_Army_(Russia) Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 185th Mechanized Division was formed March 1941 from 185th Rifle Division in Moscow Military District as part of 21st Mechanized Corps with: 257th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 280th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 145th Tank Regiment - 0 tanks 695th Motorized Howitzer Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns Reconnaissance Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Antitank Battalion Sapper Battalion The entire 21st Mechanized Corps never received any tanks before the war started, and trucks were so short most of the infantrymen were on foot. The division had 90% of its assigned personnel, but up to 3/4 of them had just arrived between April and June 1941 - there was no time for any unit, or even individual training before the division went into battle. Tankless and practically truckless, 185th 'Mechanized' Division went into action at Daugavpils against 4th Panzer Group on 26 June. Six weeks later it officially converted into 185th Rifle Division by adding 1319th (reserve) Rifle Regiment to the remnants of the original 'mechanized' division.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 185th Soviet Rifle Division was formed at Belgorod in November 1939 and in March 1941 was redesignated the 185th Mechanised Division, assigned to the 21st Mechanized Corps. The 185th Mechanised Division was rushed into action, suffered very heavy casualties, was withdrawn to be rebuilt in August 1941, and redesignated back to the 185th Rifle Division. The 185th Soviet Rifle Division was rebuilt by September, 1941, assigned to the 30th Army, Kalinin Front and fought in the defense of Moscow. In January 1945 the Division was assigned to the 77th Rifle Corps, 47th Army, 1st Belorussian Front and finished the war close to Berlin. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#181%E2%80%93190 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 186th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in 1939 and was assigned to the 62nd Rifle Corps, 22nd Army, Stavka Reserve (RVGK). At the start of the war it was in transit from the Ural Military District. The Division was close to 100% strength and in early July took up defensive positions on the east bank of the Dvina River. This sector was soon in total disarray, the Division was lucky to escape encirclement, and by the end of August had an establishment of about 2,000 men. In September 1941 the Division was rebuilt with reservists and survived the year defending Moscow as part of the Kalinin Front. The Division finished the war assigned to the 46th Rifle Corps, 65th Army, on the Oder River in Germany. Note : A second 186th Rifle Division was formed in September 1941 and renamed the 205th Rifle Division in June 1943. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 187th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in 1939 and was assigned to the 45th Rifle Corps, Stavka Reserve (RVGK), located in the Kharkov Military District. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at about 50% strength. The Division quickly received mobilised reserves and was assigned to the 21st Army. In mid July 1941 it was committed into the counter attack against Army Groups Center, suffered heavy casualties, and the remnants were wiped out in the Kiev pocket in September 1941. The Division was reformed in October 1941, assigned to the 1st Red Banner Army in the Far East, where it remained for the remainder of the war. For a time it was known as the Grodelkovskaya Rifle Division. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#181%E2%80%93190 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 188th Soviet Rifle Division was formed at Kaunas in March 1941 and was assigned to the 16th Rifle Corps, 11th Army, Northwestern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at about 70% strength. Despite receiving reinforcements the Division suffered heavy casualties and by mid July, 1941 was down to about 2,000 men. By the end of the year it was assigned to the 34th Army of the Northwestern Front. The Division fought in central Russia and in the liberation of Ukraine and Moldova. It was with the 82nd Rifle Corps of the 37th Army in Bulgaria in May 1945. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner and the Order of the October Revolution. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/46th_Rocket_Division Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 189th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in April 1941 and was assigned to the Reserves of the Southwestern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at about 50% strength. The Division was wiped out in the Uman pocket in August 1941. The Division was reformed in September 1941, from the 6th Leningrad Militia Division, and assigned to the 42nd Army, Leningrad Front, until at least July 1942. The Division fought at Tartu and in Courland and ended the war with the 67th Army of the Leningrad Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#181%E2%80%93190 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

Formed in November 1939 in Military Region (Wehrkreis) VI, the 18th Army was part of the offensive into the Netherlands (Battle of the Netherlands) and Belgium (Battle of Belgium) during Fall Gelb and later moved into France in 1940. The 18th Army was then moved East and participated in Operation Barbarossa in 1941.The Army was a part of the Army Group North until early 1945, when it was subordinated to Army Group Kurland. In October 1944, the army was encircled by the Red Army offensives and spent the remainder of the war in the Courland Pocket.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Army_(Wehrmacht)

The 18th Army was formed on 21 June 1941 on the basis of HQ Kharkov Military District and armies of the Kiev Special Military District.The Army's commander in 1941 was General-Lieutenant Ilya Smirnov. The Army composition on the beginning of the war was the 16th Mechanized Corps (15th Tank Division, 39th Tank Division, 240th Mechanized Tank Division, 64th Fighter Air Division, 45th Mixed Air Division), 17th Rifle Corps (96th Mountain Rifle Division, 60th Mountain Rifle Division, 164th Rifle Division), 18th Mechanised Corps (47th Tank Division, 218th Mechanized Division), 55th Rifle Corps (130th Rifle Division, 160th Rifle Division, 189th Rifle Division, 4th Independant Brigade).It was caught soon after the start of Operation Barbarossa in 1941 in a huge encirclement south of Kiev along with the Soviet 6th Army and 12th Army. This encirclement was part of the Battle of Uman. A further formation was shattered during the Battle of the Sea of Azov in September-October 1941.On 1 October 1943 the army consisted of 20th Rifle Corps (8th Guards Rifle Brigade, 81st and 83rd Naval Rifle Brigades), 55th Guards Rifle Division, 89th Rifle Division, 176th, 318th, 414th Rifle Divisions, 107th Rifle Brigade, 255th Naval Infantry Brigade, 10th Guards Separate Antitank Battalion, artillery, armoured forces, and engineers.

The 18th Guards Motor Rifle Division was formed originally as 133rd Rifle Division at Novosibirsk or Biysk in 1939. The division was part of 1st Shock Army on 1 December 1941 during the Battle of Moscow. It was redesignated as the 18th Guards Rifle Division in March 1942 with the 51, 53, 58 Guards Rifle Regiments and 52 Guards Artillery Regiment. The division fought in the East Prussian Offensive. The unit became 30th Guards Mechanised Division in 1945 as part of the 11th Guards Army.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Guards_Motor_Rifle_Division

Editor Name: 18th Hun. Infantry Brigade;18th Hun. Reserve Division
text: The 18th Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 18th Light Division. In March of 1943 the division was sent from Hungary to join the Hungarian Occupation Group assigned to security duties in occupied Russia. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 18th Light Division was merged with other units and renamed the 18th Reserve Division. In January of 1944 the Hungarian First Army to which the division was subordinate, mobilized to defend Hungary's northern Carpathian frontier against the advancing Red Army. The division was disbanded in August 1944.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

As part of Hoth's 3rd Panzer Group, the 18th Motorized Division fought in the Bialystok and Minsk encirclements, in the drive on Leningrad, and at Volchov, among others. It was badly mauled in the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42, losing 9,000 men and dropping to a strength of 741 combat effectives by December 22. Soon after it was put into reserve behind the northern sector of the front.In March 1942, however, it was back in the line and took part in the rescue of II Corps at Demyansk. Remaining on the northern sector in the defensive battles of 1942 and 1943, where it held a sector of the front near Tichvin, the 18th Panzer Grenadier also fought around Demyansk and Lake Ilmen and at Staraya Russa. On June 23, 1943, it added the 118th Panzer Battalion (which was equipped with assault guns), and it was redesignated 18th Panzer Grenadier Division. That autumn, it was sent to Army Group Centre, where it fought in the unsuccessful defense of Smolensk that fall. In the spring of 1944 it was officially cited for distinguished action in the central Dnieper fighting. The 18th Panzer Grenadier was virtually destroyed in the Russian summer offensive of 1944. Encircled in the Bobruisk Pocket, divisional commander Lieutenant General Karl Zutavern committed suicide, rather than surrender to the Russians. The tiny remnants of the burned-out division that escaped the destruction of the 4th Army were sent to Silesia, where they were temporarily absorbed by the 105th Panzer Brigade. The division was rebuilt as a Kampfgruppe in November and early December 1944, and absorbed both the 105th and 103rd Panzer Brigades. It had four panzer grenadier battalions, a panzer battalion and three artillery battalions, but no tank destroyer or engineer battalions. Its tank battalion was equipped with obsolete PzKw IVs. It returned to the Eastern Front in East Prussia in December and was decimated there in the winter fighting of 1944-45. Evacuated by sea to northern Germany, it fought in the battles of Seelow Heights and Berlin, where it was finally destroyed. Most of its survivors fell into Communist hands.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 18th Panzer Division first saw action in Russia, crossing the Bug in underwater tanks originally designed for Operation Sea Lion (the invasion of Britain). It spent the rest of 1941 fighting in a number of battles, including the Minsk encirlement, Smolensk, the Dniepr crossings, Kiev, Roslavl, Bryansk, Moscow, and Orel, all on the central sector of the Russian Front. It also opposed the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42, near the Soviet capital. Casualties were heavy. During the first sixty days of the campaign, it lost almost 6,000 men-more than one-third of its pre-invasion strength. By July 9, the division had only eighty-three operational tanks-39 percent of its strength just three weeks before. By late July, only twelve of its panzers were operational, compared to 212 on June 21. The division nevertheless acquitted itself very well in the winter fighting of 1941-42.On June 15, 1942, the division was reorganized and lost several units, including the 18th Panzer Regiment, which was disbanded. The division’s only remaining tank unit was redesignated 18th Panzer Battalion. Its table of organization and equipment strength was reduced from more than 17,000 men to about 14,000. This was all academic, however; its actual strength was less than 7,000. The division, however, did receive one new unit: the 292nd Army Anti-Aircraft Battalion.In the summer of 1942, the much-reduced division was sent to the southern sector of the Eastern Front, where it took part in the initial advances on Stalingrad, but it was soon returned to Army Group Center, with which it fought in the defensive battles of 1942-43. The 18th Panzer Division was virtually destroyed in the Battle of Kursk. It went into the battle with 5,432 combat effectives but lost 4,028 men in the next ten days. The division commander disbanded his supply and rear area units and sent their men to the front. By mid-September, the division had four panzer grenadier battalions, but they only averaged 130 men each. In autumn 1943, the 18th was fighting around Kiev, and in the fall suffered such heavy losses in the counteroffensive west of Kiev (in the Bryansk, Orscha and Vitebsk sectors) that it had to be disbanded on September 29, 1943. Low morale was a factor in this decision. Its Headquarters and its artillery were used to help form the 18th Artillery Division.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 18th Rifle Division was formed in November 1918 at Arkhangelsk with troops from Archangel, Belsky and Kotlassky areas. In the spring of 1920 the division was part of the Western Front and took part in the invasion of Poland. After being defeated at the Battle of Warsaw the division retreated to East Prussia where it was briefly interned. From November 1939 to March 1940 the division was part of the Winter War with Finland. The division led the attack on Uoma-Kitilya-Impilahti-Sortavala and was subsequently encircled near Lemeti and defeated. In early 1940 due to the loss of its banner and heavy losses the division was disbanded. The remains of the division were reassigned to the 71st Rifle Division. Today the divisions banner is in a museum collection in Finland. The division was reestablished at Kazan in August 1939 from the Ulyanovsk-based 86th Rifle Division as the 111th Rifle Division. In 1940 it was renamed as the 18th Rifle Division.At the start of Operation Barbarossa the division was stationed in Kazan and consisted of the 97th, 208th and 316th Rifle Regiments, 12th Howitzer Regiment, 381st Separate Tank Battalion and various support units. The division was immediately ordered west and took up positions south of Orsha on the left bank of the Dneper River covering the area from Orsha to near Shklow. Here the division found itself surrounded. Elements of the division was able to break out of the ring on in July and August 1941. The division was officially disbanded in September 1941.The division was reformed once again in September 1941 from the 18th Division of the Moscow People's Militia. It then fought at the Battle of Moscow becoming the 11th Guards Rifle Division in January 1942.A new 18th Rifle Division was formed in February 1942 at Ryazan in the Moscow Military District from a cadre of the 16th Sapper Brigade. The division was in reserve as part of the Stalingrad Front by July 1942 and assigned to the 4th Tank Army. In August 1942 the division was involved in intense fighting in a small bend of the Don River north-west of Stalingrad where it sustained heavy casualties. Due to its significant losses the division was put in reserve in September 1942. After spending three months in the Moscow Military District rebuilding near Tambov the division was sent to the Volkhov Front and before the end of 1942 was assigned to the 2nd Shock Army. In mid-January 1943 the division broke through the German encirclement, breaking the Siege of Leningrad and joining the forces of the Leningrad Front. The 18th Rifle Division is credited with capturing the first Tiger Tank. The division would participate in the Svir-Petrozavodsk Offensive. In late September 1944 the division was assigned to the Soviet-Finish border southwest of Sortavala. The division was placed in the STAVKA reserves in mid-November 1944 and assigned to the 19th Army's 132nd Rifle Corps. Reassigned to the 2nd Belorussian Front the division participated in the East Pomeranian Offensive and fought at Danzig, Poland. The division remained in Poland as part of the Northern Group of Forces and was disbanded in June 1946.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 18th Romanian Infantry Division did not participate in the opening phase of Operation Barbarossa and remained in Romania. In January of 1942 it was assigned, less its 90th Infantry Regiment, to the German XI Corps. It was one of four Romanian infantry divisions not withdrawn to Romania after the Siege of Odessa. In January of 1943 it was serving with the German4th Panzer Army.John Ellis, World War II A Statistical SurveyCharles D. Pettibone, The Organization and Order of Battle of Militaries in World War II Volume VII - Germany's and Imperial Japan's Allies & Puppet Stateshttp://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D18I.html#asEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 18th Tank Corps was formed in June 1942 in the Moscow Military District.<cr>While it was forming, 18th Tank Corps moved to Voronezh, where it temporarily included 217th Antiaircraft Regiment, but it never went into combat with this unit. Early in July 18th Tank Corps was assigned to 5th Tank Army in Bryansk Front, and then to 60th Army in Voronezh Front. In the uncoordinated Soviet tank actions around Voronezh the corps suffered heavy losses, and in October was withdrawn into Volga Military District, where the most damaged subordinate brigades were removed and replaced by new units. In November 1942 the corps was assigned to Southwestern Front.<cr>The 18th Tank Corps was in 1st Guards Army at the start of 'Malyy Saturn' Offensive on 15 December, and then part of the Southwestern Front Mobile Group known as 'Group Popov' in February 1943, when the badly-worn corps was almost annihilated at the beginning of Manstein's panzer counter-attack. At that time, in addition to the units above, the corps also contained the 1st Armored Car Battalion.<cr>In late February 1943 the remnants of 18th Tank Corps, almost completely without equipment, went into STAVKA reserves to be completely rebuilt. The corps was assigned to Steppe District (later Steppe Front) of STAVKA Reserves from April to 5 July 1943. On 6 July the corps was assigned to 5th Guards Tank Army.<cr>The 18th Tank Corps was on the right of 5th Guards Tank Army at the great tank battle at Prokhorovka on 12 July 1943. Even with support from 10th Antitank Brigade, fighting Tigers with T-70s and T-34s was costly. On 12 and 13 July, the corps lost one-third of its tanks, and when fighting died down on 17 July it took the rest of the month to repair enough tanks to rebuild the corps. In August 18th Tank Corps took part in the battles to recover Kharkov, with the 78th Motorcycle Battalion and 106th Guards Mortar Battalion (8 BM-13 launchers) being added to the units already commanded.<cr>In November 1943 the 18th Tank Corps was supposed to be turning in all the T-70 light tanks and equipping each tank brigade with 65 T-34s, but because of the continuous combat since August, the tank brigades only averaged 40 tanks each including almost 25% T-70s. By November 1943 also, 36th Guards Heavy Tank Regiment had been removed from the corps and replaced by 1543rd Heavy SU Regiment with SU-152s. By 15 December the corps only had 37 tanks left, and even by adding 1438th SU Regiment (SU-85s) the corps could not be brought up to any decent armored strength. After attacking through the Kirovograd Operation (January 1944) , Korsun-Shevchenkosvskii (January-February) and Uman (March) the corps was practically wrecked. On 9 March 1944 there were just 9 T-34s and 8 SU guns left in 18th Tank Corps.<cr>On 27 May 1944 18th Tank Corps was removed from 5th Guards Tank Army, under which it had fought since July 1943, and became a separate unit in 2nd Ukrainian Front. By this time 1543rd Heavy SU Regiment had been removed from the corps, but in July, preparing for the Lvov-Sandomir Operation, 363rd Guards Heavy SU Regiment (ISU-122s) was added to the corps, and in August 1944 18th Tank Corps received 452nd Light Artillery Regiment with 24 76mm towed guns. For the rest of the war, 452nd and 1000th Regiments were used and designated as either Light Artillery or Antitank Regiments, since they were equipped almost alike, each with 24 76mm guns. In November 1944 18th Tank Corps became part of 3rd Ukrainian Front reserves, and fought under that Front until the end of the war. The corps ended the war in Hungary in May 1945.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 18th Tank Division was formed July 1940 in Moscow Military District as part of 7th Mechanized Corps with: 35th Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Tank Bns - all light tanks 36th Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Tank Bns - all light tanks18th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns 18th Motorized Howitzer Regiment 1 light, 1 medium bn 18th Reconnaissance Battalion 18th Motorized Pontoon Battalion 18th Antiaircraft BattalionThe 18th Tank Division was formed with all light tanks, mostly BT-5 and BT-7 types. In early July it took part in the counter-attack near Orsha, and afterwards fought in 7th Mechanized Corps until mid-July. Afterwards it was in the Battle of Smolensk as a separate division in Yartsevo Direction Group until the division was disbanded in August 1941.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 190th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in March 1941 and was assigned to the Reserves of the Southwestern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at about 50% strength. The Division was wiped out in the Uman pocket in August 1941. The Division was reformed in October 1941, assigned to the 25th Army in the Far East where it spent the remainder of the war. The Division was sometimes known as the Poltavskaya (Poltava) Rifle Division. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#181%E2%80%93190 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 191st Soviet Rifle Division was formed in April 1941 and was assigned to the Leningrad Military District. At the start of Operation Barbarossa the Division was still forming and it was at about 55% strength. The Division was assigned to the Luga Operations Group in July 1941. It suffered very heavy casualties in the defence of Leningrad and had to be withdrawn to be rebuilt. By November 1941 the Division was assigned to the 4th Army. The Division ended the war with the 49th Army, 2nd Belorussian Front in Germany in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIAEntry courtesy John Tomlinson

The Soviet 193rd Rifle Division was established in the Kharkov Military District on March 14, 1941. By June 22, 1941 it was still forming near Kamenka in the Kiev Military District  and was at close to 50% strength.  The Division fought at  Rozhits and Kivertsy and by July 8th it was down to 3,500 men. It was destroyed in the Kiev pocket. 

It's Commander, Col. A.K. Berestov,  escaped the pocket, and went on to command the 124th Rifle Division, until his death in July 1942.

The division was reformed at Sorochinsk, in the South Urals Military District, in early 1942 and was held in reserve until committed at Stalingrad in September 1942, where it suffered very heavy casualties.  In November, 1942 the Division was withdrawn from the field to be rebuilt.  

The rebuilt division was assigned to the 65th Army in February 1943; it was under the command of Lieutenant General Pavel Batov, part of Colonel General K. K. Rokossovski's Central Front. The 193rd would remain under these commanders for the duration of the war.

The Division fought at Kursk, in Operation Bagration, participated in the liberation of Danzig, and finished the war on the Oder river.

The Division was awarded the honorific of  Dnepr, Red Banner, Order of Lenin, Order of Suvorov, and Order of Kutuzov.
