The 194th Rifle Division was formed from the existing 194th Mountain Division in August 1941 and was assigned to the 49th Army, Reserve Front. In October 1941 the Division suffered very heavy casualties at Kaluga but there were enough survivors for the Division to be rebuilt. The Division fought at Yelnya, Moscow, Stalingrad, Kursk, and in Belorussia, East Prussia, and Courland. It ended the war with the 48th Army of the 3rd Belorussian Front in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 195th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in March 1941 in Ovruch and was assigned to the Southwestern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at about 50% strength. The Division was wiped out in the Kiev pocket in September 1941. The Division was recreated in the Urals from 423rd Rifle Division in March 1942, fought at Stalingrad and in the Ukraine. The Division ended the war with the 37th Army in Bulgaria in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson Virus-free. www.avg.com

The 196th Infantry Division was formed in November 1939 as part of the 7th Wave. It contained the 340th and 345th Infantry Regiments, 223rd Light Artillery Battalion and various support units. In September 1940 the division was on garrison duty in Norway. It had gained the 362nd Infantry Regiment but its 345th Infantry Regiment had been sent to the 199th Infantry Division. The artillery battalion had been upgraded to the 223rd Artillery Regiment. By late 1943 elements of the division were being sent to Army Group Centre in Russia. By July 1944 the bulk of the division was in Russia although some elements remained in Norway. In September 1944 the division was largely destroyed. Some surviving elements returned to Norway and the rest were absorbed by the 361st Infantry Division.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 196th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in March / April 1941 near Dnepropetrovsk and was part of the reserves for the Southern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at about 30% strength. In mid July it was assigned to the 7th Rifle Corps of the Southwestern Front . The Division was wiped out in the Kiev pocket in September 1941. The Division was reformed at Kisner in January 1942 and fought at Stalingrad with 62nd Army. It also fought in East Prussia and Courland and finished the war with the 67th Army of the Leningrad Front in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 197th Infantry Division, was sent to the central sector of the Russian Front in July 1941, and remained there throughout the rest of its existence. It fought at Smolensk, played a prominent role in the minor battle of encirclement at Roslavl in August, defended a sector near Vyazma in September, and took part in the battles around Moscow in December 1941 and January 1942. Engaged in skirmishing and the defensive battles of Army Group Center in 1942, the 197th also took part in the Rzhev withdrawal in early 1943. By April 30, it was down to four grenadier battalions, and the 321st Grenadier Regiment had been disbanded. The division was involved in the fighting west of Smolensk in the fall of 1943, and most of it was destroyed in the huge Soviet summer offensive of 1944. The division broke up that July near Vitebsk, along with much of the 3rd Panzer Army and the bulk of the 4th Army. The last commander of the 197th Infantry Division, Colonel Hans Hahne, is still missing and was presumably killed. The divisional staff, however, was pulled out of the battle after Hahne disappeared on June 24 and was used to form Staff, Corps Detachment H.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 197th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in April 1941 in Kiev, and was part of the reserves for the Southwestern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at about 50% strength and it was assigned to the 49th Rifle Corps. The Division was wiped out in the Uman pocket in August 1941. The Division was reformed at Krasnodar in March 1942. In August 1942 it was assigned to the 63rd Army and went on to fight at Stalingrad where it was renamed the 59th Guards Rifle Division in January 1943. The Division was formed for the third time at Kuybyshev in February 1943, fought at Bryansk and in Poland. It was with the 3rd Guards Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 198th Infantry Division was formed in November 1939 as part of the 7th Wave. It contained the 305th, 308th and 326th Infantry Regiments, 235th Light Artillery Battalion and various support units. In January 1940 the artillery battalion was upgraded to the 235th Artillery Regiment. In May 1940 one battalion from the 326th Regiment was detached for garrison duty in Copenhagen but was replaced. In April 1941 the division participated in the invasion of Greece. During Operation Barbarossa the division was attached to the 11th Army in Romania. In the summer of 1944 the division was withdrawn to France and rebuilt with the Bohemian Shadow Division. By November 1944 the division had been pushed back into Germany and absorbed numerous independent units including the 1432nd Fortress Infantry Battalion, 40th Fortress Machine Gun Battalion, 8th Ship's Company Battalion and one company from the 687th Naval Artillery Battalion. The division subsequently withdrew to the Neckar River in southern German where it was taken prisoner by the Americans. George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 198th Soviet Rifle Division was formed in October 1941 from the remnants of the 198th Mechanised Division and the newly raised 1027th and 1029th Rifle Regiments. It was assigned to the 23rd Army, Northern Front. It was with the 10th Guards Army of the Kurland Group (Leningrad Front) in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 199th Soviet Rifle Division was established in the Ukraine, in March, 1941, assigned to the Southwestern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was approximately 50% (6,700 men) in strength and by August, 1941, it was down to 1,900 men. It was one of the few rifle divisions that did not suffer the fate of encirclement in 1941. The Division fought at Lake Ilmen and Kharkov and was disbanded in September 1942. The Division was recreated at Kalinin from the 126th and 128th Rifle Brigades, in February 1943. It fought at Smolensk and in East Prussia. With the 49th Army of the 2nd Belorussian Front in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy John Tomlinson

The 19th Guards Rifle Division was formed from the first formation of the 366th Rifle Division on March 17, 1942. At this time it was in the 52nd Army of Volkhov Front, taking part in the Lyuban Offensive Operation, which was planned to encircle and defeat the enemy forces laying siege to Leningrad. However, just at that time the German 18th Army was in the process of cutting off the Soviet Lyuban grouping in a pocket, and over the following months the division was nearly destroyed. Enough survivors emerged from the swamps in June and July to rebuild the unit, and it fought in the Second Sinyavino Offensive before it was shifted south into Kalinin Front to take part in the battle and siege of Velikiye Luki in December. In the summer of 1943 the 19th Guards fought in the battles for Smolensk, and won its first battle honor, 'Rudnya'. in September. During the offensive in the summer of 1944 it was awarded the Order of the Red Banner for its successes in the fighting around Vitebsk. It was further honored in February, 1945, with the Order of Lenin for its role in the victories in East Prussia. In the summer the division was moved by rail with its 39th Army to the Far East and saw action in the Soviet invasion of Manchuria in August, winning its second battle honor, 'Khingan', for its services.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_Guards_Rifle_Division

Editor Name: 19th Hun. Infantry Brigade;19th Hun. Reserve Division
text: The 19th Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 19th Light Division. The Hungarian Government reluctantly agreed to support the Germans 1942 summer offensive Fall Blau and allocated the Hungarian Second Army to the task. Each light division in the Second Army was reinforced with three battalions from sister divisions in Hungary but nonetheless each division was only slightly larger than half the size of its German counterparts. Second Army's role in the offensive was to guard the German northern flank on the Don River. During the Stalingrad Campaign the Second Army suffered over 60% casualties but was generally able to retreat in good order. By 1943 the division was part of the Hungarian Occupation Group assigned to security duties in occupied Russia. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 19th Light Division was merged with other units and renamed the 19th Reserve Division. In January of 1944 the Hungarian First Army to which the division was subordinate, mobilized to defend Hungary's northern Carpathian frontier against the advancing Red Army. The division was disbanded in August 1944.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

Sent to Russia in 1941, the 19th Panzer Division fought in the Bialystock, Minsk and Smolensk encirclements, at Nevel, and in the Battle of Moscow. Losses were so heavy that two of its three panzer battalions had to be disbanded. It nevertheless remained on the central sector in the defensive battles of 1942 and was sent to the critical southern sector in late 1942.In January 1943, it escaped to Army Group Don after the 8th Italian Army, which it had been supporting, collapsed. The division took part in the Donets battles of early 1943, the Kharkov counteroffensive of March 1943, and the Battle of Kursk offensive of July 1943, and suffered heavy casualties in these battles and in the subsequent retreats. It was fighting near Kiev in November 1943, at Zhitomir in December, and was heavily engaged in the withdrawal through the northern Ukraine in March 1944. It formed part of General Hube's 'Floating Pocket' in March and April. Rushed north after Army Group Centre was crushed, the 19th and two other panzer divisions surprised and destroyed the III Soviet Tank Corps north of Warsaw and thus halted the Russian summer offensive of 1944. It was cited for this action. In autumn 1944, the 19th Panzer was resisting west of the Vistula. Now at battle group strength, the division retreated through southern and eastern Poland, fought in the Baranov Bridgehead battles on January 1945, and the subsequent retreat through Warthegau, Silesia and southern Germany, and ended the war in the Deutsch-Brod pocket east of Prague.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 19th Rifle Division was originally formed in 1922 as a territorial unit. In 1923 it was renamed the 19th Voronezh Rifle Division. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it consisted of the 32nd, 282nd and 315th Rifle Regiments, 90th Artillery Regiment, 103rd Howitzer Regiment and various support units. It entered combat against the Germans on July 19, 1941 near Yelnya as part of the 24th Army of the Western Front. It participated in the Elninskaya Offensive, the Battle of Moscow, Rzhev Offensive in 1942, the Rzhev-Sychevka Offensive, Third Battle of Kharkov and Belgord-Kharkov Offensive in 1943 as part of the 7th Guards Army. The division also participated in the Poltava-Kremenchuk Offensive, Pyatihatskoy Offensive, Bereznegovatoe-Snigirevskaya Offensive, Odessa, Chisinau and Izmail Offensives, Belgrade Offensive and Bratislava-Brnovskoy Offensive. In 1944 its combat path took it through Romania, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia where it ended the war. The division was awarded the Order of Suvorov 2nd degree in January 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_Motor_Rifle_DivisionEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 19th Romanian Infantry Division did not participate in the opening phase of Operation Barbarossa and remained in Romania. In August of 1942 it was in the Crimea. It subsequently served in the Kuban and Caucasus regions. By mid 1944 it was back in Romania preparing for the defense of the homeland. http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D19I.html#asEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 19th Tank Corps HQ was formed in December 1942.<cr>The 19th Tank Corps formed up and trained in Bryansk Front reserves from February to April 1943, and then was transferred to Central Front. It was one of the first reserve units moved to counter the German 9th Army's attack on the northern flank of the Kursk salient in July, by which time the improvised Armored Car Battalion had been replaced by 91st Motorcycle Battalion in the corps. 19th Tank Corps suffered heavy losses in the Battle of Kursk, and in
late July was sent back to Moscow Military District, where it spent two months reforming to the 1943 Tank Corps standard. The corps went to the South Front in September.<cr> The 19th Tank Corps fought across southern Russia with South Front (in October 1943 renamed 4th Ukrainian Front) until the spring of 1944. While the basic composition of the corps remained the same, the assigned SU regiments fluctuated depending on the mission. In October-November 1943 as the corps took part in the Melitopol Operation, 1452nd SU Regiment (SU-85s) was part of the corps. In April - May 1944 when the corps was the Mobile Group for the break in to the Crimea, the corps had two SU Regiments.<cr> After the fall of the Crimea, 19th Tank Corps went into STAVKA Reserve, and then back to Moscow Military District in June 1944. At this time the tank brigades were probably re-equipped with T-34/85 tanks all or in part, because the corps was generally built up while in reserve. It went back to the front in the Baltic in early July.<cr> Even after it was committed in the Baltic, 19th Tank Corps continued to receive reinforcements. The 19th Tank Corps remained in the Baltic theater until the end of the war in May 1945.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 19th Tank Division was formed December 1940 in Kiev Special Military District as part of 9th Mechanized Corps. On 22 June 1941 included:<cr>
37th Tank Regiment
1st, 2nd, 3rd Tank Bns - each 20 to 30 light tanks
38th Tank Regiment
1st, 2nd, 3rd Tank Bns - each 20 to 30 light tanks
19th Motorized Rifle Regiment
1st, 2nd, 3rd bns
19th Motorized Howitzer Regiment
1 light, 1 medium bn
19th Reconnaissance Battalion
19th Motorized Pontoon Battalion
19th Antiaircraft Battalion<cr><cr>This was one of the two divisions formed separately, between the two great 'waves' of Soviet armored formations of July 1940 and February-March 1941. In February 1941 19th Tank Division became part of the newly-formed 22nd Mechanized Corps and moved to near the border, at Rovno.<cr>On 22 June 1941 the division was nearly at full strength for personnel, with 9347 men present for duty. However, it was short almost 50% of the NCOs authorized, and over 33% of the offiicers and technicians. The two tank regiments had a total of 34 BT tanks, 122 T-26s, and 7 OT-26s. The howitzer regiment had all of its authorized guns, but the division had only 20% of its
trucks and a little over half the tractors required. This meant that in the initial marches, most of the division was on foot and could not keep up with the tanks, and when tanks broke down there was no way to recover them. The division went into battle on 24 June, and by 26 June 1941 had only 4 working tanks left, and had lost half the howitzers in the division.<cr>Fighting under 22nd Mechanized Corps throughout June and July to mid- August, the division was reduced to less than 1500 men and less than a halfdozen
armored cars and light tanks by 20 August. Shortly afterwards, 19th Tank Division was disbanded.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 1st Air Army was formed on May 10, 1942, within the Soviet Western Front.When it was formed, the 1st Air Army was made up of two fighter aviation divisions (with four fighter aviation regiments each), two mixed aviation divisions (with two fighter aviation regiments, two assault aviation regiments and one bombing regiment each) a training aviation regiment, a long-range reconnaissance aviation regiment, a communications squadron, and a night close-range bombing aviation regiment.In March 1943, the Air Army also included the French Normandie Niemen squadron, which was later reorganized into a regiment. In 1942, the 1st Air Army fought alongside the troops of the Western Front, supporting them near Yukhnov, Gzhatsk and Rzhev. The Air Army later participated in the Rzhev-Sychevka, Rzhev-Vyazma, Oryol, Smolensk, Belarusian, Memel and East Prussian offensive operations.Throughout the war, the 1st Air Army made 290,000 sorties. Five of the Air Army's formations where reorganized as 'Guards Units', 50 formations were given 'honourable titles', 44 formations received various awards, 145 pilots and navigators received the title 'Hero of the Soviet Union' and over 17,000 of its servicemen were also given various medals and decorations.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Air_Army

The corps was formed in April 1941 and consisted of the 1st, 204th, and 211th Airborne Brigades. In 1941, it fought as a part of Southwestern Front to defend Kiev. It was destroyed with the collapse of the Kiev pocket in August and was reformed in December 1941. It was assigned to Western Front. Between December and February 1942, it participated in airborne operations in the central region, culminating in an unsuccessful operation to seize airfields in the Demyansk Pocket that reduced the corps to about 900 effectives. In August, it was reorganized into the 37th Guards Rife Division. The corps was reformed in fall 1942, and in December it was used to form two new guards airborne divisions, the 4th Guards Airborne Division and the 9th Guards Airborne Division. Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 1st Artillery Division of the Reserve of the Supreme High Command (RGK) in October 1942 with the Southwestern Front, under the command of Colonel Vikenty Mazur. It was composed of the 274th, 275th, and 331st Howitzer, the 1162nd and 1166th Gun, and the 468th, 501st, and 1189th Anti-Tank (Tank Destroyer) Artillery Regiments. In addition to its regiments, the division included the organic 816th Separate Reconnaissance Artillery Battalion and the 45th Separate Corrective Aviation Squadron. It was sent into combat on 9 November in the area of Kletskaya and Serafimovich, supporting the 21st Army of the Southwestern Front in the final stage of the Soviet defensive phase of the Battle of Stalingrad. From the second half of November to January 1943, the units of the 1st Artillery, operationally subordinated to the 24th and 65th Armies of the Don Front, provided artillery support in the encirclement and defeat of the German troops in the Stalingrad area. After the Battle of Stalingrad, the 1st Artillery was transferred to the Central Front during February, where it was subordinated to the 65th Army and later the 70th Army. The division was reorganized on 20 February 1943, with its regiments combined into three brigades – one howitzer, one gun, and one anti-tank (tank destroyer). In recognition of its 'courage and heroism', the division was converted into the 1st Guards Artillery Division RGK on 1 March 1943.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Breakthrough_Artillery_Division

The First Baltic Front was a major formation of the Red Army during the Second World War. It was commanded by Army General Andrey Yeryomenko, succeeded by Army General Ivan Bagramyan. It was formed by renaming the Kalinin Front in October 12, 1943, and took part in several important military operations, most notably Operation Bagration in the summer of 1944. The 1st Baltic Front also assisted in lifting the Siege of Leningrad on January 27, 1944, as well as in Operation Samland, at that time known as the Samland Group, captured Königsberg in April 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Baltic_Front

Initially, the Belorussian Front was created on 20 October 1943 as the new designation of the existing Central Front. It was placed under the command of General Konstantim Rokossovsky, who had been commanding the Central Front. It launched the Gomel-Rechitsa Offensive in 1943 and then the Kalinkovichi-Mozyr Offensive in 1944.It was then renamed the 1st Belorussian Front (1BF) on 17 February 1944 following the Dniepr-Carpathian Offensive. A few days later, on 21 February, the Rogachev-Zhlobin Operation commenced, which continued until 26 February. The next operation was the Bobruysk Offensive, part of Operation Bagration, and on 26 June the attacks of 1BF encircled Bobruisk, trapping 40,000 troops of the German 41st Panzer Corps (part of 9th Army). From 18 July-2 August the Front was part of the Lublin-Brest Offensive. From 2 August to 30 September, the Front was engaged cleaning out Germans to the east of the Vistula (during which the Battle of Radzymin took place from 1-10 August). Its 8th Guards, 28th, 47th, 65th, 69th, and 70th Armies were involved at Radzymin. Later during that same period, on 14 September, 1BF with the support of Polish forces it captured Praga, a suburb of Warsaw.The next attack was the Warsaw-Poznan Operation, a part of the Vistula-Oder Offensive. On 13 January, 1BF began an offensive toward Schlossberg in East Prussia, against which they met stiff resistance from the 3rd Panzer Army.The 1st Belorussian Front opened its attack on the German Ninth Army from the Magnuszew and Pulawy bridgeheads at 08:30 on 14 January, again commencing with a heavy bombardment. The 33rd and 69th Armies broke out of the Pulawy bridgehead to a depth of 30 km, while the 5th Shock and 8th Guards Armies broke out of the Magnuszew bridgehead. The 2nd and 1st Guards Tank Armies were committed after them to exploit the breach. On 25 January, the Front cut off the fortress city of Poznan which held 66,000 Germans, and continued its 80 km a day advance, leaving the 8th Guards Army to lay siege to the city, which they finally took on 23 February. While Adolf Hitler dealt with home issues in Germany, Stalin had defeated the German Army near Warsaw.Along with the 1st Ukrainian Front, 1BF then stormed Berlin in the climatic Battle of Berlin.They finished the encirclement of Berlin on 25 April when units of the 1BF and 1UF met at Kietzen west of Berlin. After heavy street by street and house to house fighting, General Helmuth Weidling, the commander of Berlin's garrison, met with Marshal Vasily Chuikov and surrendered Berlin unconditionally at 15:00 hours local time on 2 May.Wikipedia 1st Belorussian Front

The 1st Cavalry Division fought in the battles of Minsk, Gomel, and Kiev (1941), and was used in anti-partisan operations in the Pripjet marshes. It took part in the huge battle of encirclement at Bryansk in October 1941, as part of the 2nd Panzer Army. The 1st Cavalry was sent back to East Prussia the following month and was reorganized as the 24th Panzer Division. The 1st Cavalry Division officially ceased to exist on November 28, 1941.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 1st Guards Airborne Division was formed in accordance with an order from 8 December 1942 from the 4th Airborne Corps headquarters and the 1st Airborne Brigade.<cr>                  
The division became part of the Special Group commanded by Mikhail Khozin. In mid-February 1943, it was concentrated south of Zaluceni. Its objective was to advance into a breach in the German lines in the 1st Shock Army offensive zone. In March, the division fought in the Staraya Russa operation, but was unable to capture the town. In August, it made another attempt and cut the Staraya Russa-Kholm road on 18 August. It then advanced to the Porus River at the villages of Chirikov and Kotov. The division entrenched in positions there. After the end of the fighting, it was sent to the rear to rest and refit; in September, it was transferred to the Steppe Front.<cr>
It fought in the capture of Left-bank Ukraine in the area east of Kremenchug. On 9 October, it crossed the Dnieper near Moldavan Island and the villages of Soloshino and Perevolochna. October 9, 1943, crossed the Dnieper near the island of Moldovans, Soloshino, Perevolochna, advancing in the second echelon of the 37th Army. From October to December, the division advanced towards Krivoy Rog and Kirovograd.<cr>
In January and February 1944, the division fought in the Korsun-Shevchenkovsky Offensive and took part in the encirclement of German troops around Zvenigorod. The division was awarded the honorific 'Zvenigorod' for its actions during the fighting on 13 February. Between March and April, it fought in the Uman-Botosani Offensive. During the offensive, the division reached the Dniester and Dubasari. During the summer it fought in the Jassy-Kishinev Offensive. During the offensive, it advanced in the second echelon of 53rd Army towards Focsani. On 31 August, it entered Bucharest. At the end of September, the division reached the Hungarian border northwest of Arad. On 6 October, it launched an offensive from there during the Battle of Debrecen and reached the Tisza. The division crossed the Tisza in November during the Budapest Offensive.<cr>
By February 1945, the division was positioned on the Hron. It fought in the Bratislava-Brno Offensive in April and the Prague Offensive in May.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Airborne_Division</url>

On August 6, 1942, the army formed from the 2nd Reserve Army with five Guards Rifle Divisions, the 37th, 38th, 39th, 40th and 41st. On August 9, the army was incorporated into Southeastern Front. On August 18, it was transferred to the Stalingrad Front (renamed Don Front on September 30).On October 16, 1942, the headquarters of the army transferred into Stavka reserve and its troops transferred to the 24th Army. On 25 October 1942 the army was disbanded, its headquarters was converted to the field management of the 2nd formation of Southwestern Front according to the Stavka directive of 22 October 1942.On November 5, 1942, 1st Guards Army was reformed from 63rd Army according to the Stavka directive of November 1. The army was a part of Southwestern Front. When the German troops were making their attack on Stalingrad, the First Guards Army was facing the Italian Eighth Army in the upper part of the Don River. The Army participated in Stalingrad strategic offensive Operation Uranus. As the right flank of the front shock group, 1st Guards Army with 5th Tank Army created the appearance of the Stalingrad encirclement 'boiler'.On December 5, 1942, 1st Guards Army is split, its left wing being renamed 3rd Guards Army of the Southwestern Front.The 1st Guards Army was created on December 8, 1942, according to the Stavka directive of December 5, 1942. The troops of the army was formed from the part of the operational group of Southwestern Front, and the headquarters of the army formed of management of 4th Army Reserve. It is composed of units of the right wing of the previous version of the 1st guard army and some reinforcement units : the 4th Guards Rifle Corps, the 6th Guards Rifle Corps, the 153rd Rifle Division, and the 18th Tank Corps. After the German relief operation was held, the 1st Guards Army, along with the 6th Army and 3rd Guards Army, launched an attack in Operation Little Saturn. During the operation the Soviets defeated the Italian Eighth Army and gained a respectable amount of territory. By the end of the year, the 1st Guards Army was outside Millerovo.The 1st Guards Army also took part in Operation Saturn, where the Red Army successfully drove back Army Group South to the Donets Basin in the Ukraine. The 1st Guards Army was part of the Soviet Southwestern Front, and took part in the victorious Soviet pushing into Germany in 1943 to 1945. Also, in 1943, the 1st Guards Army was the first unit of the soviet army to operate the new T-34/85 tank. Among its units when the war ended in 1945 was the 81st Rifle Division. In August, the 1st Guards Army became the headquarters of the Kiev Military District.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Army_(Soviet_Union)

Text Display Name: 1st Guards Artillery/1st Guards Breakthrough Artillery Division
text: In recognition of its 'courage and heroism, the 1st Artillery Division was converted into the 1st Guards Artillery Division RGK on 1 March 1943. The 1st Guards Artillery Division included the 1st Guards Gun, 2nd Guards Howitzer, and 1st Guards Light Artillery Brigades, which in turn included the 201st and 205th Guards Gun, 169th and 203rd Guards Howitzer, and 167th, 200th, and 206th Guards Light Artillery Regiments. During the defensive phase of the Battle of Kursk, the division supported the 13th and 70th Armies with massed artillery fire, helping to repulse German tank and infantry attacks. It received the Glukhov honorific on 31 August. In October the division was assigned to the 1st Ukrainian Front. In July of 1944 the division was assigned to the 7th Artillery Corps. From 16 April to 20 May 1944 3rd Guards Light Artillery Brigade commander Colonel Viktor Zhagala temporarily commanded the division after Arkady Volchek was wounded. 76th Rifle Corps Artillery commander Colonel Viktor Khusid (promoted to major general on 18 November 1944) was appointed to lead the division on 21 May, while it was part of the 1st Ukrainian Front. The division then fought in the Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive. The division was redesignated as the 1st Guards Breakthrough Artillery Division in November 1944, reflecting its role of providing artillery concentrations for offensives. In 1945 the division fought in the Sandomierz-Silesian Offensive, the Lower Silesian Offensive, the Berlin Offensive, and the Prague Offensive, and in fighting for the cities of Szydlöw, Kielce, Steinau, Lüben, Sprottau, Cottbus, and Dresden.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Breakthrough_Artillery_Division

Formed 11/26/1941 from 5th Cavalry Division as part of I Guards Cavalry Corps, it was part of Southwestern Front reserve. It was awarded the honorific titles 'Stavropol' and 'Zhitomir' in December 1943. Fought in the Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive and the Dniepr-Carpathian Offensive in 1944 and in the Battle of Berlin in 1945 as part of 1st Ukrainian Front. Pettibone, Charles D., The Organization and Order of Battle of Militaries in World War II: volume V - Book B Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Trafford, 2009Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 1st Guards Mechanized Corps was formed in November 1942 in the Tambov region during the re-establishment of the Mechanized Corps as a formation in the Red Army. It was then assigned to the Southwestern Front which was under the command of General Nilolai F. Vatutin to participate in the encirclement of German Army Group A in Operation Saturn, which was undertaken during the Battle of Stalingrad.The corps consisted of the following units:Combat Units 1st Guards Mechanized Rifle Brigade 2nd Guards Mechanized Rifle Brigade 3rd Guards Mechanized Rifle Brigade 16, 17, 18, 19 Guards Tank Regiments (combined into the 9th Guards Tank Brigade by 1945) 116th Guards Artillery Regiment 1504th Guards Anti-Tank Regiment 267th Mortar Regiment 407th Guards Mortar BattalionSupport Units 54th Guards Signalling Battalion Corps TrainChanges to unit organization The 116th Guards Artillery Regiment had been replaced by the 382nd Guards, 1453rd, and 1821st self-propelled gun regiments by 1945. The 1504th Guards Anti-Tank Regiment was no longer with the corps in 1945. The 11th Guards Motorcycle Battalion and 1699th Anti-Aircraft Regiment had been added to the corps by 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Mechanized_Corps_(Soviet_Union)

The 1st Guards Special Rifle Corps was created on 4 October 1941 by special request of the STAVKA supreme command, in an area of the city of Mtsensk (the Oryol Oblast). Initially its structure included the 6th Guards Rifle Division, 5th Airborne Corps, 4th Tank Brigade, 11th Tank Brigade, the Tula military school, several Border Guard Regiments, two artillery regiments, two rocket artillery battalions and the 6th reserve aviation group. Major General Dmitri Lelyushenko was appointed the commander of the corps. The corps was given several tasks: to destroy the nearby enemy, to break through into Oryol, to slow the progress of the German tank armies, and to block the way to Tula.<cr>The Soviet government and STAVKA command highly valued the efforts and sacrifices of the 1st Guards Rifle Corps in the Oryol-Bryansk defensive operation, which took place from 4 to 18 October 1941. On 11 November the National Commissioner of Defense renamed the 4th Tank Brigade, which played a vital role in the battle of Mtsensk, the 1st Guards tank brigade. The Commander of the brigade, Colonel Mikhail Katukov, was eventually promoted to commander of the Soviet 1st Guards Tank Army, and was twice awarded the Hero of the Soviet Union award.<cr><cr>On 12 October 1941, by the order of STAVKA supreme command, the corps was transformed into the 26th Army. On 25 October 1941, its field HQ was disbanded, and its constituent formations were transferred to the 50th Army of the Bryansk Front.<cr>A new 1st Guards Rifle Corps was formed on 31 December 1941. Its first commander, Col. Afanasii Sergeevich Gryaznov, was appointed the same day; he would be promoted to Major General ten days later. As of 1 February it was under the direct command of Northwestern Front, with the following units in its order of battle:

7th Guards Rifle Division
14th, 15th, 52nd Rifle Brigades
72nd Naval Rifle Brigade
203rd, 204th and 205th Ski Brigades
878th Corps Artillery Regiment (re-designated 37th Guards Artillery Regiment later that month, with 4 batteries of 4 122mm guns each.)<cr><cr>The Corps saw action around the Demyansk Pocket for most of 1942, with a number of rifle brigades under command, but also with 7th Guards Rifle and 37th Guards Artillery under command as well. In October the Corps headquarters went into the Reserve of the Supreme High Command, where it was assigned to the 1st Reserve Army, which later became the 2nd Guards Army. For the duration of the war it served as an administrative command, with no assigned support units.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Special_Rifle_Corps</url>

On 22 June 1941 the 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division was part of the 7th Mechanised Corps, alongside the 14th and 18th tank divisions in the Moscow Military District, assigned to the 20th Army.
23 June 1941, the 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division was replenished to the full strength of 10831 men. It was the first Soviet formation to use T-34 tanks, at Borisov, on June 30, 1941.
11 July 1941, after suffering heavy losses, the 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division was moved to the reserve of 20th army and placed north of Orsha, and was completely encircled by the German forces 14 July 1941.
25 July 1941, the elements of 6th and 175th motor rifle regiments of 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division break encirclement near Mogilev, but have suffered more losses in the heavy rearguard fighting by 30 July 1941. During that period, heavy personnel flow left few if any of the initial combatants.
By 5 August 1941, remnants of the 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division were wiped out after being encircled again in Smolensk region, in unclear circumstances.
5 August 1941, the 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division was re-formed anew within 20th army, 18 August 1941 renamed 1st armoured division and on September 21, 1941, it was renamed the 1st Guards Moscow Motor Rifle Division. The division was renamed (again) as the 1st Guards Rifle Division, in January 1943.
30 August 1941, the 1st armoured division was participating in the Yelnya Offensive, forcing back 28th Jager Division. Due heavy losses, the division was stopped advancing 10 September 1941 and was withdrawn to behind of Vop River.
18 September 1941, the 1st armoured division was withdrawn to Mozhaysk for replenishment and subordinated directly to Stavka.
30 September 1941, the 1st Guards Moscow Motor Rifle Division was assigned to 40th army and sent to Sumy region. After initial advances, the 1st Guards Moscow Motor Rifle Division started to retreat 6 October 1941 as First Battle of Kharkov was being lost by Soviet forces. After losing Sumy 10 October 1941, the division was withdrawn to the reserve and sent back to Moscow.
21 October 1941, the division was assigned to 3rd army and arrived to Naro-Fominsk. The 1st Guards Moscow Motor Rifle Division lost 70% of personnel in urban warfare before retreating from Naro-Fominsk 25 October 1941. Attempt to re-take Naro-Fominsk 28 October 1941 have failed. The division remained in Naro-Fominsk area until end of November 1941.
29 January 1942, the division liberated the village of Myatlevo in cooperation with the 415th Rifle Division during the winter counteroffensive in front of Moscow.
In 1942, the 1st Guards Moscow Motor Rifle Division was participating in Battle of Rzhev.
In July 1943, the 1st Guards Rifle Division was participating in Operation Kutuzov, in October 1943 - in Bryansk offensive, and in December 1943 - in Haradok offensive.
In January–July 1944, the 1st Guards Rifle Division was advancing in Vitebsk - Minsk direction with heavy fighting, and was awarded 'Minsk' honorific 13 July 1944.
In November 1944, the division invaded East Prussia in Gusev area, and finally stormed Königsberg in April 1945.
21-26 April 1945, the 1st Guards Rifle Division ended the war by storming Baltiysk as part of 11th Guards Army of the 3rd Belorussian Front.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Motor_Rifle_Division</url>

The 1st Guards Romanian Infantry Division was formed in 1940 and was intended to be an elite division in the Romanian Army. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was attached to the Romanian V Army Corps at the southern end of the front. It participated in the 73 day Siege of Odessa. At the end of 1941 it was transferred from the front to Romania where it remained until the Soviets threatened Romania in 1944. It was decimated in the defensive battles that followed and disbanded. In the Spring of 1945 it was again mobilized under Soviet control and sent to Czechoslavkia.http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D1G.htmlEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The First Guards Tank Army was created by awarding the Guards title to the 1st Tank Army in April 1944. It participated in the in the Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive, the Vistula-Oder Offensive and the Battle of Berlin. It was commanded by Mikhail Katukovhttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Tank_Army_(Russia)

On 8 December 1942, the 26th Tank Corps became the 1st Guards Tank Corps for its actions at Stalingrad. The 216th Tank Brigade became the 15th Guards, the 19th became the 16th Guards, the 157th became the 17th Guards and the 14th Motor Rifle Brigade became the 1st Guards.<cr>On 27 January 1943, the corps was awarded the honorific 'Don' for its actions. Alexey Rodin was promoted to Lieutenant general and became commander of the 2nd Tank Army in early February. 6th Army Tank Troops commander Major General Alexander Kukushkin took command. During February and March, the corps fought in the Third Battle of Kharkov. It defended positions north of Pavlohrad and fled to escape an encirclement on 24 February. On 25 April, Kukushkin was killed during an enemy air raid. 2nd Guards Army Tank Troops commander Major General Mikhail Panov took command. During the summer it fought in Operation Kutuzov. From October 1943, it fought in Belarus during the Gomel-Rechitsa Offensive. The corps captured Rechytsa in November and cut off the German line of retreat west of Gomel. For its actions, the corps was awarded the Order of the Red Banner on 18 November.<cr>The corps fought in the Kalinkovichi-Mozyr Offensive in January 1944. The corps captured Kalinkavichy on 14 January after outflanking defending German troops. On 15 January, the corps was awarded the Order of Suvorov 2nd class for its actions. From June, the corps fought in Operation Bagration. On 24 June, the corps advanced through the gap made by the advance of the 65th Army. By 27 June, the corps linked up with elements of the 9th Tank Corps, completing the encirclement of five German 9th Army divisions in the Bobruysk Offensive. The corps continued to advanced towards Pukhavichy and Osipovichi. On 3 July, the corps was on the southeastern outskirts of Minsk and helped complete the encirclement of the German 4th Army around Minsk. After the capture of Minsk, the corps advanced toward Baranovichi and Brest. The corps helped capture Slonim.<cr>From mid-November 1944, the corps was part of the 2nd Belorussian Front. From January 1945, the corps fought in the East Prussian Offensive. During the offensive, the corps helped capture Plonsk and Tuchola. On 19 February, the corps was awarded the Order of Lenin for its capture of Plonsk. At the end of March, the corps fought in the capture of Gda?sk during the East Pomeranian Offensive. From April, the division fought in the Berlin Offensive. It reached the Baltic coast near Rostock and Ribnitz at the end of the war.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Tank_Division</url>

The first commander of the Hungarian First Army was Lieutenant-General (or Altábornagy according to the Hungarian army rank) Vilmos Nagy. After 30 August 1940, under Nagy, the Hungarian First Army took part in Hungary's annexation and occupation of northern Transylvania. This region of Romania was awarded to Hungary as a condition of the Second Vienna Award.From 1940 to mid-1944, the Hungarian First Army saw little action other than occupation duties.By 30 April 1944, the Hungarian First Army was used to bolster Army Group South Ukraine. This army group was pushed back during the Second Battle of Târgu Frumos in May 1944. The Hungarians were placed in defensive positions north of the 4th Romanian Army and south of Army Group North Ukraine.From 13 July to 29 July 1944, the Hungarian First Army fought against the Soviet Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive. At this time the Hungarians were attached to the German 1st Panzer Army commanded by Colonel-General (Generaloberst)Gotthard Heinrici, which, in turn, was part of Army Group North Ukraine.Later in 1944, Soviet troops entered Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary. The Romanians capitulated. The Bulgarians capitulated. The Hungarians tried to capitulate twice, but unsuccessfully. In the end, the Hungarian First Army continued its precarious existence.On 28 December, a newly formed Hungarian government, under acting Prime Minister Béla Miklós, officially declared war against Nazi Germany. But the Germans and the pro-German Hungarians in Hungary fought on against the Soviets. However, there are indications that some elements of the Hungarian First Army went over to the Soviets at about this time. Béla Miklós had been the commander of the Hungarian First Army from 1 August 1944 to 16 October 1944.Between 1 January and 16 February 1945, most of what remained of the Hungarian First Army was overrun, bypassed, or destroyed about 200 kilometers north of Budapest when the 40th Soviet Army advanced through the area. But, even after this, the Hungarian First Army did not cease to exist. The remnants fought on as an attachment to Heinrici's German First Panzer Army. Fighting as they went, they moved progressively westward into Slovakia. The army was not officially disbanded until 8 May 1945, the end of the war.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Army_(Hungary)Photo courtesy Slobodsky family archive.

The 1st Hungarian Cavalry Brigade was formed in 1938. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was assigned to the Hungarian Mobile Corps or Gyorshadtest which in turn was part of the Carpathian Group. The Carpathian Group invaded Ukrainian Galicia on June 29th, 1941. Shortly thereafter the Carpathian Group was disbanded and the Hungarian VIII Corps was assigned occupation duties while the 1st Hungarian Cavalry Brigade, still part of the the Hungarian Mobile Corps, continued the drive deep into the Soviet Union. The brigade along with the rest of the Corps were recalled to Hungary in October of 1941. Shortly after arriving home the 1st and 2nd Hungarian Cavalry Brigades were merged into the 1st Hungarian Cavalry Division. In September 1944 the division was renamed the 1st Hussar Division.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IICharles D. Pettibone, The Organization and Order of Battle of Militaries in World War II Volume VII - Germany's and Imperial Japan's Allies & Puppet StatesEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 1st Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 1st Light Division. In January of 1943 the division was transferred to Russia for security duties with the Hungarian Occupation Group. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 1st Light Division was merged with other units and disbanded.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

Editor Name: 1st Hun. Motorized Brigade;1st Hun. Armored Division
text: The 1st Hungarian Motorized Brigade was formed in 1938. The brigade participated in the German Invasion of Yugoslavia in early 1941. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was assigned to the Hungarian Mobile Corps or Gyorshadtest which in turn was part of the Carpathian Group. The Carpathian Group invaded Ukrainian Galicia on June 29th, 1941. Shortly thereafter the Carpathian Group was disbanded and its Hungarian VIII Corps was assigned occupation duties while the 1st Motorized Brigade, still part of the the Hungarian Mobile Corps, continued the drive deep into the Soviet Union. The brigade along with the rest of the Corps were recalled to Hungary in October of 1941. By this time the brigade had lost most of its armor. In early 1942 the brigade was reorganized and became the 1st Armored Division.The Hungarian Government reluctantly agreed to support the Germans 1942 summer offensive Fall Blau and allocated the division as part of the Hungarian Second Army to the task. Second Army's role in the offensive was to guard the German northern flank on the Don River. During the Stalingrad Campaign the Second Army suffered over 60% casualties but was generally able to retreat in good order with the 1st Armored Division being the last unit in the Hungarian Second Army to withdraw from the fighting in February 1943.In September 1944 the division was part of the Third Hungarian Army defending Hungary's southern border. The division was one of the defenders of the Hungarian capital when In November 1944 the Russians commenced their 102 day Siege of Budapest. The division was disbanded in February 1945 when the city surrendered.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 1st Hungarian Mountain Brigade was formed in September of 1939. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was assigned to the Hungarian VIII Corps which in turn was part of the Carpathian Group. The Carpathian Group invaded Ukrainian Galicia on June 29th, 1941. Shortly thereafter the Carpathian Group was disbanded and the Hungarian VIII Corps was assigned occupation duties however the 1st Hungarian Mountain Brigade was back in Hungary by the end of 1941. It did not participate further in the fighting until Russian armies approached the Carpathian Mountains and Hungary proper in 1944. The brigade surrendered to Soviet forces in Styria, Austria in May of 1945.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IICharles D. Pettibone, The Organization and Order of Battle of Militaries in World War II Volume VII - Germany's and Imperial Japan's Allies & Puppet StatesEntry courtesy Chris Munson

In June 1941, the 1st Infantry Division crossed into Russia with Army Group North and was heavily engaged in the Baltic States during the drive on Leningrad. By October 1941, its strength had been reduced by two-thirds; nevertheless, it continued to fight on the northern sector of the Russian Front, primarily as a part of the 18th Army, for more than two years. During this time, it took part in the Battle of Lake Peipus, the Battles of Lake Ladoga, and the Battle of the German Corridor (east of Leningrad), as well as the siege of Leningrad itself. In October 1943, the 1st Infantry was attached to Army Group South and fought in the Battle of Krivoi Rog in the Dniepr campaign in southern Russia. Later it saw action in the Ukraine and was encircled with the 1st Panzer Army between the Bug and the Dnestr rivers in March 1944. In the subsequent breakout it formed the rear guard of the XXXXVI Panzer Corps and suffered heavy casualties. Later, after a period of rest and rebuilding, it was sent to the central sector in August 1944. The survivors of the 1st Infantry remained with Army Group Center and ended the war fighting the Soviets in the division's home territory of East Prussia, including the battles of Schlossberg, Königsberg, Samland, and Pillau.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 1st Mechanized Corps was initially formed in March 1940 it was attached to the Leningrad Military District, and held in reserve near the Pskov Fortified Region. It was under the command of Major General Mikhail Chernyavski when the German Operation Barbarossa began in June 1941. It initially comprised the 1st and 3rd Tank Divisions, and the 168th Mechanized Division. On 22 June 1941, 1st Mechanized Corps consisted 31,439 Men, 1037 Tanks, 239 Armored Cars, 148 Artillery Pieces, 146 Mortars, 4730 Vehicles, 246 Tractors & 467 Motorcycles including lighter models T-26, BT-7, & T-28's.After the invasion began the Leningrad Military District was renamed Northern Front, Commanded by Lieutenant General Markian Popov. The front fielded 14th Army, 7th Army, 23rd Army, the 65th Rifle Corps & the Leningrad Military District forces including the 2nd Division of NKVD troops. The 1st Mechanized Corps was heavily engaged in the first battles of Operation Barbarossa, particularly during the Baltic Operation (1941). On 29 June 1941 the 1st Mechanized Corps was ordered to reinforce new defenses anchored on the Velikaya River near Ostrov on the former Stalin Line after the spectacular advances by Georg-Hans Reinhardt's XLI Panzer Corps which had crossed the Daugava River. However it was unable to hold the line. On 11 July 1941 Col P Poluboiarov, Northwestern Front armoured directorate reported that the 1st Mechanized Corps had at the present moment fewer than 100 Tanks remaining. Pskov and Ostrov were captured within weeks & Leningrad invested. On 2 August 1941 Colonel Limarenko, Chief of Staff of the 1st Mechanized Corps reported that the Corps 'possessed no T-34 or Kv-1s when sent into action 20 were delivered only after combat began. The 1st Mechanized Corps was disbanded in August 1941, although 1st Tank Division remained in 14th Army.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Mechanized_Corps_(Soviet_Union)

The 1st Mechanized Division was formed from the 1st Rifle Division in May 1940 in Moscow Military District.<cr>
The 1st was one of the earliest Mechanized Divisions formed, and even though it was assigned to 7th Mechanized Corps, it retained some of the personality of the 1st 'Moscow Proletariat' Rifle Division, which had been a Parade or showpiece unit permanently stationed in Moscow.<cr>
By 22 June 1941 the 1st Mechanized was actually stationed just outside of Moscow in Vyazma, with 12,000 men (actually overstrength in authorized personnel), 100% of authorized artillery and heavy weapons, and 225 BT-7M tanks in the tank regiment - the newest and most modern 'light tanks' available in quantity.<cr>
Before the rest of 7th Mechanized Corps, 1st Mechanized Division was alerted to move to the front on the morning of 22 June. On the way forward through Orsha (west of Smolensk) the division added 10 KVs and 30 T-34s from Tank Training units in Western Military District. When the division went into battle for the first time 26 - 30 June, it also had under command a battalion of students from the Borisov Tank-Technical School. Because of these additions, the Germans mistakenly thought that this division had been authorized a special complement of heavy and medium tanks not found in other mechanized divisions. To add to the confusion, German intelligence variously identified the unit as the 'Moscow' division, the 'Stalin Guards' division, or the 'Moscow Guards' division.<cr>
For a time in August 1941, both the Germans and the Red Army (unofficially)identified it as the 1st Tank Division - chiefly because it still had a functioning tank regiment after almost all the other tank and mechanized divisions in Western Front had been destroyed.<cr>7th Mechanized Corps staff was used to form a new headquarters for 16th Army near Smolensk in early July, so 1st Mechanized Division became an independant 'fire brigade' unit for Western Front, fighting frequently under either 16th or 20th Army command east of Smolensk throughout July and August, 1941. Its division commander, Col A. I. Lizyukov, was one of the first wartime recipients of the Hero of the Soviet Union medal - the Soviet equivalent of the Medal of Honor or Victoria Cross.<cr>
By 15 September, 1st Mechanized Division was in Western Front reserveswith 45 tanks total and 600 riflemen left in each motorized rifle regiment. In recognition of the division's combat record - in persistant survivability, if not strategic success - on 21 September 1941 1st Mechanized Division became the 1st Guards Motorized Division.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 1st Moscow Rifle Division was formed from a single regiment in September 1939 and reformed as the 1st Moscow Motor Rifle Division in January 1940. Its honorific title was 1st Moscow Proletariat Red Banner Rifle Division. Training was complete by June 1940 and the division took part in the Soviet occupation of the Baltic States. After several months on occupation duty the division returned to Russia. At the start of Operation Barbarossa the division was assigned to the 20th Army in the Moscow Military District. The division was rapidly replenished to its full complement of 10,831 men. On June 30, 1941 at Borisov the division was the first Russian unit to use T-34 tanks against the Germans invaders.In July 1941 the division was encircled near Mogilev. Some elements escaped only to be encircled near Smolensk the following month and destroyed. The division was reformed almost immediately in August 1941 as the 1st Tank Division and in September 1941 was renamed the 1st Guards Moscow Motor Rifle Division. The division was severely mauled in October 1941 in street fighting at Naro-Fominsk.The division fought in the Battle of Rzhev in 1942. The division was again renamed in January 1943 becoming the 1st Guards Rifle Division. The division fought in many other engagements throughout 1944 and crossed into East Prussia in November 1944. In April 1945 it participated in the storming of Königsberg and then Baltiysk.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Motor_Rifle_DivisionEntry courtesy Chris Munson

In June 1941, the 1st Mountain Division crossed into Russia as part of Army Group South, and on July 15-16 broke through the Stalin Line. During this battle, the division lost 31 men killed and 74 wounded, but killed several hundred Russians and captured 281 more. It also captured 100 machine guns, eight guns, a tank and three airplanes. Two days later, it was fighting on the Bug, where it held a twenty-seven mile front with only two infantry regiments. As the Soviet forces tried to escape from Vinniza, the division was able to take 10,000 prisoners, but was unable to block the escape of 30,000 more.Later, the 1st Mountain took part in the Battle of the Uman Pocket (where it suffered 759 casualties), and by the end of the month, the division’s strength had dropped from 17,801 men to 13,636. It had also lost about 500 of its 6,487 horses. The division nevertheless launched a major assault across the Dnieper River at Berislav, where it built a bridge 431 meters long. It took part in the capture of Kiev and the subsequent liquidation of the Kiev Pocket, then pushed south to help capture Stalino (now Donetsk, Ukraine) in September, and took part in the encirclement of Mogila Tokmak (also known as the Chernigovka Pocket and the Battle of the Sea of Azov) from October 5 to 10. During this battle, the Red Army lost 100,000 men captured and 212 tanks and 672 guns captured or destroyed. From September 6 to October 10, 1941, however, the 1st Mountain Division had lost 573 men killed and 1,975 wounded. Even more seriously, 75 percent of its vehicles had broken down or were in need of major overhauls. The division nevertheless took part in the drive on and retreat from Rostov and helped defend the Mius River Line against Stalin's winter offensive of 1941-42.By May 1942, it was with the III Panzer Corps and fought in the Battle of Kharkov and in the eastern Donetz. Later, it was at the spearhead ofGeneral von Kleist's Caucasus campaign, but was checked in the high mountains. After the disaster of Stalingrad, Kleist’s Army Group A was forced to retreat into the Kuban, and the 1st Mountain Division was involved in the first of a long series of withdrawals and rear-guard actions on the road back to Germany. In April 1943, the division was withdrawn from the front and sent to Serbia and northern Greece, where it was rebuilt and engaged in anti-partisan operations. Later it was reported on the Greco-Albanian frontier, and subsequently in western Serbia, Bosnia, Croatia and Montenegro. The division was still fighting south of Belgrade in October 1944. Following the loss of this city, it fought in Hungary (November 1944–March 1945) and in the Austrian Alps. It was redesignated 1st Volks Mountain Division on March 12, 1945, but with no change to its table of organization. The 1st Mountain Division ended the war as part of Army Group South, fighting the Russians in central Styria. It ended up in Soviet captivity in May 1945.German Order of Battle Vol II 291st - 999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions and Special Divisions in WWII

Formed 7/31/41 from 1st Cavalry Division, it was part of Separate Coastal Army and fought in the Siege of Odessa. Later redesignated 2nd Rifle Division.The Organization and Order of Battle of Militaries in World War II: volume V - Book B Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Trafford, 2009 Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 1st Panzer Division crossed into the Soviet Union when Operation Barbarossa began on June 22, 1941, with a strength of approximately 155 tanks. It formed part of Army Group North’s 4th Panzer Group (later Army) and took part in the annihilation of the Soviet III Armored Corps at Dubysa in June. The 1st Panzer was seriously depleted by casualties, and by August 16 had only forty-four serviceable tanks; nevertheless it took part in the drive on Moscow (it came to within twenty miles of the Soviet capital) and opposed the Russian winter offensive, where it was surrounded and forced to break out. By February 18, the 1st Panzer Regiment had only eighteen operational tanks; most of the regiment was used to form two ad hoc ski companies. The division nevertheless fought in the critical Rzhev salient and helped save the 9th Army, which was nearly surrounded.In early July, the 1st and 2nd Panzer Divisions surrounded and destroyed or captured 218 Soviet tanks, 592 guns, and 1,300 anti-tank guns near Pushkeri. In a two day period in August, the division destroyed sixty-five superheavy KV-1 and KV-2 tanks and wiped out a Soviet penetration. Greatly reduced by losses, the 1st Panzer was withdrawn for resting and refitting in January 1943. Initially it was sent to Amiens, France, but spent that summer in Greece. Here it was brought up to full strength; by autumn it had a full battalion of PzKw V (Tiger) tanks and about 100 PzKw VI (Panther) tanks. When Italy defected to the Western Allies in September 1943, the 1st Panzer Division played a major role in subduing the Italian 11th Army, which put up little resistance. In October 1943, it returned to the Russian Front, fighting on the southern sector, took part in the Battle of the Kiev Salient and the counteroffensive west of Kiev (November–December 1943).It also spearheaded the attempt to rescue the XI and XXXXII Corps, which were surrounded at Cherkassy in February 1944. It could not penetrate the last six miles to the pocket but was still successful in saving half the trapped Germans. The next month the 1st Panzer rescued the 96th and 291st Infantry Divisions from the Soviet spring offensive of 1944. Casualties were again heavy and, as of March 14, 1944, the division’s panzer grenadier battalions were at 25 percent of their authorized strengths, and the 1st Panzer Regiment had fewer than sixty operational tanks. The division nevertheless remained in the line and fought in the battles of the Dnieper Bend, the north Ukraine, and eastern Poland in 1944. Retreating behind the Vistula, it was transferred to Hungary and was cited for its counterattack against the Russians at Debrecen. Most of the division was trapped and destroyed at Szekesfehervar, Hungary, in December 1944, when the 6th Army collapsed; despite its losses, however, the remnants of the 1st Panzer Division continued fighting on the southern sector of the Eastern Front until the end of the war. The division then extricated itself from the Red Army and surrendered to the Americans at Mauerkirchen in Upper Bavaria on May 8, 1945. The Americans dissolved the division five days later. Most of its soldiers were released and sent home by the end of July.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

1st Panzer Group (Panzergruppe 1), which was attached to Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt's Army Group South at the beginning of Operation Barbarossa. At the start of Operation Barbarossa in June 1941, Panzer Group 1 included the III, XIV and XLVIII Army Corps (mot) with five panzer divisions and four motorized divisions (two of them SS) equipped with 799 tanks. Panzer Group 1 served on the southern sector of the Eastern Front against the Red Army and was involved the Battle of Brody which involved as many as 1,000 Red Army tanks. On October 6, 1941, Panzer Group 1 was enlarged to the 1st Panzer Army.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Panzer_Army

Part of the 10th Army in the Western Front, it consisted of the 2nd and 8th Rifle Divisions. It was encircled in the Minsk Pocket and was destroyed in June 1941. The corps was reformed in to the North Caucasus Front in August 1942 and its subsequent history is unclear. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Army_Corps_(Soviet_Union)Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 1st Romanian Armored Division was formed in April of 1941. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was assigned to the Romanian Cavalry Corps. As with most Romanian units it was withdrawn to Romania after the Siege of Odessa. In late 1942 the division was deployed to Southern Russia with Army Group B The first armored regiment had been reequipped with imported German tanks, primarily the PzKw 35t, PzKw III and PzKw IV. The 2nd Armored Regiment, equipped with obsolete Renault R-35 tanks, was left behind in Romania in the role of training unit. After its losses in the Battle of Stalingrad the division was out of action for more than a year as it waited for replacement equipment from Germany and did not see action again until February of 1944.http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D1B.htmlhttp://philonworldwartwo.blogspot.com/2011/11/romanian-1st-armored-division.htmlPicture: 'Armata Romana in al doilea razboi mondial', Meridiane, 1995Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 1st Romanian Cavalry Brigade was attached to the Romanian VI Corps at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In March of 1942 it was reorganized as the 1st Romanian Cavalry Division. As the 1st Cavalry Division it participated in the Stalingrad Campaign where much of the division was encircled and destroyed. By April of 1943 the surivors, with only 189 horses and one tank remaining, had returned to Romania. It was envisioned the division would be transformed into an armored cavalry or motorized cavalry division but due to a lack of tanks and vehicles this was only partially complete prior to Romania's signing an armistice with Russia in 1944.http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D1C.htmlhttp://worldwar2.ro/oob/?article=70Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 1st Romanian Infantry Division did not participate in the opening phase of Operation Barbarossa and remained in Romania. It was activated in September of 1941 and assigned to the V Romanian Army Corps. At the end of 1941 it was assigned to the German 1st Panzer Army to assist in repeling Soviet winter counterattacks. In 1942 it particpated in the German summer campaign Fall Blau. The division was down to a few hundred survivors after the Battle of Stalingrad and returned to Romania. When the Soviets threatened Romania in 1944 it was again activated and participated in many defensives battles until it was merged with other units in late 1944.http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D1I.htmlEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 1st Romanian Security Division was formed in February of 1942 to perform security operations in occupied Russia near the Romanian border. In May of 1943 it was merged with the 5th Romanian Infantry Division.http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D1P.htmlEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 1st Shock Army was formed as part of the Reserve of the Supreme High Command (RVGK, the Stavka reserve) at Zagorsk (now Sergiyev Posad) in the Moscow Military District in November 1941. Taking part in the Battle of Moscow in December 1941, on 1 December the Army consisted of the 133rd Rifle Division, 29th, 44th, 47th, 50th, 55th, 56th, 71st, and 84th Rifle Brigades, 17th Cavalry Division, two tank battalions, an artillery regiment of the Stavka reserve, and other support units.[2] All the rifle brigades were formed from the naval personnel of the Pacific Fleet.1st Shock Army was then airlifted to Staraya Russa and fought at Demyansk in 1942. Fighting in the north-central areas of the front, the 1st Shock Army again fought near Staraya Russa in 1944. From 1942 through 1944, the army took part in many attacks such as the Leningrad-Novgorod, Pskov-Ostrov, Tartu, and Riga offensives. Fighting through the Baltic States, the 1st Shock Army finished the war as part of the Courland Group of Forces that had trapped the German Army Group Kurland in the northern reaches of Latvia.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Shock_Army

The 1st Slovak Infantry Division was part of the Slovakian Corps at the start of Operation Barbarossa. It was disbanded in August of 1941 and elements were used to form the Mobile Division (aka Fast Division). The Mobile Division was in turn disbanded in August of 1943 and a new 1st Slovak Infantry Division formed from its elements. After being mauled at Melitopolin the Southern Ukraine the division was disbanded in the summer of 1944 and its personnel assigned to construction units.http://www.axishistory.com/axis-nations/slovakia/army/75-slovakia-army/slovakia-army-unsorted/889-field-corps-slovakiahttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovak_Republic_(1939%E2%80%9345)Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 1st SS Panzer Division crossed into southern Russia with Army Group South in July 1941. It advanced along the Black Sea coast in August, took part in the opening phases of the Crimean campaign, and was devastated in the Battle of Rostov during the Soviet winter offensive of 1941–42. After seeing some action in the summer of 1942, the Leibstandarte was pulled out of the line and sent to northern France in August.Returned to the Eastern Front in the spring of 1943, the division took part in the Kursk offensive and suffered heavy casualties in the Battle of Kharkov (1943) before being transferred to northern Italy.Returning to southern Russia in the autumn, the 1st SS was involved in heavy combat west of Kiev, at Tarnopol, and in the Dnieper battles. It unsuccessfully tried to prevent the encirclement of the 1st Panzer Army in 1944. The division was itself surrounded at Skala in the spring of that year and suffered ruinous losses in the ensuing breakout.THe division was sent to Belgium and fought in the west until after the Ardennes offensive. The division was subsequent withdrawn and sent to Hungary, where it fought in the unsuccessful Lake Balaton counterattack. Hitler, displeased with the failure of one of the Leibstandarte’s attacks, ordered it to remove the Adolf Hitler cuffband from the uniforms of its troops. The division responded by sending him a pile of their medals—in a latrine bucket. The survivors of the division retreated into Austria in 1945, and fought in the Battle of Vienna. It ended the war on the southern sector of the Eastern Front, although most of the men of the division managed to surrender to the Americans.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 1st Tank Army was first formed within the Stalingrad Front from 38th Army in July 1942, under the command of Major General Kirill Moskalenko. The army was encircled and partially destroyed, and was disbanded as a result in August 1942, its headquarters becoming the Southeastern Front headquarters.The 1st Tank Army was formed a second time on 30 January 1943 (order No.46021) from the headquarters of the 29th Army, under the command of famous armoured troops commander Lieutenant General of Tank Troops Mikhail Katukov, personally appointed by Stalin. The army was transferred to the Northwestern Front. 3rd Mechanized Corps (later to become 8th Guards Mechanized Corps) and 6th Tank Corps (later to become 11th Guards Tank Corps) joined it on formation, and served with the army throughout the war. It was quickly transferred to Voronezh Front for the defense of the Kursk salient's southern shoulder. It was awarded a Guards title and became the 1st Guards Tank Army in April 1944, and Katukov was promoted to Colonel General.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Guards_Tank_Army_(Russia)

The 1st Tank Corps was formed in March 1942 in the Moscow Military District, started receiving units in April 1942 in the same District.<cr>The first Corps commander was Major General M. E. Katukov, the commander of 4th Tank Brigade when it became 1st Guards Tank Brigade in 1941, and later commander of 1st Guards Tank Army. The 1st Tank Corps went right to Bryansk Front in May, before receiving any unit training or any other supporting units. It was badly chewed up trying to attack the flank of German panzer forces south and east of Voronezh, and by late August was assigned to 5th Tank Army with only 89th Tank Brigade left in the corps.<cr>The 1st Tank Corps was part of the 'Mobile Group' of 5th Tank Army that seized Kalach-na-Don and surrounded the 6th German Army at Stalingrad, unfortunately, the actual seizure of Kalach was done by 26th Tank Corps, so that unit received the 'Guards' designation, not 1st Tank Corps. In January 1943 the 1st Tank Corps went into reserve, first in Volga Military District (east of Stalingrad) and then, in March, it shifted to Western Front reserves near Moscow. While in reserve the corps was stripped of its supporting elements, leaving just the brigades.<cr>In June 1943 the Soviet High Command began rebuilding the Corps for the anticipated campaigns of the late summer. When llth Guards Army went over on the attack north of Orel in July, 1st Tank Corps was assigned to it as part of the Army Mobile Group.<cr>The 1st Tank Corps fought under Bryansk Front through the summer of 1943. Since Bryansk Front had no major breakthroughs in which to commit the tank corps, in September it added two more support units.<cr> In January-March 1944 1st Tank Corps fought under llth Guards Army in 1st Baltic Front, sometimes with 2nd Guards Heavy Tank Regiment (KV-85 tanks) attached. In late March 1944 the corps went into STAVKA Reserves to prepare for the major operations planned for the summer. While in the reserves in April-May 1944, the corps was completely re-equipped with new tanks and the antitank and SU units in the corps were reorganized.<cr>The 1st Tank Corps formed the Mobile Group for 6th Guards Army in June-July 1944, and formed its own Corps Forward Detachment to lead the advance deep into the German rear.<cr>Even while the fighting was going on in the Baltic, 1st Tank Corps was
being reinforced. In August 1944 the corps received 354th Guards Heavy SU Regiment (21 ISU-122s) and in September 1944 the 120th Light Artillery Regiment (24 76mm guns) was added. These were the last additions to 1st Tank Corps, which ended the war in May 1945 in East Prussia with 3rd Belorussian Front.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

On October 20, 1943, the Voronezh Front was renamed to the 1st Ukrainian Front. This name change reflected the westward advance of the Red Army in its campaign against the German Wehrmacht, leaving Russia behind and moving into Ukraine.During 1944, the front participated with other fronts in the battles of Korsun-Shevchenkovsky, and the battle of Hube's Pocket in Ukraine. It conducted the Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive, during which the Front was controlling the Soviet 1st Guards Tank Army, 3rd Guards Tank Army, 4th Tank Army, 3rd Guards, 5th Guards Army, 13th, 38th, and 60th Armies. It then took part in the battle for Ternopil'.In 1945 the front participated in the Vistula-Oder Offensive, and conducted the Silesian and Prague Operations, and the siege of Breslau. It also participated in the Berlin operations in Germany and Poland. The front also conducted the major part of the Halbe Encirlement, in which most of the German 9th Army was destroyed south of Berlin. By this time the Polish 2nd Army was operating as part of the Front. Finally 1st Ukrainian Front provided the defence against the counter-attacks by Armee Wenck which aimed to relieve Berlin and the 9th Army. The Prague Offensive was the final battle of World War II in Europe.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Ukrainian_Front

The 200th Soviet Rifle Division was established at Belokorovichi, Ukraine, in March, assigned to the Southwestern Front. At the start of Operation Barbarossa it was at approximately 50% strength and was wiped out at Kiev, in September 1941. Recreated at Busulusk in February 1942 by renaming the 425th Rifle Division. Fought in Belorussia, at Gydnia, and at Berlin. With the 49th Army of the 2nd Belorussian Front in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#191%E2%80%93200 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy John Tomlinson

The 201st Rifle Division was formed as an Red Army national unit during August 1941 in Gorki, Moscow Military District from the remains of the 24th Territorial Rifle Corps, and assigned to the 33rd Army. It was originally designated as the 201st Latvian Rifle Division, as the basis of the division was the 76th Independent Latvian Rifle Regiment. By December 1941 the division had 10,348 personnel, of whom 51% were ethnic Latvians, 26% ethnic Russians, 17% Jews and 6% others. The first combat the division experienced was during the counter-offensive at Moscow in the areas of Naro-Fominsk and Borovsk where it suffered 55% casualties. It also fought in the battle for Staraya Russa (from 16 February 1942 until 4 April), and for the Demyansk bridgehead. By June 1942 only 36% of the division were Latvian-speaking, and a year later this figure was reduced to 32%. The division was renamed as the 43rd Guards Rifle Division in October 1942 and was known as the Latvian Guards. A new 201st Rifle Division was raised from the 27th Rifle Brigade at Shlisselburg, near Leningrad, in November 1943, assigned to the 23rd Army. It served in the Leningrad and Baltic coast areas. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_201st_Military_Base Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa Vol IIIB Entry courtesy 56 ajax

When 12th Mechanized Corps went into battle, the division simply could not organize itself fast enough to join the tank divisions. The Division fought Sol'tsa, Kiev, and Korsun and ended the war assigned to the 27th Army of the 3rd Ukrainian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%9357#201%E2%80%93210 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The Divisional and Regimental commanders were relieved of their command. The Division fought at Stalingrad, the Donbass, Odessa and Budapest, amongst others. The 204th Mechanized Division had only 1 battalion of 44 light BT-5 tanks, but was full strength in armored cars left over from 9th Armored Car Brigade. Just to complete the dismal story of the unit, on the first day of the war, while trying to move to the front, the 204th was caught by the Luftwaffe and lost over 50% of its remaining equipment.
