The 205th Mechanized Division was formed February - March 1941 at Berez in Western Special Military District as part of 14th Mechanized Corps with: 577th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 721st Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns Tank Regiment 1 Tank Bn - with 6 BT, 35 T-26 tanks 672nd Motorized Howitzer Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns Reconnaissance Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Antitank Battalion Sapper Battalion The 205th Mechanized Division was at full strength in artillery, heavy weapons, mortars, and even antitank and antiaircraft guns, but had only 1 battalion of tanks and was missing most of the authorized trucks and tractors on 22 June 1941. In addition, the division was in action straight out of its barracks a few miles from the frontier in the first hours of the war. After losing what vehicles it had, the division was caught in the Minsk pocket and annihilated by early July.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 205th Soviet Rifle Division started forming in the Far East from October 1941. In July 1942 it was assigned to the 64th Army at Stalingrad where it was overrun and destroyed by October 1942. The Division was reformed from the 1st Polar Division and 186th Rifle Division and ended the war with the 19th Army of the 2nd 2nd Belorussian Front in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%9357#201%E2%80%93210 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 206th Infantry Division was involved in the Russian campaign from the beginning. It fought at Duenaberg, Velikije-Luka and Kalinin, and, along with the 26th Infantry Division, took Rzhev on the Volga River between Moscow and Leningrad in October 1941; however, the division was shattered by Russian counterattacks near Moscow from December 22, 1941 to January 4, 1942. Later that month it was briefly surrounded, along with the XXIII Corps, south of Lake Volga.In the spring of 1942, the 312th Infantry Regiment was disbanded, along with three infantry battalions, and the 206th Tank Destroyer and 206th Reconnaissance Battalions were combined to form a single schnelle battalion. The division remained with Army Group Center for the rest of its existence, taking part in the defensive battles around Rzhev (1942-43), the Rzhev withdrawal in March 1943, and the Battle of Smolensk (August 1943), among others. The 312th Grenadier Regiment was reconstituted in April 1944 (from elements of the 52nd Security Division), but the other grenadier regiments were reduced to two battalions each. As part of LIII Corps, 3rd Panzer Army, the division was crushed by the massive Soviet summer offensive of 1944. Encircled at Vitebsk and ordered to stay there by Adolf Hitler himself, the divisional commander, Lieutenant General Alfons Hitter, ordered a breakout on his own responsibility. Only a few of the division's 12,000 men managed to escape, however; the division was overwhelmed and destroyed on June 28. General Hitter was among those taken prisoner. On July 18, 1944, the demobilization office officially declared the historic East Prussian 301st, 312th, and 413th Grenadier Regiments disbanded and the 206th Infantry Division dead.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 206th Rifle Division was an infantry division of the Red Army, which began forming in March 1941, as a reserve division for what was to become the Southern Front. When the German invasion began it was only at 40% strength, still organizing well away from the front, near Krivoi Rog. The Division was sent North to the Kiev Fortified Sector where it was completely destroyed in the Kiev pocket in September, 1941. A small group led by the commander, Colonel Gorshkov, managed to escape, along with another led by the divisional chief of staff, Lt. Col. P. I. Kulizhski. It was not officially stricken from the Soviet order of battle until 27th December 1941. The 206th was reformed in early 1942 and went on to have a distinguished military history. It fought at Battle of Kursk, Korsun where it suffered heavy casualties, Uman, Budapest and Vienna amongst others. It lost 2 commanders due to military action and was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov, Kutuzov and Order of Bogdan Khmelnitsky. Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/206th_Rifle_DivisionEntry courtesy of 56ajax

The 207th Rifle Division was partly formed for the first time as a standard Red Army rifle division in the spring of 1941 but was disbanded by June 1941. The second 207th Rifle Division began forming in April, 1942, in the North Caucasus Military District, based on a cadre from the 52nd Rifle Brigade. In August it was thrown into a series of desperate and costly counter attacks against the north flank of the German 'corridor' at Stalingrad. It suffered very heavy casualties and was disbanded. The third 207th Rifle Division was formed on June 6, 1943, in the 5th Army in Western Front, based on a cadre from the 40th Rifle Brigade and the 2nd formation of the 153rd Rifle Brigade. It was involved in the battles for Smolensk, Riga and Berlin, amongst others. The 207th Rifle Division ended the war with the official title of 207th Rifle, Pomerania, Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov, Division. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/207th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 208th Mechanized Division was formed March 1941 near Gainovka in Western Special Military District as part of 13th Mechanized Corps with: 435th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 760th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 578th Motorized Howitzer Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns Reconnaissance Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Antitank Battalion Sapper Battalion The 208th Mechanized Division had a full strength howitzer regiment, -antiaircraft and antitank battalions - at least in weapons. Unfortunately, it had no tanks at all, and was missing most of its other motorized transport. As a result, ithin a few days after the war started, the division was stripped out of 13th Mechanized Corps and fought directly under 10th Army as a regular rifle division. The division was destroyed in the Minsk pocket, but a core of the unit, hiding in the forests east of Minsk, formed 208th Partisan Regiment. The 578th Howitzer Regiment was detached from the rest of the division when the pocket closed, and elements of it fought with 5th Mechanized Corps near Orsha in late June and early July, before the regiment was dissolved and its elements used to reinforce other artillery units.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 208th Rifle Division was a Soviet infantry division in the Red Army during World War II. It began Operation Barbarossa as the 208th Mechanized Division under Colonel V.I. Nichiporovich and was part of the 13th Mechanized Corps, 10th Army, Western Front. The division was trapped and destroyed in the Minsk pocket. Unusually, Colonel Nichiporovich managed to keep a large group of men together after the destruction of his division during the border battles, and kept on the fight as 'Detachment No.208,' one of the first units of the Soviet partisans in Belorussia. The Division is listed as being assigned to the 25th Army, Far East, as of November 1941. In 1942 the Division, under Col. K. M. Vysokoboinikov, was part of the 64th Army which fought in the Battle of Stalingrad. On 6 April 1945, now under the title 'Siberian,' it was part of the divisions of the encirclement of Königsberg, located at the northwest sector as part of 124th Rifle Corps, 43rd Army. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/208th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 209th Mechanized Division was formed March 1941 in Western Special Military District as part of 17th Mechanized Corps with: Motorized Rifle Regiment Motorized Rifle Regiment Howitzer Regiment Antitank Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Sapper Battalion The 209th Mechanized Division had a full-strength howitzer regiment and most of the heavy weapons for the rifle regiments, but not a single tank or armored car, and very few vehicles of any kind. In addition, like the entire the division was desparately short of NCOs and experienced officers, and had had no time to train the men that were on hand before the war started. The division was officially disbanded 19 September 1941.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 20th Army was first formed in the Orel Military District in June 1941. On 22 June 1941 the Army was part of the Reserve of the Supreme High Command and was located west of Moscow.On 27 June 1941 it was proposed to Joseph Stalin that the Soviet armies (13th, 19th, 20th, 21st, and 22nd Armies) would defend the line going through the Daugava-Polotsk-Vitebsk-Orsha-Mogilev-Mazyr as part of the Reserve Front.Committed as part of Western Front in defensive battles in Belarus, Battle of Smolensk, and Vyazma. By 5 August 1941 the army had been seriously reduced. The strength of the 289th Rifle Division had fallen to 285 men, 17 machine guns, and one anti-tank gun, the 73rd Rifle Division to 100 men and 4 to 5 machine guns, 144th Rifle Division to 440 men, and 153rd Rifle Division to 750 men. The Army HQ was disbanded having been encircled and destroyed in the Vyazma Pocket.Reestablished in November 1941 from Operational Group Liziukov. Reformed November 1941 for the Battle of Moscow, comprising 331st and 350th Rifle Divisions, and three separate brigades. Fought as part of the Western Front. In 1942-43 it operated on the Rzhev-Vyazma bridgehead, and took part in the Rzhev-Vyazma offensive operation. In 1944 it became part of the Stavka Reserve and was then reassigned to Kalinin Front and Leningrad Front. It was disbanded in April 1944 by being dispersed within the formations of 3rd Baltic Front.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Army_(Soviet_Union)

The 174th Rifle Division, became the 20th Guards Rifle Division in 1942. The 20th Guards Rifle Division fought at the Battle of Stalingrad, Krivoi Rog, Odessa, Budapest, and Vienna. It was with the 57th Army of the 3rd Ukrainian Front in May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Tank_Brigade_(Ukraine)

The 20th Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 20th Light Division. The Hungarian Government reluctantly agreed to support the Germans 1942 summer offensive Fall Blau and allocated the Hungarian Second Army to the task. Each light division in the Second Army was reinforced with three battalions from sister divisions in Hungary but nonetheless each division was only slightly larger than half the size of its German counterparts. Second Army's role in the offensive was to guard the German northern flank on the Don River. During the Stalingrad Campaign the Second Army suffered over 60% casualties but was generally able to retreat in good order. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 20th Light Division was merged with other units and renamed the 20th Infantry Division. In September 1944 the division was part of the Third Hungarian Army defending Hungary's southern border.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 20th Mechanized Corps was formed in March and April 1941 from elements of the 4th Don Cossack Cavalry Division and the Borisov Automobile, Tank, and Cavalry Schools. Corps headquarters was located in Borisov. It included the 26th and 38th Tank Divisions, and the 210th Motorized Division. The 26th Tank Division was located at Krasnoye Urochishche, the 38th Tank Division at Novoborisov, and the 210th Motorized Division at Osipovichi. The corps was commanded by Major General Andrei Nikitin.<cr>The corps fought in the Battle of Bialystok-Minsk. The corps was not yet fully formed and was at cadre strength. Between 22 and 27 June the corps fought in battles in the Minsk area, unsuccessfully attempting to stop the German advance towards the city. On 26 June it was ordered to conduct a counterattack with the 4th Airborne Corps at Slutsk. The corps attacked with its 93 outdated light tanks (80 T-26 tanks and 13 BT tanks) and the 4th Airborne Corps advanced on foot instead of conducting an air assault due to a lack of transport aircraft. Both units were unable to stop the German advance. On 30 June the Svisloch Railroad Bridge, defended by the 4th Airborne Corps, was captured by the 4th Panzer Division, cutting off most of the 20th Mechanized Corps and a 4th Airborne Corps brigade. The corps and other remnants of Soviet units delayed the advance of the XXXXVI Motorized Corps with their resistance.<cr>By 1 July it was part of the 13th Army. On 7 July the corps included about 12,000 men with 27 guns and no tanks. From 9 to 27 July it fought in and was destroyed in the Mogilev pocket. By the end of 15 July the corps was defending Mogilev alongside the 61st Rifle Corps and remnants of several divisions. On 21 July deputy corps commander Major General Nikolai Vedeneyev took command after Nikitin was wounded and evacuated. At this time the corps defended Mogilev's eastern approaches. By 25 July, the Soviet troops in Mogilev were running out of ammunition, food and fuel. 61st Rifle Corps commander Fyodor Bakunin made the decision to withdraw against orders and called a meeting with Vedeneyev and three of the division commanders on the breakout plan. The 20th Mechanized Corps would lead the breakout towards the general direction of Roslavl. That night, the corps began the breakout. In the morning, the corps ran into the German 78th Infantry Division at the village of Samulki. Supported by vehicles from an attached reconnaissance battalion, the corps fought on foot and attacked the German positions. The attack was stopped by heavy German machine gun fire. Bakunin ordered the destruction of remaining equipment and ordered the survivors to disperse and break out in small groups. Between 27 and 28 July the corps broke out of the pocket with 100 to 200 men left. The perechen (list of Soviet units during World War II) does not state that the corps was disbanded, although it lost most of its men during the battles in the Mogilev Pocket. The corps last appears on the combat composition of the Soviet Army list for 10 July 1941.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Mechanized_Corps_(Soviet_Union)</url>

On the Eastern Front in 1941, the 20th Motorized Division fought with Army Group Centre at Bialystok, Minsk, Smolensk, and the Dniepr crossings, before being sent to the northern sector, where it fought its way across the Dvina River and spearheaded the 16th Army's drive on Oreshek, on the road to Leningrad. The 20th remained on the northern sector until December 1942, fighting in the Volkhov sector (February-July 1942), at Staraja Russa (July-August), and at Volkhov again (September-October). In December 1942, it was sent to Army Group Center, where it held a sector near Welish (December 1942-June 1943) and fought in the defensive battles of Orel (August) and Bryansk (September). Meanwhile, it was redesignated a panzer grenadier division on July 23, 1943. Transferred south that autumn, the 20th suffered heavy losses in the Battle of Kiev and the subsequent retreat to the Dniepr in November 1943. It nevertheless remained in the line and fought at Winniza (January 1944), in the Hube Pocket (March-April 1944), in the defensive victory at Brody> (i.e., in the first battle of Brody) (May 1944), in the retreat across southern Poland to the Vistula (June-August 1944), and in the efforts to eliminate and then contain the Baranov Bridgehead (August-January 1945). After the Soviets broke out of the Baranov sector, the 20th Panzer Grenadier Division was forced into Silesia in February 1945. It was transferred to the north in March (i.e., the Oder sector), where the remnants of the division defended Seelow Heights in the Third Reich's last stand (April 16-19, 1945) and were crushed there after a gallant defense. The remnants of the division surrendered to the Americans at Tangermünde on the Elbe River.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 20th Panzer Division first saw action on the central sector of the Eastern Front, took part in the Minsk encirclement, took Vitebsk by coup de main (July 10), stormed Ulla and fought in the Battle of Smolensk (July 16–August 5). In late August it fought in the Battle of Mga and took the city, which was a major junction on the Moscow-Leningrad Railroad. Later that year, it suffered heavy losses in the Battle of Moscow and in the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42.Reorganized in March 1942, two of its tank battalions, an infantry battalion and its motorcycle battalion had to be dissolved due to heavy losses. The Headquarters, 20th Rifle Brigade was taken from the division in early 1943 and used to form Staff, 20th Bicycle Brigade. The Staff, 21st Panzer Regiment (which had been upgraded to a brigade headquarters, despite the fact that it only controlled one tank battalion) was also taken from the division and sent north, where it became HQ, Panzer Division Norway. The 20th Panzer Division, meanwhile, remained on the central front from 1942 to 1944, taking part in the defensive battles of 1942 and the Kursk offensive, and in the battles around Gshatsk, Orel, Toropez, Bryansk, Vitebsk, Nevel, Bobruisk, and Kholm. In June 1944, it was encircled by the massive Soviet offensive and had to fight its way out, with ruinous losses. Transferred to Army Group South Ukraine (a supposedly quiet sector), the 20th Panzer again suffered heavy casualties when the Romanians defected and the front collapsed. In November 1944 the division (or what was left of it) was in East Prussia, and the following month was transferred to the Hungarian sector. After fighting in Austria, the burned-out division was sent to Silesia. It was overrun by the Red Army in April 1945, and was pushed into Bohemia, and it ended the war surrounded in the Deutsch-Brod pocket in May 1945.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The corps was in STAVKA reserve in June 1941 and consisted of 137th and 160th Rifle Divisions. It was reorganized as 20th Assault Corps, part of 18th Assault Landing Army at Novorossiysk in February 1943 ahead of planned amphibious operations in the Black Sea. It fought in the Kuban Bridgehead as part of 18th Army in 1943. In spring 1944, it was part of 4th Ukrainian Front, and fought in the Belorussian Offensive as part of 28th Army. In April 1944 it consisted of 55th Guards Rifle and 20th Rifle Divisions. It fought in Germany in 1945 and participated in the Battle of Berlin in April 1945. The 20th Rifle Division was formed during World War II on 21 April 1944 from the 20th Mountain Rifle Division. Fought at Krasnodar, Novorossiysk, Crimea, and near Berlin. With 28th Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front May 1945. The division inherited the 20th Mountain Rifle Division's Order of the Red Banner, was awarded another Order of the Red Banner during the war, and received the honorific 'Baranovichi'. It was also awarded the Order of Suvorov 2nd class. Thus its final title was the 20th Baranovichi twice Red Banner Order of Suvorov Rifle Division.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 20th Romanian Infantry Division did not participate in the opening phase of Operation Barbarossa and remained in Romania. In May of 1942 it was with the German XI Corps. During the Battle of Stalingrad it was part of the ill fated German Sixth Army.http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D20I.html#asEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 19th Tank Corps HQ was formed December 1942  and added units in early 1943 in the Bryansk Front.<cr>The 20th Tank Corps was an improvised unit in Bryansk Front that never really got formed until it was sent back to the training establishment in Moscow Military District in May 1943. By July 1943 when it was sent back to Bryansk Front.<cr> The 20th Tank Corps was in Bryansk Front briefly, then returned to Moscow Military District in late August. There 1419th SU Regiment was removed to refit with SU-85s.<cr> In September 1943 20th Tank Corps was sent south, first to South Front and then to 2nd Ukrainian Front by the end of the year. In October, the corps received the 406th Guards Mortar Battalion (8 BM-13 launchers).<cr>On 18 January 1944 20th Tank Corps was assigned to 5th Guards Tank Army, under which it fought during the Korsun-Shevchenkovskii Operation Jan-Feb 1944. By this time, continuous operations since September had worn the entire corps down: it started the Korsun offensive with only serviceable 51 tanks.
The fighting in the Ukraine remained heavy throughout the winter and spring of 1944: by 9 March 20th Tank Corps had just 15 T-34 tanks left operating. The 20th Tank Division was formed December 1940 in Kiev Special Military District as part of 9th Mechanized Corps. on 22 June 1941 included:<cr>
39th Tank Regiment - 1 tank bn only

20th Antiaircraft Battalion<cr><cr>The 20th Tank Division never received any modern tanks, nor in fact many tanks of any kind. On 22 June 1941, the division had only 30 BT-5, 3 T-36, and 8 OT-26 tanks on hand, and while there were 8997 total personnel assigned to the division, 20th Tank Division was short almost 75% of its required NCOs and 50% of the officers and technicians. In addition, although the howitzer and rifle regiments had all their authorized guns and heavy weapons, the division had only 244 trucks of all types and 38 tractors, so the bulk of the division's men and equipment could not be moved except on foot! If there was a bright spot anywhere in the division, it was the commander, Colonel M. Y. Katukov. Katukov was one of the best tank men in the Red Army, and ended the war as a Hero of the Soviet Union and Guards Tank Army commander.<cr>Unfortunately, Katukov was on sick leave on 22 June 1941, and the best leadership cannot make up for endemic deficiencies in training and equipment. 20th Tank Division fought under 9th Mechanized Corps across the Ukraine until early September, when both were destroyed in the Kiev encirclement. By then the division was little more than a rifle brigade; in one of its last official strength returns, on 25 August the 'division' reported a total of 2400 men, 12 guns, 6 mortars, and 0 tanks on hand.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 210th Mechanized Division was formed in March-April 1941 from 4th Cavalry Division at Osipovichi in Western Special Military District as part of 20th Mechanized Corps with: 644th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 649th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns Howitzer Regiment - 1 light bn only Antiaircraft Battalion Antitank Battalion Sapper Battalion The 210th was another division that was 'mechanized' in name only. Formed from a cavalry division, it had no tanks, no medium artillery, very few trucks, and was short over 25% of its authorized personnel on 22 June 1941. By 1 July the Soviet general staff was listing it as 'without equipment' - meaning that it had lost virtually all of its transport and heavy weapons. The last division strength report, on 7 July, listed just 5000 men and 9 guns. The division was disbanded in mid-July.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 211th Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 3rd Wave. It contained the 306th, 317th and 365th Infantry Regiments, 211th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was heavily damaged in fighting around Rozan Poland in November 1944 and was reformed as the 211th Volksgrenadier Division.<cr><cr>George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War II<cr><cr>Entry courtesy Chris Munson

At the start of the war, the 211th Soviet Rifle Division was still forming at Zagorsk, north of Moscow. In August 1941 it was assigned to the 43rd Army, Reserve Front. The division was rushed into combat and was completely destroyed in the Vyazma Pocket. It was removed from the Soviet Order of Battle by early October 1941. In late December 1941, the barely raised 429th Rifle Division was redesignated the 211th Rifle Division. The Division fought at Voronezh, Kursk (assigned to the 28th Rifle Corps, 70th Army, Central Front) and Chernigov. At the end of the war it was assigned to the 1st Guards Army, 4th Ukrainian Front, in the Balkans. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#211%E2%80%93220 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 212th Mechanized Division was formed March-April in Kiev Special Military District as part of 15th Mechanized Corps with: 587th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 669th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 131st Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Tank Bns - total 220 old light tanks 665th Howitzer Regiment - only 1 light bn Reconnaissance Batalion - included 1 light tank company with 17 tanks Antitank Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Sapper Battalion The 212th Mechanized Division had no trucks or tractors, only one medium artillery battalion (which could not move), and a collection of old light tanks inherited from a disbanded tank brigade. It fought as a part of 15th mechanized Corps until mid-July, then became a separate division in 6th Army. The fiction of its being a mechanized division was dropped in late July, when it was redesignated as 212th Rifle Division in 26th Army. Shortly afterwards, it was destroyed at Uman.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

On the 29th of July 1941, the 212th Soviet Rifle Division was formed by renaming the remnants of the 212th Mechanised Division, which had lost most of its transport. In early August 1941 it was assigned to the 38th Army, and by November 1941 was assigned to the 21st Army, Southwestern Front. The division suffered heavy losses in the defence of Stalingrad and was disbanded in November 1942. The Division was raised for the second time in June 1943, based on the 4th and 125th Rifle Brigades, and fought at Kursk assigned to the 50th Army, Western Front. At the end of the war it was assigned to the 61st Army, 1st Belorussian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#211%E2%80%93220 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

When the war started on 22 June 1941 213th Mechanized Division was almost full strength in men, but in nothing else. It had 10,021 men assigned on 1 June 1941, but only 140 trucks of all types in the division - the rifle units were virtually unmotorized, and missing about half their heavy weapons (light and medium mortars and machine guns). The howitzer and antiaircraft units were almost completely unequipped, and there were no antitank guns in the entire division. Only 48 hours after the war started, on 24 June, it was already being identified as a Rifle Division, fighting with Group Lukin to protect the big Red Army supply depot at Shepetovka.<cr>
By 10 July the tank regiment, which was never more than a single battalion, was detached to the Kiev Fortified Sector, and the rest of the division was under 6th Army as a Rifle Division when it was destroyed at Uman in early August.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

At the start of Operation Barbarossa the 213th Mechanised Division was completely lacking in transport, heavy weapons and most armoured vehicles and by the end of June 1941 was being referred to as the 213th Rifle Division. The Division was assigned to the 38th Army, Southwestern Front and was destroyed in the Uman pocket in August 1941. The Division was raised for the second time in December 1941, based on the 585th, 702nd and 793rd Rifle Brigades, at Kattakurgan in the Central Asia Military District. It took 15 months to complete its formation and in March 1943 was assigned to the 7th Guards Army, where it fought at Kursk in July 1943. The division spent most of 1944 with the 48th Rifle Corps of the 52nd Army and fought in the Vistula-Oder Offensive in January 1945, the Upper Silesia in March, the Siege of Breslau, and the Prague Offensive in May. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/213th_Rifle_Division Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 213th Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 3rd Wave. It contained the 318th, 354th and 406th Infantry Regiments, 213th Artillery Regiment and various support units. In August 1940 after the fall of France the division stood down. In March 1941 each of its three regiments was used as the foundation to form three new divisions; the 213th, 286th and 403rd Security Divisions. The 213th Security Division was attached to the German Sixth Army at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In September 1943 the division consisted of the 177th and 318th Security Regiments, 213th Cossack Battalion (mounted) and various support troops. In June 1944 the 180th Security Regiment was added. In the fall of 1944 during the withdrawal from northern Ukraine the division was heavily damaged and was disbanded in September 1944.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

At the start of the war, the 214th Soviet Rifle Division, assigned to the Kharkov Military District, was still forming at Voroshilovgrad, and was at only 40% strength. In July 1941 it was filled up with reservists, and assigned to the 22nd Army, east of Velikie Luki. By August 1941 the division was down to 2,500 men and was rebuilt in September and assigned to the 16th Army, Western Front. The division was trapped at Vyazma in October 1941 and completely destroyed. In January 1942, the division was formed for a second time at Ufa. The Division fought at Stalingrad, assigned to the 24th Army, Don Front, and at Voronezh, Kremenchug, and Kirovograd. At the end of the war it was assigned to the 52nd Army, 1st Ukrainian Front, near Prague. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#211%E2%80%93220 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 215th Mechanized Division was short about 70% of the officers needed for the tank regiment and reconnaissance battalion, and was missing almost 75% of the mechanics and technicians required in the division maintenance and supply organizations. This made the division very fragile, so that within 5 days after it went into action on 23 June 1941, 5th Army HQ was reporting that the division had 'apparently (only) remnants' left.<cr>
Nevertheless, a steady trickle of reinforcements and replacements kept a small 'rump' of the division in action with 22nd Mechanized Corps all through June, July, and early August. The unit was officially redesignated as 215th Rifle Division on 22 August. At that time the 'division' was down to 1200 men, 8 repaired T-37 tankettes, and a dozen each artillery pieces and mortars. The 215th was wiped out fighting with 5th Army in the Kiev pocket in September.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

In May 1942 the 215th Soviet Rifle Division was formed from the 48th Rifle Brigade and assigned to the reserves of the Kalinin Front. Sharp

At the start of the war, the 216th Mechanised Division, severely lacking in armored vehicles and transport, was referred to as the 216th Rifle Division. The 217th Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 3rd Wave from Landwehr personnel in East Prussia. It contained the 311th, 346th and 389th Infantry Regiments, 217th Reconnaissance Battalion, 217th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division crossed into Poland with the German Third Army in September 1939 but was not heavily engaged. The division was then assigned to garrison duty in Poland. Part of the OKH reserve during the invasion of France in 1940 it was not committed. In July 1940 the division returned to East Prussia.The division was part of the XXVI Corps in Army Group North at the start of Operation Barbarossa. It performed costal defense duties and participated in the sieges of Oranienbaum and Leningrad. In the fall of 1943 the division was sent to the Kiev region and participated in several heavy engagements. At the start of the war, the 217th Soviet Rifle Division, assigned to the 30th Rifle Corps, Orel Military District, was still forming at Voronezh, and was at only 30% strength. In July 1941 it was assigned to the 28th Army, and was fortunate to avoid encirclement at Roslavl. The Division was brought up to strength by October 1941 and survived the year assigned to the 50th Army in the Tula region. It had suffered heavy casualties and was down to 2,500 men. By late 1942 the Division was assigned to the 16th Army and in mid 1943 the division fought at Kursk with the 11th Guards Army (renamed 16th Army), Western Front. The Division fought in Belorussia, East Prussia and Courland and at the end of the war was assigned to the 48th Army, 3rd Belorussian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#211%E2%80%93220 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 218th Mechanized Division was formed February 1941 from 12th Motorized Rifle Brigade in Odessa Military District as part of 18th Mechanized Corps with: 658th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 667th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 135th Tank Regiment - 0 tanks 663rd Howitzer Regiment - 1 bn only of 12 122mm howitzers Reconnaissance Battalion Antitank Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Sapper Battalion The 218th Mechanized Division was understrength and tankless, but it did have enough trucks to motorize most of the infantry it did have, and so quickly became a Mobile Reserve division for Southern Front. As such, it fought across the southern Ukraine and Donbass until late September, when it was officially redesignated as 218th Rifle Division by adding 182nd (Reserve) Rifle Regiment to the existing divisional units.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

At the start of the war the 218th Mechanised Division was assigned to the 18th Mechanised Corps, 9th Army, Southern Front, and was close to 80% establishment, though lacking in tanks and armoured cars. In early September, 1941, this mechanised division was renamed as the 218th Rifle Division, withdrawn to the reserves of the Southern Front, and ended 1941 assigned to the 12th Army. The division was deactivated in July 1942 and was formed for a second time in mid 1943 where it assisted in the recapture of Kiev and Zhitomir, for which it was awarded the Order of the Red Banner. At this time the divisional commander, S.F. Skliarov, was killed in an air raid. At the end of the war it was assigned to the 6th Army, 1st Ukrainian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#211%E2%80%93220 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIA A. A. Maslov, Fallen Soviet Generals Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 219th Mechanized Division was formed in March 1941 in Kharkov Military District as part of 25th Mechanized Corps with: 710th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 727th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 136th Tank Regiment 673rd Howitzer Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns Reconnaissance Battalion Antitank Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Sapper Battalion The 219th Mechanized Division may have had a few tanks assigned to it by 22 June 1941, as there were some 300 tanks in the 25th Mechanized Corps. Major General Krivoshein, the corps commander, quickly grouped all his tanks in the tank divisions of the corps before they went into action, so the point is mute: 219th mechanized Division fought as a reinforced motorized rifle brigade, chronically short, as was the entire 25th Mech Corps, of artillery, antiaircraft, and trucks. The division was in action by early July, and by 14 August was effectively a rifle division, assigned to 28th Rifle Corps. By 1 September it was officially redesignated as 219th Rifle Division by adding 375th (reserve) Rifle Regiment, just in time to get caught in the Kiev pocket and destroyed in early September.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 219th Mechanised Division, assigned to the 25th Mechanized Corps, 21st Army, was mechanised in name only and fought as a rifle division in the first few months of the war. On the 9th September 1941 it was redesignated the 219th Rifle Division and was destroyed in the Kiev pocket by the end of the month. The division was formed for a second time in May 1942 and by the end of the year was assigned to the 6th Army, Voronezh Front. It fought at Kursk assigned to the 52nd Rifle Corps, 40th Army. It ended the war assigned to the 22nd Army in reserve. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#211%E2%80%93220 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 21st Army was also known as the Army Norway.The 21st Army was formed on 19 December 1940. The units of the army were absorbed by the 20th Mountain Army on 18 December 1944.On 27 April 1945, towards the end of the war in Europe, the 21st Army was reformed as part of Army Group Vistula (Heeresgruppe Weichsel) and fought until 2 May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Army_(Wehrmacht)

21st Army was a part of the Second Operational Echelon of the Red Army. It was formed from the forces of the Volga Military District in May 1941 and was initially based on 63rd Rifle Corps (53rd, 148th, and 167th Rifle Divisions) and 66th Rifle Corps. <cr>On 24 July, 21st Army came under command of the newly formed Central Front. Fedor Kuznetsov was assigned to the command of this new Front, and Lieutenant-General Mikhail Eframov was assigned as the new commander of 21st Army.<cr>21st Army, continuing to retreat to the south, became caught up in a vast encirclement that became the Battle of Kiev. During the second week of September a significant portion of 21st Army was able to escape eastwards through gaps in 2nd Panzer Group's lines between Priluki and Piriatin, but the bulk of the army found itself, together with the rest of South Western Front, in a tightening encirclement east of Kiev. Only a few thousand soldiers, mainly from 21st Army and 5th Army, together with 500 men from the headquarters staff, escaped from the final encirclement of South Western Front in the second half of September.<cr>On 26 September Colonel-General Yakov Cherevichenko was appointed to the command of the residual forces of 21st Army that had escaped encirclement at Kiev. The army grew rapidly in strength as reserves were fed into the Ukraine from the Soviet strategic reserve, so that by the beginning of October the army included three rifle divisions and five cavalry divisions.<cr> By late June 1942, 21st Army, with nine rifle divisions and a tank corps, occupied the northern flank of Southwestern Front along 100 kilometres of frontline east of Belgorod. Facing the left flank of the German Sixth Army and the right flank of the newly introduced Hungarian Second Army, was still flanked on its right by 40th Army, but 40th Army at this time constituted the southern wing of Bryansk Front which was responsible for the defence of the Voronezh axis.<cr>At the beginning of May 1943 the designation of the army, in recognition of the part it had played in the battle of Stalingrad, was changed from 21st Army to 6th Guards Army. This change of designation was not made public until July.<cr>On 12 July 1943 the 3rd Reserve Army, part of the Red Army's strategic reserve, was designated as the new formation of 21st Army. On 23 July it was transferred from the reserve to the operational army and at the beginning of August was assigned to Western Front to participate in an offensive to retake Smolensk (Operation Suvorov).<cr>At the end of October, 21st Army Headquarters was returned to the high command reserve, the army's rifle divisions having been assigned to Western Front's 33rd Army and 68th Army.<cr>At the beginning of May 1944 the headquarters of 21st Army, under the command of Lieutenant-General Dmitrii Gusev, was assigned from the reserves to Leningrad Front. Its task was to take command of forces facing the Finnish army's IV Corps in the western half of the frontline in the Karelian Isthmus north of Leningrad.<cr>Within days some of 21st Army's best units were being withdrawn for deployment to other Soviet armies further south, and by mid-July the offensive in the Karelian Isthmus had been terminated. 21st Army remained with Leningrad Front until the end of September 1944, when it was again returned to the high command reserve.<cr>On 11 December 1944 21st Army was assigned to 1st Ukrainian Front from the high command reserve. From this date 21st Army remained operationally active throughout the remainder of the war.<cr>In early May, as representatives of the German government were beginning to discuss with the Allies a general surrender of German forces, Soviet high command decided to launch a final offensive against Army Group Centre. The main objective was the capture of Prague, but other Soviet armies facing Army Group Centre's frontline further east, including 21st Army, were required to participate in placing the whole of Army Group Centre under pressure. The hurriedly prepared offensive by more than twenty Soviet armies was launched on 5 May and made rapid progress everywhere. Over the subsequent four days 21st Army advanced 70 kilometres, taking Walbrzych and crossing the Czech border to reach Jaromerz by the war's end on 9 May.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Army_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 21st Guards Rifle Division was an elite infantry division of the Red Army during World War II. It was formed from the 361st Rifle Division on March 17, 1942, in recognition of that division's successes in the attempt to encircle the German 9th Army in the Rzhev area during the Soviet winter winter counteroffensive of 1941-42. After being partially encircled itself in the spring of 1942, the division was withdrawn for rebuilding, and then played a major role in the Battle of Velikiye Luki in 1942-43. It distinguished itself in the battle for Nevel in October, 1943, for which it was awarded a battle honor. The division went on to complete a combat path through northwestern Russia and into the Baltic States, ending its war containing the German forces trapped in the Courland Peninsula.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Guards_Rifle_Division

Editor Name: 21st Hun. Infantry Brigade;121st Hun. Infantry Brigade
text: The 21st Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In the fall of 1941 the brigade was one of five brigades reduced in size and stripped of their artillery that was assigned to the Hungarian Occupation Group for security duties on the Eastern Front. At this time it was redesignated the 121st Hungarian Infantry Brigade but in February of 1942 was redesignated the 121st Light Division. In May of 1943 the unit became the 21st Light Division. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 21st Light Division was designated to be disbanded but the division remained with the Hungarian Occupation Group. In January of 1944 the Hungarian First Army to which the division was then subordinate, mobilized to defend Hungary's northern Carpathian frontier against the advancing Red Army. The division was disbanded in May 1944.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 21st Infantry Division crossed into Russia with Army Group North, swept through the Baltic States, fought in the battles of Tilsit, Volkhov and Grusino, and broke through the Soviet defensive positions on the Msta River, the last natural barrier before Leningrad. The division spent the next three years in northern Russia, participated in the Siege of Leningrad, fought in the Battle of Volkhov (1942), and in the Second Battle of Lake Ladoga in early 1943. It was reorganized as a six-grenadier-battalion (Type 44) division on October 2, 1943. After distinguishing itself during the retreat from Leningrad, the 21st was transferred by Army Group Center in the fall of 1944. It was smashed in the Russian invasion of East Prussia, but the survivors of the unit continued to resist-at battle group strength-until the fall of the Third Reich. The remnants of the 21st Infantry Division were still in East Prussia (in the Hela sector) at the end of the war.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 21st Mechanized Corps was initially formed in March 1941, in response to the German victories in the West it was attached to the newly forming 27th Army, and held in reserve near Opochka in Soviet Union 130 kilometres (81 mi) South of Pskov in the Special Baltic Military District. It was under the command of Major General Lelyushenko when the German Operation Barbarossa began in June 1941. It initially consisted of the 42nd and 46th Tank Divisions, and the 185th Mechanized Division. After the Invasion began the Special Baltic Military District was renamed Northwestern Front, Commanded by Colonel General Kutznetsov. The front fielded 8th and 11th Armies with the 27th Armies in its second echelon. The 21st Mechanized was heavily engaged in the first battles of Operation Barbarossa, particularly during the Baltic Operation (1941). After the spectacular advances by 4th Panzer Group Kutznetsov asked Stavka for the release of Berzarin's 27th Army and the 21st Mechanized Corps on 25 June and was ordered to halt Erich von Manstein's LVI Panzer Corps which was closing up to the Daugava River later that day both units engaged near Dvinsk.<cr>Next Army Group North sent a special force which captured the bridges at Daugavpils and consolidated with 8th Panzer Division. As the fighting intensified elements of 21st Mechanized Corps broke into the Northern suburbs of the town, with fierce house-to-house fighting. After failing to clear Daugavpils further fighting and attacks by the Luftwaffe succeeded in wearing down its forces during the next two days to the extent that by 29 June it had only seven operational tanks, 74 artillery pieces and slightly more than 4,000 men left and was exhausted as a fighting force. On 30 June the Soviet Air Force put in an all out effort which resulted in the loss of 43 aircraft (27 DB-3s and SBs for only four Bf 109s) but did not succeed in destroying the principal river crossings over the Daugava River but did succeed in destroying some pontoon bridges. After continuing a fighting retreat through the Baltic states in July, but in remnants, the 21st Mechanized Corps was disbanded in August 1941.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Mechanized_Corps_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The corps was at Vitebsk in June 1941 as part of 13th Army and consisted of 17th, 24th, 37th and 50th Rifle Divisions. It advanced into the vicinity of Minsk and was cut off and destroyed in July. The corps was reformed in January 1943 at Voronezh and fought in the Kiev Operation as part of 38th Army. In January 1944, it consisted of 100th, 135th and 155th Rifle Divisions. It fought in Hungary in 1944 andtook part in the Siege of Budapest. Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 21st Romanian Infantry Division was attached to the Romanian V Corps at the start of Operation Barbarossa. As with most Romanian infantry divisions it was withdrawn to Romania after the Siege of Odessa. The division was on garrison duty in Russia and Romania until it participated in the defense of Romania in 1944.http://www.geocities.ws/dangrecu/D21I.html#asEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 21st Tank Corps was formed in early April 1942 in Southwestern Front as 1st Mechanized
Corps with the 198th and 199th Tank Brigades. By the end of April the corps was redesignated as 21st Tank Corps, and consisted of:<cr>
64th Tank Brigade
297th, 298th Tank Battalions
64th Motorized Rifle Battalion
198th Tank Brigade
196th, 197th Tank Battalions
198th Motorized Rifle Battalion
199th Tank Brigade
291st, 292nd Tank Battalions
199th Motorized Rifle Battalion
21st Motorized Rifle Brigade (not added until early May)
1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Battalions
1st Motorcycle Battalion<cr><cr>The 21st Tank Corps was formed by Southwestern Front in 6th Army. The Southwestern Front command apparently had not gotten the word that the new multibrigade formations would be called 'Tank Corps', and not named after the Mechanized Corps of 1941 - for a month the Front command was referring to 3
'mechanized corps' in various stages of formation before they renamed them. 21st Tank Corps had the shortest career of any of the wartime tank corps. It was barely formed with brand-new brigades, all of them formed early in 1942, when it was committed to the Kharkov Operation in May 1942. The corps was cut off by the German counter-attack and destroyed early in June. Some of its component brigades survived, at least as a cadre for later units, but 21st Tank Corps was never reformed.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 220th Mechanized Division was formed in March-April 1941 in Orel Military District as part of 23rd Mechanized Corps with: 653rd Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 673rd Motorized Rifle Regiment1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 137th Tank Régiment - 0 tanks 660th Howitzer Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Bns Reconnaissance Battalion Antitank Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion 381st Sapper Battalion The 220th Mechanized Division was 'effectively a rifle division', since the majority of the moorization and all the tanks in 23rd Mechanized Corps went into the tank divisions of that corps. Even its artificial designation as a mechanized unit did not survive the first counterattacks launched by the corps under 19th Army in early July: by mid-July 220th was officially reformed as 220th Rifle Division by adding 376th (reserve) Rifle Regiment to the division.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 220th Mechanised Division, assigned to the 23rd Mechanized Corps, Orel Military District, was mechanised in name only and fought as a rifle division in the first few months of the war, assigned to the 19th Army. On the 21st of July 1941 it was redesignated the 220th Rifle Division. It was withdrawn from the front to be rebuilt but was destroyed in the Vyazma pocket in October 1941. The division was formed for a second time in November 1941, from remnants that escaped the pocket, and was assigned to the 22nd Army, Kalinin Front. In May 1942 it was withdrawn to regroup and be rebuilt and was assigned to the 31st Army. It fought with distinction at Rzhev, the liberation of Smolensk where it had to be reinforced no less than four times, and at Orsha, Minsk and Grodno. It ended the war near Prague. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov and the honorifics of Orsha and Minsk. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/220th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 221st Mechanized Divison was formed March-April 1941 from 19th Cavalry Division in Central Asia Military District as part of 27th Mechanized Corps with: 625th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 671st Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 659th Howitzer Regiment 2 light bns only Reconnaissance Battalion Antitank Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Sapper Battalion The 221st.Mechanized Division was formed from a Mountain Cavalry Division, which meant that the cadre of the division had no motorized equipment and no experience with it. The division's tank regiment was never formed, since the division never received any tanks. Along with the rest of 27th Mechanized Corps, the division went to the front in July, to 28th Army. While the two tank divisions of the corps (9th and 53rd Tank Divisions) were used to form 104th Tank Division, 221st went into action as a rifle division and was annihilated in the Smolensk battle in July 1941.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 221st Rifle Division was established at Krasnoufimsk 3.42, fought at Stalingrad and inactivated 11.42. Recreated 6.43 from the 79th Rifle Brigade. Fought in East Prussia. With 39th Army of the RVGK 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 221st Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 3rd Wave. It contained the 350th, 360th and 375th Infantry Regiments, 221st Artillery Regiment and various support units. In August 1940 after the fall of France the division stood down. In March 1941 each of its three regiments was used as the foundation to form three new divisions; the 221st, 444th and 454th Security Divisions. The 221st Security Division was attached to the German 4th Army at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In October 1942 the 1st East and 2nd East Cavalry Hundertschaft as well as the 221st Cavalry Hundertschaft were added to the division. By February 1944 the division was in West Ruthenia and consisted of the 34th and 75th Security Regiments, two attached security battalions and various support troops. One battalion of the 75th Regiment was Lithuanian. In July 1944 the division was destroyed. It was officially disbanded in November 1944.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 222nd Rifle Division was established at Starodub Apr 1941. Fought at Yelnya, Moscow, Mozhaisk, Smolensk, Lenino, Kalinin, and Mogilev. With 33rd Army of the 1st Belorussian Front May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 223rd Rifle Division was a Azeri national formation. Established at Kuba 9.41, fought at Terek River, and in the Caucasus and the Ukraine, and later in Yugoslavia. With 46th Army of the 2nd Ukrainian Front in May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 225th Rifle Division was established at Yerevan 10.41, fought at Novgorod and Kattowitz. With 21st Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 226th Rifle Division was established at Orochevo 6.41, fought at Kharkov, inactivated 7.42. Recreated at Bugurusslan 9.42 and became 95th Guards Rifle Division 4.5.43. Created again at Lgov 7.43, fought at Kiev and Debica. With 38th Army of the 4th Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 227th Rifle Division was established at Slavyansk 4.41, wiped out at Kharkov 5.42. Recreated from 19th Rifle and 84th Naval Rifle Brigades summer 1942, fought at Kursk and in the Crimea. With 53rd Army of the 2nd Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 228th Rifle Division was established at Zhitomir prior to 6.41 and wiped out at Kiev 9.41. Recreated at Kansk 11.41, fought at Stalingrad and in the Ukraine. With 53rd Army of the 2nd Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 229th Rifle Division was established at Noginsk 5.41, fought at Stalingrad and wiped out at Kalach 8.42. Recreated at Volokolamsk 12.42, fought at Opole. With 1st Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

In the Russian invasion the 22nd Air Landing was equipped as a standard line unit and fought as a regular infantry force under the 11th Army, Army Group South. Attacking out of Romania, it was the first German division to penetrate the Dnieper line and also fought on the Pruth, Dnestr, and Bug. It overran the Perekop Isthmus and took part in the initial assault on Sevastopol, where it suffered heavy losses. On June 28, 1942, combat elements of the 22nd Air Landing, along with the 24th Infantry Division, crossed a thousand-yard-wide stretch of North Bay in rubber rafts and landed in the Russian rear, east of the city. Russian resistance in Sevastopol, which had been fierce, crumbled rapidly after this highly successful surprise attack.Following the clearing of the Crimea in early July, the 22nd Air Landing was returned to Germany, once more re-equipped as an air landing division and was sent to Crete.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 22nd Army was formed in June 1941 and it comprised 51st Rifle Corps (98th, 112th, and 153rd Rifle Divisions) and 62nd Rifle Corps (170th, 174th, and 186th Rifle Divisions), and several separate regiments, including the 336th and 545th Corps Artillery Regiments. Headquarters was at Velikiye Luki by 22 June 1941, and General Lieutenant F. A. Yershakov took command (who would direct the army until August 1941).<cr>During the Battle of Smolensk (1941), six rifle divisions of the army fought fiercely against sixteen Wehrmacht divisions, including three tank and three motorized, and under their assault 22nd Army was forced to retreat. On July 16, 1941, the Germans managed to surround the 51st Rifle Corps, and on July 20, to seize Velikiye Luki. 48th Tank Division joined the Army by August 1, 1941.<cr>As part of the Soviet Western Front, since October, 17th the Kalinin Front, the Army conducted defensive operations on the Idritsa-Drissa-Vitebsk frontier, participated in the Battle of Smolensk, the Kalinin defensive operation, and the Battles of Rzhev - Operation Mars in 1942. General Major V. A. Yushkevich again took command in April 1942, after previously commanding the army in August-October 1941. 3rd Mechanised Corps under General Major M. Ye. Katukov joined the Army in September 1942 when it was formed, though it was later reassigned.<cr>The Army's task as part of Operation Mars was as part of what in Soviet parlance was the Bely Offensive Operation in conjunction with 39th Army. Spearheaded by the 3rd Mechanised Corps, the army was tasked to: 'advance eastward up the Luchesa River valley, pierce the German defenses, assist in the capture of Bely, and encircle German forces around Olenino in conjunction with 39th Army. Early on 25 November, 22nd Army, with over 50,000 men and 270 tanks of 3rd Mechanised Corps, assaulted eastward up the Luchesa River valley. Attacking along a narrow corridor flanked by forests and frozen swamps, Soviet forces tore a gaping hole through German defences and drove German forces eastward up the valley. General Yushkevich's attack was spearheaded by Colonel I. V. Karpov's 238th Rifle Division and two regiments of Colonel M. F. Andryushenko's 185th Rifle Division, supported by a tank brigade of General Katukov's mechanised corps. The combined force routed a regiment of the German 86th Infantry Division and punctured the German front.'<cr>In 1943, the Army fought as part of the North-Western Front since April 21, then from October 13 as part of the Baltic Front, which became 2nd Baltic Front on October 20, 1943. 22nd Army defended the river Lovat, and participated in operations at Kholm, Velikiye Luki, Leningrad-Novgorod, Staraya Russa-Novorzhev, and Rezhitsa-Dvina. It then took part in the Riga Offensive Operation, part of the Baltic Offensive. In October 1944, together with the other armies of the Front it carried out the blockade of the German Army Group Courland in the Courland Pocket. One of the Army's rifle corps was the Latvian 130th Rifle Corps that included two rifle divisions in which served a large number of Latvians in their ranks who would soon be facing their opposites in the Latvian 19th Waffen Grenadier Division of the SS.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22nd_Army_(Russia)</url>

The 22nd Guards Rifle Division was unique in being the only Guards rifle division formed twice during WWII. It was first formed from the 363rd Rifle Division in March, 1942. Soon after forming it provided a command cadre for the second formation of the 53rd Army in Kalinin Front. Later, in the fall of that year, the division provided most of its personnel and equipment to form the new 2nd Guards Mechanized Corps, and was then disbanded. In April, 1943, a new 22nd Guards was formed from the second formation of the 150th Rifle Division in the Moscow Military District, and went on to serve for the duration in 10th Guards Army, winning a battle honor for its part in the liberation of Riga, before ending the war in Lithuania, helping to contain the German forces trapped in the Courland Pocket.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/363rd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 22nd Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 22nd Light Division. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 22nd Light Division was merged with other units and disbanded.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The corps was created after the occupation of Estonia in 1940 as the Estonian Territorial Corps, and it consisted of the 180th and 182nd Rifle Divisions. It was part of 27th Army. It fought in the vicinity of Pskov in July and saw many Estonian personnel defect after the Germans captured Estonia. The corps fought around Staraya Russa on the Lovat River in August and was disbanded at the end of August. The corps was reformed in February 1943 and consisted of 112th, 135th, 181st and 273rd Rifle Divisions. In November 1943, it participated as part of 18th Army in the Kerch-Eltigen Operation. At that time, it consisted of 117th and 129th Guards Rifle Divisions and 317th and 318th Rifle Divisions. It was part of 3rd Guards Army from July 1944 to the end of the war. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22nd_Rifle_Corps Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 22nd Tank Corps was formed in early April 1942 in Southwestern Front as 2nd Mechanized Corps. Renamed as 22nd Tank Corps by the end of April with:<cr>
13th Tank Brigade
1st, 2nd Tank Battalions
13th Motorized Rifle Battalion<cr>36th Tank Brigade
173rd, 174th Tank Battalions
36th Motorized Rifle Battalion
133rd Tank Brigade
1st, 2nd Tank Battalions
133rd Motorized Rifle Battalion<cr><cr>The 22nd Tank Corps was committed with 38th Army in the Kharkov Operation, and managed to survive that fiasco despite being barely formed when the battle started. Retreating across southern Russia, 22nd Tank Corps went through the same shuffling of its tank brigades that 13th Tank Corps did.<cr>In July, 22nd Tank Corps was part of 4th Tank Army when that army was formed. At that time the entire army had so little armor left it was derisively referred to as the 'Four-Tank Army' by Soviet officers!<cr>Unfortunately, most of these brigades had been rushed forward from across the Volga River with little training or cohesion. They melted away in battles west of the Don River in front of Stalingrad, and by the end of August 22nd Tank Corps was in Stalingrad Front reserves as a 'holding' unit controlling various tank brigades that had been shot up in battle and were awaiting replacement tanks and crews. In September 22nd Tank Corps HQ was evacuated to Moscow Military District to form cadre for 5th Mechanized Corps.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 22nd Tank Division was formed February 1941 from 29th Tank Brigade in Western Special Military District as part of 14th Mechanized Corps. On 22 June 1941 included: 43rd Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Tank Bns - each 30 to 33 T-26 tanks 44th Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Tank Bns - each 30 to 33 T-26 tanks 22nd Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns 22nd Motorized Howitzer Regiment 1 light, 1 medium bn 22nd Reconnaissance Battalion 22nd Motorized Pontoon Battalion 22nd Antiaircraft Battalion - 2 batteries of 37mm onlyThe 22nd Tank Division 'was essentially just a tank brigade' according to the official Soviet report on the division. It never received any more tanks than the 235 T-26 tanks in the old 29th Tank Brigade. It did have all its authorized artillery and heavy weapons, but the division was stationed so close to the border that it came under German artillery fire while still in barracks on the first morning of the war! At 0500 hours on the 24th of June the divisional commander, V P Puganov, was killed by artillery fire and buried in a communal grave.After that inauspicious beginning, the division went into action against Guderian's 2nd Panzer Group as unsupported light tank battalions, since most of the howitzers were captured while still sitting in garrison and the rifle regiment dispersed into the Pripyet marshes. By 1000 hrs on 22 June 1941 the division was down to just 60 T-26 tanks. The last of the division elements were destroyed in the Minsk encirclement in mid-July.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 230th Rifle Division was established at Dnipropetrovsk Jul 1941. Fought in Uman Pocket Aug 1941. Inactivated Aug 1942. Recreated from 229th Rifle Brigade Jun 1943. Fought at Stalino and Berlin. With 5th Shock Army of the 1st Belorussian Front May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#221%E2%80%93230

The 231st Rifle Division was established Kungur 1941, near Stalingrad 8.42 and inactivated 11.42. Recreated; with the 1st Red Banner Army of the independent coastal group in the Far East 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#231%E2%80%93240

The 232nd Rifle Division was established at Chernigov prior to 6.41 and wiped out at Kiev 9.41. Recreated at Biysk 1.42, fought at Voronezh, Kiev, and Iasi. With 40th Army of the 2nd Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#231%E2%80%93240

The 233rd Rifle Division was established at Zvenigorod 5.41 and wiped out at Smolensk 9.41. Recreated at Naro Fominsk 8.42, fought at Stalingrad, Kremenchug, Iasi, and in Hungary. With 26th Army of the 3rd Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#231%E2%80%93240

The 234th Rifle Divisoin was established at Kostroma from Yaroslavl Home Guard Division 6.41, fought on central part of front and in Warsaw. With 61st Army of the 1st Belorussian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#231%E2%80%93240

The 235th Rifle Division was established at Nikopol May 1941. Wiped out vicinity Luga Sep 1941. Recreated at Novosibirsk Mar 1942. Fought on central part of front, and at Vitebsk and Königsberg. With 43rd Army of the 2nd Belorussian Front Front May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#231%E2%80%93240

The 239th Infantry Divison crossed into Russia in July 1941 and took part in the battles in the Ukraine. It was especially heavily engaged at Kharkov. The 239th was disbanded on January 1, 1942, because of the excessive age of its men and the casualties it suffered in Russia.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 23rd Guards Rifle Division was reformed as an elite infantry division of the Red Army in March, 1942, based on the 1st formation of the 88th Rifle Division, and served in that role until after the end of WWII. It was one of just two Guards divisions to be formed in the far north, the 10th Guards being the other. It continued to serve in Karelian Front, where it was formed, until October when it was railed south to join the 1st Shock Army of Northwestern Front; it would remain in that Army until nearly the end of 1944. Over the next several months it took part in the dismal fighting around the Demyansk salient until March, 1943. During the rest of the year the division continued battling through the forests and swamps south of Lake Ilmen, occasionally under command of the 14th Guards Rifle Corps, until the Leningrad-Novgorod Offensive began in late January, 1944. The 23rd Guards took part in the liberation of Staraya Russa in mid-February and went on to win a battle honor about a week later at Dno. 1st Shock Army (now in 2nd Belorussian Fronts) closed up to the German Panther Line south of Lake Peipus during the spring and then helped break through it at the start of the Baltic Campaign in July. For its part in the liberation of Ostrov the division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner before gradually advancing through Latvia towards Riga, which it helped to liberate in October. By now it was in the 12th Guards Rifle Corps which was transferred in late November to the 3rd Shock Army in 1st Belorussian Front. The 23rd Guards would remain under these commands for the duration of the war, advancing across Poland and eastern Germany into Berlin in 1945 and winning a second honorific after the fighting ended. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd_Guards_Rifle_Division

Editor Name: 23rd Hun. Infantry Brigade;23rd Hun. Reserve Division
text: The 23rd Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 23rd Light Division. The Hungarian Government reluctantly agreed to support the Germans 1942 summer offensive Fall Blau and allocated the division as part of the Hungarian Second Army to the task. Each light division in the Second Army was reinforced with three battalions from sister divisions in Hungary but nonetheless each division was only slightly larger than half the size of its German counterparts. Second Army's role in the offensive was to guard the German northern flank on the Don River. During the Stalingrad Campaign the Second Army suffered over 60% casualties but was generally able to retreat in good order. By February of 1943 the division had been assigned to security duties with the Hungarian Occupation Group. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 23rd Light Division was merged with other units and renamed the 23rd Reserve Division. In September 1944 the division was part of the Third Hungarian Army defending Hungary's southern border. The division was disbanded in May 1945.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 23rd Infantry Division crossed the Dnieper with the 2nd Panzer Army on the central sector and fought at Bialstok, Minsk and Smolensk. It took part in the Siege of Mogilev on the Dnieper from July 20-26, where it lost more than 1,000 men, and in the defensive battle of Vyazma (September-October). The 23rd Infantry pushed on to the gates of Moscow, suffering heavy casualties along the way. By January 1942, it had barely 1,000 infantrymen left, and its nine infantry battalions were consolidated into three because of casualties. The divisional artillery was down to one 50mm anti-tank gun and three howitzers. It was surrounded south of Fedorovka by the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42. Relieved, the 23rd Infantry remained on the central sector around Gshatsk until summer 1942, when it was sent to Amiens, France, to reform as the 26th Panzer Division.The second 23rd Infantry Division was assembled in Denmark and Potsdam on October 23, 1942. It adopted the regimental numbers of the original 23rd. Cadres for the new division were provided by the old 23rd Infantry Division. The 67th Grenadier Regiment received the honorary title 'von Seeckt' to honor Colonel General Hans von Seeckt, who had created the Reichswehr in the early 1920s. The 68th Regiment received the honorary title 'Fusilier' in late 1942, but its organization and equipment were no different from that of a standard grenadier regiment.The new division was sent into action on the Eastern Front in early 1943 and fought on the northern sector. It was involved in the Siege of Leningrad from February to August 1943. Because of heavy casualties, three of its grenadier battalions were dissolved in September 1943. Briefly sent to Army Group Center in the fall of 1943, it fought in the defensive Battle of Nevel but was returned to Army Group North in February 1944 after the Russians broke the siege of Leningrad. Later the division withdrew through Estonia, and defended Saareman Island (Osel) in autumn 1944, against overwhelming Russian landings. It was, however, successfully evacuated by the German Navy. After this battle, the 9th Grenadier Regiment was disbanded. By October, it was defending in the Courland Pocket, but in January 1945, the remnants of this veteran but depleted division were evacuated by sea to northern Germany and sent to Army Group Center in East Prussia, where it remained until the fall of Berlin. It surrendered to the Russians.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 23rd Mechanized Corps was formed in March 1941 in the Oryol Military District at Voronezh. The corps included the 48th and 51st Tank Divisions, and the 220th Motorized Division. The 48th was at Voronezh, the 51st at Bryansk, and the 220th at Yelets. The corps was commanded by Major General Mikhail Myasnikov.<cr>The corps was assigned to support the 24th Army on 27 June, but due to the slow deployment of the 25th Mechanized Corps was reassigned to the 19th Army on 1 July. The corps moved to the Vitebsk and Liozno region.  At this time the corps had 413 tanks. These included 21 new KV tanks and T-34 medium tanks. The 51st Tank Division was sent to Rzhev to support the reserve armies. On 9 July the 220th Motorized Division was ordered into action with the 19th Army, without the rest of the 23rd Mechanized Corps, which had not yet arrived in the area. On 10 July, the 51st Tank Division was assigned to the 31st Army. The 57th Tank Division was assigned to the corps to replace the 51st Division but never joined it, instead moving to Orsha in support of the 20th Army. On 11 July, the corps became part of 19th Army reserve in the Mogilno and Berezino region. The 48th Tank Division was sent to the Nevel region and became part of the 22nd Army on 12 July to lead the army's counterattack. As a result of these changes, the corps did not fight as a unit.<cr>The perechen (list of Soviet units during World War II) states that the corps was converted into the 23rd Rifle Corps (Second Formation) on 20 July. Corps deputy commander Yakov Sharaburko became commander of the 23rd Rifle Corps, part of the 24th Army. On 1 August it included the 100th Rifle Division and the 194th Mountain Rifle Division.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd_Mechanized_Corps_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 23rd Rifle Division was formed in July 1922 from the predecessor Zavolzhskaya Rifle Brigade. In May 1932 the division was awarded the Order of Lenin for helping to construct the Kharkov Tractor Factory. For its service at Stalingrad it was renamed the 71st Guards Rifle Division. A new 23rd Rifle Division was formed in May 1943 from the 7th Rifle and 76th Naval Infantry Brigades in the Steppe Military District. The division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, the Order of Suvorov 2nd class, and the Order of Kutuzov 2nd class for its actions. The division also received the honorifics 'Kiev' and 'Zhitomir'. The division was disbanded in Germany at the end of the war.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 23rd SS Panzergrenadier Division began its career as the SS Volunteer Legion 'Niederlande'. It was formed in Krakow (Krakau), Poland, from Dutch volunteers who joined the SS to fight communism. Initially it consisted of the 1st and 2nd SS Volunteer Panzer Grenadier Regiments 'Nederland', as well as a two battalion artillery regiment, tank destroyer, engineer and field replacement battalions, a reconnaissance company and a signal company. It distinguished itself in its first action (on the northern sector of the Eastern Front) where, in June 1942, it attacked and destroyed a much larger Soviet force, taking 3,500 prisoners in the process, including General Andrey Vlasov, the future commander of the Russian Liberation Army (ROA). The Legion was then shifted north, where it took part in the Siege of Leningrad and in the Second Battle of Lake Lagoda.The Legion was sent back to the Netherlands in early 1943 to rest, recruit and expand. It was upgraded to the 4th SS Volunteer Panzer Grenadier Brigade on October 23, 1943, and its panzer grenadier regiments became the 48th SS Volunteer Panzer Grenadier Regiment 'General Seyffardt' and the 49th SS Volunteer Panzer Grenadier Regiment 'De Ruiter', respectively. The Dutch Legion/Brigade served in the Balkans until December 1943, when it was sent to the Leningrad sector. It joined the III Panzer Corps and fought in the Siege of Oranienbaum, in the retreat from Leningrad, in the fierce battles on the Narva, and in the first battles of the Courland Pocket. The 48th SS Volunteer Panzer Grenadier Regiment and most of the division’s artillery regiment were destroyed in Operation Bagration (June–July 1944). The division was transported to Stettin, Pomerania, by ship in early 1945, and, on February 10, was upgraded to divisional status as the 23rd SS Volunteer Panzer Grenadier Division 'Nederland', although without any change to its table of organization and equipment and without any reinforcements.
