(It had only about 1,000 men left at this time, and its 48th SS Volunteer Regiment had been reduced from a strength of 2,000 men to eighty men.) It was sent to the Oder sector and was trapped in the huge Halbe Pocket southeast of Berlin. Here it surrendered to the Soviets on or about April 29, 1945.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 23rd Tank Corps was formed April 1942 in Southwestern Front as 3rd Mechanized Corps.<cr>The 23rd Tank Corps was formed with experienced tank brigades, at least:130th and 131st were both formed from the 8th Tank Division in 1941, and 6th Tank Brigade was formed from the 6th Tank Division. Unfortunately, in its first actions in the Battle of Kharkov in May, the Soviet command switched brigades back and forth between direct support missions in the rifle armies and operational missions with the tank corps. At various times in May and June 1942 23rd Tank Corps not only controlled its 'own' tank brigades, but also 57th, 65th, or 114th Tank Brigades.<cr>At that time the entire 4th Tank Army only had a handful of tanks left. As tank brigade remnants were evacuated to the rear to reform, 23rd Tank Corps was moved to 1st Tank Army in late July.<cr>From late August to October 1942, 23rd Tank Corps was under 62nd Army, acting as a 'holding HQ' for shot-up tank brigades.<cr>Finally, in October 1942 the corps was evacuated across the Volga into the tank training areas of Volga Military District. There, in November - December 1942, the corps was rebuilt. In late December it went back to the front in
Southwestern Front reserves.<cr>The 23rd Tank Corps took part in operations in the Donbass with Southwestern Front and 3rd Guards Army. As a result of the heavy casualties suffered in these battles, the corps went into reserve in Southwestern Front in March 1943. It remained in reserve until August 1943, when the advance to the Dnepr River began. By that time the corps had been built up to the 1943 standard.<cr>The 23rd Tank Corps kept these same components for the rest of 1943 and most of 1944, only adding a third tank battalion to each tank brigade late in 1943 and gradually replacing the light tanks in the brigades with all T-34s. The corps also spent the rest of the war in the southern portion of the front, with either 2nd or 3rd Ukrainian Front. From July to Octoberl944 the 23rd Tank Corps was paired with 5th Guards Cavalry Corps in Gorshkov's Cavalry Mechanized Group for the lasi-Kishinev Operation and the advance through Rumania into Hungary. In November the corps received its first structural change in over a year when 1669th Light Artillery Regiment (24 76rnm guns) was assigned. The 23rd Tank Corps ended the war in May 1945 in 2nd Ukrainian Front reserves in Austria.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 23rd Tankd Division was formed February 1941 from 6th and 22nd Tank Brigades in Baltic Special Military District as part of 12th Mechanized Corps. On 22 June 1941 included:<cr>
45th Tank Regiment
46th Tank Regiment
23rd Motorized Rifle Regiment
23rd Motorized Howitzer Regiment
23rd Motorized Pontoon Battalion
23rd Reconnaissance Battalion
23rd Antiaircraft Battalion<cr><cr>Formed from existing tank brigades, by 22 June 1941 23rd Tank Division was at nearly full strength in personnel, artillery, heavy weapons, and had over 75% of its authorized trucks - a much better percentage than normal in Soviet motorized units in 1941. Unfortunately, it only had about half its authorized tanks, and of the 230 tanks, all were light BT and T-26 tanks and 16% of them were in need of repair before the war even started. In other specific shortages, the divisional reconnaissance battalion had no headquarters or staff organized, and there were less than 20% of the authorized armored cars available.<cr>23rd Tank Division was ordered to counterattack German advancing units on the first day of the war in the Baltic. In moving to the front, the division came under heavy air attacks. To build up more armor for the attack, 28th Tank Division's 55th Tank regiment was added to the division late on 23 June. In the ensuing tank battles throughout 24 June, most of the tanks in all three tank regiments were either destroyed or overrun by the German armor.<cr>23rd Tank Division remained in the Soviet order of battle under 12th Mechanized Corps until early August, when it was officially disbanded.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 240th Rifle Division was established at Kupyansk prior to 6.41 and wiped out at Kiev 9.41. Recreated at Kupyansk 10.41, fought at Kursk, Kiev, Targul Frumos, and in the Carpathians. With 40th Army of the 2nd Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#231%E2%80%93240

The 240th Mechanized Division was formed in March-April 1941 at Kupyansk in Kharkov Military District with: 836th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 842nd Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Rifle Bns 692nd Howitzer Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Bns Reconnaissance Battalion Antitank Battalion Antiaircraft Battalion Sapper Battalion The 240th Mechanized Division moved to Kamenets-Podolsk in Kiev Special Military District in May to become part of 16th Mechanized Corps in 12th Army. Since it was missing any semblance of armor and most of its motorization, the division mostly fought as separate supporting rifle units with the tank divisions in 16th Mechanized Corps. By August the division was reduced to a handful of rifle troops, and was sent back to Kharkov to be reformed as a Rifle Division by 1 September 1941.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 241st Rifle Division was established at Vishniy Volocheck 10.41, fought at Kursk, Vinnitsa, and in the Carpathians. With 38th Army of the 4th Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#241%E2%80%93250

The 242nd Mountain Rifle Division was established at Moscow 7.41 and inactivated 10.41. Recreated at Grozny 3.42, fought at Mount Elbrus, in the Kuban and Taman Peninsula, at Kerch and Sevastopol. With 60th Army of the 4th Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#241%E2%80%93250

The 243rd Rifle Division was one of a series of 15 divisions formed from cadres of NKVD border troops as standard Red Army rifle divisions, very shortly after the German invasion, in the Moscow Military District. It served in the heavy fighting around Smolensk in Smolensk, then later in the defensive operations around Kalinin. It then saw extensive service in the severe fighting around Rzhev, before being moved south in the winter of 1942-43. In the following winter the division was recognized for its role in the liberation of Nikopol, receiving that place name as an honorific. After battling through Ukraine, Romania, Hungary and Austria, the 243rd completed a very complex combat path by ending the war in Manchuria and earning a second honorific.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/243rd_Rifle_Division

The 244th Rifle Division was established at Dimitrov 7.41 and wiped out at Vyazma 10.41. Recreated and merged with 469th Rifle Division at Stalingrad, fought at Zaporozhye. With 37th Army in Bulgaria 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#241%E2%80%93250

The 245th Rifle Division was established at Vishniy Volocheck 7.41, fought at Kattowitz. With 59th Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#241%E2%80%93250

The 246th Rifle Division was established at Rybinsk 7.41, fought at Kursk, in the Crimea, and at Krakow. With 60th Army of the 4th Ukrainian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#241%E2%80%93250

The 247th Rifle Division was established at Murom 7.41, fought at Kursk, the Pulawy bridgehaed, and Berlin. 69th Army of the 1st Belorussian Front 5.45.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#241%E2%80%93250

The 248th Rifle Division was established at Vyazma Jul 1941; wiped out there Oct 1941. Recreated at Astrakhan May 1942. Fought near Kharkov May 1942 and wiped out at Izyum May 1942. Recreated at Astrakhan Jul 1942. Fought at Stalingrad, in the Ukraine and Pomerania, and at Berlin. With 5th Shock Army of the 1st Belorussian Front May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#241%E2%80%93250

The division began organizing on June 26, 1941, in the Urals Military District. It was one of a series of rifle divisions numbered in the 240–260 range that were built on cadres taken from the NKVD.<cr><cr>The division was assigned to 31st Army of Reserve Front until October, giving its troops more time to form up and train than many other divisions in that period. During that month it was assigned to 22nd Army in Kalinin Front, which was rebuilding after being partly overrun by the Germans in September. In December the 249th was transferred again to 27th Army, which was soon renamed 4th Shock Army.<cr><cr>The division led the attack of its Army in January 1942, advancing over 100 km through deep snow and without regular supplies until capturing the German supply base at Toropets on January 21. For its efforts in this offensive, the 249th Rifle Division was re-designated as the 16th Guards Rifle Division on February 16.<cr><cr>A new division, originally designated the 423rd Rifle Division, then the 2nd Estonian Rifle Division, began forming on Feb. 10, 1942 in the Chelyabinsk Oblast of the Urals Military District. On Feb. 28 it was finally re-designated as the 249th Estonian Rifle Division. The division stayed in the Urals until September, then was shipped to the Moscow Military District where it joined the 7th Estonian and the 19th Guards Rifle Divisions to form the 8th Estonian Rifle Corps. The 249th remained in that Corps for the duration.<cr><cr>In November the corps was assigned to Kalinin Front, and reinforced 3rd Shock Army in its attack against German Third Panzer Army in and around the city of Velikiye Luki. Its first battle was costly, and in spite of receiving the 162nd Machinegun Battalion and a training battalion as replacements in December, by the end of the battle on Feb. 1, 1943, the 249th was at about 50% strength, with a total of 4,213 officers and men. The division and its corps remained directly under Front command (in October Kalinin Front became 2nd Baltic Front) for the remainder of the year, attacking alongside 4th Shock Army towards Vitebsk in the Battle of Nevel in November and December.

In February, 1944, 8th Corps was reassigned to the reserves of Leningrad Front, following the breaking of the German siege and that Front's advance towards the Baltic States. Once the 249th entered Estonia it could draw on the local population for replacements. By August it was at a strength of 7,946 officers and men, making it a very strong rifle division for that stage of the war. In September, 8th Corps became part of 8th Army, which was clearing the coasts of Estonia and Latvia as well as the islands offshore. On Oct. 6, the 1st Battalion of the 925th Rifle Regiment, along with the 328th Reconnaissance Company, staged an amphibious assault on one of these islands, mounted on US Lend Lease DUKW amphibious trucks of the 283rd Special Purpose Truck Battalion. During this year the division as a whole was awarded the honorific 'Tartu' for assisting in the liberation of that city, as well as the Order of the Red Banner on October 22.<cr><cr>In February, 1945, 8th Corps returned to 2nd Baltic Front, now in Lithuania. On Mar. 17 a strength return showed the 249th still with 8,996 officers and men, nearly twice the strength of the average 1945 Red Army rifle division. They spent the last two months of the war helping to keep guard over the German forces trapped in the Kourland Pocket.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/249th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 24th Army headquarters, formed from Headquarters Siberian Mlitary District; under General Staff instructions of 25 June 1941 arrived on 28 June 1941 at Vyazma, and was assigned six Siberian rifle divisions of the high command reserve (RVGK). The 24th participated in the Yelnya Offensive, August-September 1941. It was disbanded 10 October 1941, having been destroyed in the Vyazma Pocket.Reformed from 9 December 1941 to 4 January 1942 when it was redesignated as 1st Reserve Army. The army was assigned the 385th Rifle Division for less than a month. The army remained in the Moscow Defense Zone through April 1942 with no assigned forces.Reformed again on 20 May 1942, from an Operational Group under the command of Major General Aleksei Grechkin while assigned to the Southern Front. The army was concentrated in the area of Salsk, Rostov Oblast. The army was then transferred to the North Caucasus Front on 28 July. In early August the units assigned were transferred to the 12th and 37th Armies, and its headquarters relocated to Grozny, Chechen Republic, where it was assigned to the Transcaucasian Front. The army was disbanded on 23 August and the headquarters personnel were used to form the 58th Army on August 28, 1942.Soon afterwards reformed again as part of the Stalingrad Front from 9th Reserve Army on 1 September 1942. The army participated in the Battle of Stalingrad as part of both the Stalingrad and Don Fronts. In March-April 1943 relocated to the Voronezh area and was assigned to the Steppe Military District as part of the STAVKA reserves for rebuilding. Was redesignated 4th Guards Army in May 1943.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24th_Army_(Soviet_Union)

Editor Name: 24th Hun. Infantry Brigade;124th Hun. Infantry Brigade;24th Hun. Infantry Division
text: The 24th Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In the fall of 1941 the brigade was one of five brigades reduced in size and stripped of their artillery that was assigned to the Hungarian Occupation Group for security duties on the Eastern Front. At this time it was redesignated the 124th Hungarian Infantry Brigade but in February of 1942 was redesignated the 124th Light Division. In May of 1943 the unit became the 24th Light Division. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 24th Light Division was merged with other units and renamed the 24th Infantry Division. In January of 1944 the Hungarian First Army to which the division was then subordinate, mobilized to defend Hungary's northern Carpathian frontier against the advancing Red Army.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 24th Infantry Division crossed into Russia in June 1941, fought its way across eastern Galacia and the Ukraine and into the Crimea with von Manstein's 11th Army, and took part in the Siege of Sevastopol for several months. With the 22nd Air Landing Division it was involved in the amphibious assault that led to the fall of the city in early July 1942. Transferred to Army Group North with the 11th Army, the division helped repulse the Russian counteroffensives in the Lake lImen area in the latter part of 1942. The 24th remained in the northern sector of the Eastern Front for the remainder of the war. It was reorganized as a Type 44 division in September 1943, when each of its grenadier regiments were reduced to two battalions each. It was part of the 18th Army when the Soviets broke the Siege of Leningrad in mid-January 1944. Unlike several other divisions, the 24th kept its composure and was later officially cited for its bravery in the withdrawal through the Baltic States. In July 1944 it held its line against the Russian summer offensive, withdrew into western Latvia at its own pace in October 1944, and fought in the six battles of the Courland Pocket (1944-45).German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The corps was created after the occupation of Latvia in 1940 as the Latvian Territorial Corps, and it consisted of the 181st and 183rd Rifle Divisions. It was part of 27th Army. It was disbanded in July and reformed in spring 1943 as part of 60th Army and consisted of 121st Guards, 112th, 140th, 149th, 287th, and 328th Rifle Divisions. It fought at Kursk, in Operation Polkovodets Rumyantsev, and at the liberation of Kiev. In 1944 it became part of 13th Army and fought in the Lvov-Sandomierz Operation. In 1945, as part of 3rd Guards Army, it fought in the Berlin Strategic OffensivePoirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 24th Rifle Division was formed from volunteers in July 1918 as the 1st Simbirsk Infantry Division. In November of the same year it was renamed as the 24th Simbirsk Rifle Division. During the Russian Civil War it was active in the Volga region, Southern Ural Mountains, Polissya and Volhynia. In 1922 it was renamed as the 24th Samaro-Simbirsk Iron Rifle Division. In 1924 it was once again renamed becoming the 24th Samaro-Ulyanovsk Iron Rifle Division. During the Winter War the division distinguished itself during the breaking of the Mannerheim Line on the Karelian isthmus.The division was active in the fighting from the first days of Operation Barbarossa. It took part in the Kiev and then in heavy fighting in Belarus. The division was disbanded in December 1941. In February 1942 a new 24th Rifle Division was formed in the area of Vologda as part of the 17th Guards Rifle Corps. The Division participated in the Battle of Stalingrad, the Donbass offensive operation, in Zhytomyr - Berdychiv, Khmelnytskyi - Chernivtsi, Lviv - Sandomierz, East - Carpathian, Western - Carpathian, Moravia - Ostrava and the Prague offensive operations. The division ended the war near Prague and was disbanded in July 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24th_Mechanized_Brigade_(Ukraine)Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 24th Romanian Infantry Division was not mobilized until 1943. It undertook security duties until merged with the 4th Mountain Romanian Division in September 1943.<cr><cr>John Ellis, World War II A Statistal Survey<cr><cr>Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 24th Tank Corps was formed in April 1942 at Voroshilovgrad in the Kharkov Military District.<cr>The 24th Tank Corps was another corps, like the 2lst, 22nd, and 23rd, formed
in Southwestern Theater from existing tank units in the spring of 1942 with their numbers out of sequence. Quite possibly, like the others, 24th Tank Corps was originally known as a Mechanized Corps, but in the earliest Soviet records it is referred to as a Tank Corps. Like the other corps on the southern front, the command played 'musical brigades' with the corps HQ in May and June as the German summer offensive started. 2nd Tank Brigade was quickly removed from the brigade, and it was late June before the corps composition stabilized.<cr>Note that all three of the corps' tank brigades had a good cadre of experienced personnel: 54th and 130th were both formed from prewar Tank Divisions, and 4th Guards had distinguished itself in the Battle of Moscow. In addition, by October at the latest the corps had picked up a good collection of supporting
units.<cr>The 24th Tank Corps was in reserve when the Stalingrad Counteroffensive started on 19 November. In mid-December the corps went into the attack with 1st Guards Army. Operating as an independent Mobile Group, 24th Tank Corps broke deep into the German rear and overran the airfield at Tatsinskaya - the main base for the airlift supplying 6th Army in Stalingrad. While the air supply operations had certainly not been succeeding before this, the raid broke the back of the Luftwaffe effort. Counterattacks by panzers forced most of the corps to abandon their equipment and 'exfilitrate' back to Russian lines, but the corps' exploits in the raid earned it the honorific title: 'Tatsinskaya' and redesignation as 2nd Guards Tank Corps on 26 December 1942.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 24th Tank Division was formed February 1941 in Leningrad Military District in 10th Mechanized Corps with: 47th Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Tank Bns - each 22 to 30 light tanks 48th Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Tank Bns - each 22 to 30 light tanks 24th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns 24th Motorized Howitzer Regiment 1 light, 1 medium bn 24th Reconniassance Battalion 24th Motorized Pontoon Battalion 24th Antiaircraft BattalionThe 24th Tank Division had about 200 old T-26 and BT tanks on hand on 22 June, and was stationed east of Leningrad in Northern Front reserves. 24th Tank Division was shifted south as a separate tank division against the German assaults south of Leningrad, and fought from late July until early September as a mobile reserve for the Luga and Southern Operational Groups of Leningrad Front. In early September the division was disbanded, and personnel from it used to form 123rd Tank Brigade.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 250th Infantry Division consisted of Spanish soldiers who volunteered to fight for Germany against the communists. It was 14,000 strong when it was mustered in at the Grafenwoehr Troop Maneuver Area in July 20, 1941. Quickly sent into action at Novgorod on the northern sector of the Russian Front, the so-called 'Blue Division' fought very well in all of its engagements. In the Novgorod-Leningrad-Lake Ilmen battles of late 1941-early 1942, the Spanish Fascist volunteers played a major role in turning back the Russian winter offensive in the northern sector but lost 8,000 men killed, wounded, captured, or incapacitated by frostbite. After receiving replacements from Spain, it continued in action with Army Group North, fought at Volchov, and lost another 3,200 men in the Second Battle of Lake Ladoga in January and February 1943. Here its Fusilier battalion lost 90 percent of its soldiers, but the division again held its positions against massive Soviet attacks. The 250th continued to serve in northern Russia and in the siege of Leningrad until October 1943. At that time Spanish dictator Francisco Franco requested that the division be returned to Spain; however, about half of its veteran warriors volunteered for service in the Waffen-SS and continued to fight against the Russians until the end of the war. The Blue Division was officially disbanded on October 20, 1943.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 250th Rifle Division began forming within days of the start of the German invasion on June 26, 1941, at Vladimir, in the Moscow Military District, based on a cadre of 1,500 officers and men of the NKVD Internal Troops.The division was first assigned to 30th Army in Western Front.<cr><cr>The 250th was almost immediately committed to heavy fighting north of Smolensk. After about two weeks of combat, the division had lost about half its strength. As well, by Aug. 5 the tank battalion was down to eight T-34s, one T-26, two BT-7s and six BT-5s, when the division was transferred to 29th Army. By early October the 250th had lost all its armor, and was reduced to 500 men fighting at Olenino.<cr><cr>While retreating to the Kalinin area from Rzhev, the division became part of the newly formed Kalinin Front, under command of Col. Gen. Ivan Konev. On October 15 the 250th was ordered to 'stubbornly defend' its sector, alongside the 220th Rifle Division. On the 18th, Konev reported that both divisions were falling back under German pressure. On October 21, the two divisions were assigned to 22nd Army.<cr><cr>The 250th spent the winter in Kalinin Front, and in April 1942 was reassigned to the newly-forming 53rd Army in Northwestern Front, where it remained in the vicinity of Demyansk until February 1943. After a brief posting to 1st Shock Army in the same Front, in early March the 250th got new orders to re-deploy to the new 2nd Reserve Army, in the Yelets, Lepetsk and Lebedian regions. In April, 2nd Reserve became the 63rd Army, assigned to Bryansk Front, and the division was also assigned to 35th Rifle Corps, where it would remain for the duration. In this Front (Belorussian Front after October 20) the 250th would take part in the difficult fighting through Bryansk and towards the Dniepr River until February 1944.<cr><cr>On February 18, 63rd Army was dissolved, and 35th Rifle Corps was reassigned to 3rd Army, where it would remain for the duration. At the outset of Operation Bagration, on June 23, 35th Rifle Corps, under command of Major General Viktor Zholudev, formed one of the two assault corps of 3rd Army, packed into less than ten kilometres of front opposite the northern half of the sector held by the German 134th Infantry Division. On the second day of the offensive, at 0400 hours, the assault force unleashed a massive 2-hour bombardment on the defenders in the Rogachev area. As the weather cleared towards evening, further lines were taken, and the 9th Tank Corps prepared to exploit a breakthrough. Northwest of Bobruysk on June 26, the tankers cut the road to Mogilev behind the German XXXV Corps, with 35th and 41st Rifle Corps close behind and the 134th Infantry shattered and in flight. On the following day Bobruysk was surrounded, along with most of German 9th Army, and it fell to the 250th to help clear and liberate the city, for which the men and women of the division received the name of that city as an honorific. On Aug. 9, the 250th was also awarded the Order of Suvorov II Class.<cr><cr>Also, in August, the division, along with its army and corps, were transferred to 2nd Belorussian Front, where it would remain for the next six months, assisting in the liberation of the remainder of Belorussia and eastern Poland. It was still in this front at the outset of the Vistula-Oder Offensive in January 1945, but in February was reassigned to 3rd Belorussian Front, fighting in East Prussia. In April, 3rd Army was once again reassigned, this time to back to 1st Belorussian Front, in preparation for the assault on the German capital. When the shooting stopped, the division was in the enemy's lair of Berlin, and the final full title of its men and women was '250th Rifle, Bobruysk, Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov Division'.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/250th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 251st Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 451st, 459th and 471st Infantry Regiments, 251st Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the XXIII Army Corps in Army Group North at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In November 1943 the division was disbanded. It was reformed in September 1944 from the 'E' Corps Detachment. The new division had the 184th, 448th and 451st Grenadier Regiments, 186th Artillery Regiment and various support units. In January 1945 the division was destroyed near the Warka bridgehead in Poland. It was disbanded in March 1945.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

On the order of Stavka, the 251st Rifle Division was one of the first 10 Rifle Divisions created from NKVD cadre in late June 1941. L.P. Beria was personally responsible for raising these divisions. The division was established at Kolomna in the Moscow Military District, finished formation on 13th July, and was assigned to the 30th Army. The division lacked trained personnel, equipment and transport and was considered to be of low combat value. The division fought at Smolensk and was trapped in the Vyazma pockrt, but successfully broke out with heavy losses. The division was formed for a second time in November 1941, based on the 2,000 men that had escaped the pocket. In late 1942 the division was assigned to the 20th Army, Western Front, and participated in Operation Mars where it suffered heavy casualties. In June 1944, assigned to the 5th Guards Rifle Corps, 39th Army, the division fought in Operation Bagration, where it was awarded the honorific of Vitebsk for the liberation of that city. It fought in Courland and ended the war assigned to the 2nd Guards Army, 3rd Belorussian Front. It had also been awarded the Order of the Red Banner and Order of Suvorov. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/251st_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB David Glantz, Colossus Reborn Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 252nd Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 452nd, 461st and 472nd Infantry Regiments, 252nd Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the XXXXIII Army Corps in Army Group Centre at the start of Operation Barbarossa. By February 1943 the 452nd Regiment had been replaced by the 7th Regiment and the 472nd Regiment was disbanded and its survivors distributed to the other two regiments. In September 1943 the division consisted of the 7th and 461st Grenadier Regiments, 252nd Artillery Regiment and various support troops. In July 1944 the 472nd Regiment was reformed. The division was taken prisoner by the Russians near Danzig.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

On the order of Stavka, the 252nd Rifle Division was one of the first 10 Rifle Divisions created from NKVD cadre in late June 1941. L.P. Beria was personally responsible for raising these divisions. The division was established at Serpukhovin the Moscow Military District, finished formation on 13th July, and was assigned to the 29th Army. The division fought at Smolensk and suffered heavy casualties and in October 1941 was assigned to the 39th Army in the defense of Kalinin where it fought with some distinction. The following year the division fought in the battles around Rzhev and in July 1942 barely escaped entrapment. The division was withdrawn to be rebuilt and in October was assigned to the Don Front at Stalingrad, but by November it was depleted and was withdrawn into the Reserve. The Division fought with success in the Stalingrad counter offensive but by January 1943 was assigned to mopping up operations. In April the division was reorganised and fought successfully at Kharkov where it was awarded the honorific of 'KHARKOV' . In January 1944, assigned to the 53rd Army, it fought in the liberation of Uman and pursued the Axis forces to the Danube. It fought in the capture of Bratisalva for which it was awarded the honorific of 'BRATISLAVA' and ended the war linking up with the U.S. 2nd Infantry Division near Pilsen. A highly distinguished Division, it had been awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov and Order of Bogdan Khmelnitsky. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/252nd_Rifle_Division Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB David Glantz, Colossus Reborn Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 253rd Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 453rd, 464th and 473rd Infantry Regiments, 253rd Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was attached to the German 16th Army's in Army Group North at the start of Operation Barbarossa. The division was reorganized several times alternating between two regiments of 3 battalions each or 3 regiments of 2 battalions each. The division was taken prisoner by the Russians near Deutsch-Brod.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 253rd Soviet Rifle Division started forming on the 10th July at Volchansk in the Odessa Military District. It completed formation on the 15th of August and was assigned to the Southern Front. It was not a strong formation and was destroyed at Krivoi Rog and was disbanded on the 19th September, 1941. The Division was formed for a second time in October 1941 and was assigned to the 37th Army and then in January the 38th Army. The division was trapped and destroyed at Izyum in May 1942. The Division was formed for a third time in September 1942 at Chapaevsk and assigned to the Voronezh Front. It fought along the Dnieper and at Kalinkovichi and ended the war assigned to the 3rd Guards Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#251%E2%80%93260 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 254th Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 454th, 474th and 484th Infantry Regiments, 254th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the XXIII Army Corps in Army Group North at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In May 1944 the 474th Grenadier Regiment (most infantry regiments in the German Army by this point were designated grenadier regiments) was disbanded and replaced by survivors of the 82nd Infantry Division now called the 82nd Divisional Group. In July 1944 the 82nd Divisional Group became a new 474th Grenadier Regiment. The division was captured by the Russians in the Deutsch-Brod region.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

On the order of Stavka, the 254th Rifle Division was one of the first 10 Rifle Divisions created from NKVD cadre in late June 1941. L.P. Beria was made personally responsible for raising these divisions. The division was established at Tetnitsky Camp, north of Tula, in the Moscow Military District, finished formation on 13th July, and was assigned to the 11th Army, Northwestern Front. The division was rushed to Staraya Russa without it's artillery and many of its machine guns and fought with distinction. The division fought at Demyansk and at the end of 1942 was assigned to the 27th Army, Northwestern Front. In 1944 The Division was the first Soviet Unit to cross into Romanian territory and it's last major action was the Battle of Bautzen in 1945, near Dresden, assigned to the 52nd Army. On the 21st April, 1945, its commanding officer, Major General M.K. Puteiko, one of the youngest Soviet Generals at that time, died from wounds, and now lies in a cemetery in L'vov. A highly distinguished Division with many Heroes of the Soviet Union, it had been awarded the honorific of 'CHERKASSY', Order of Lenin, Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov, Order of Kutuzov and Order of Bogdan Khmelnitsky. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/254th_Motor_Rifle_Division Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB David Glantz, Colossus Reborn A.A. Maslov, Fallen Soviet generals Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 255th Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 455th, 465th and 475th Infantry Regiments, 255th Artillery Regiment and various support units. One company in each regiment was equipped with bicycles. The division was attched to the 2nd Panzer Group in Army Group Centre at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In May 1942 the 455th Infantry Regiment was disbanded and an additional battery composed of two captured Russian 152mm howitzers joined the artillery regiment. In August 1943 the survivors of the disbanded 332nd Infantry Division were absorbed into the division. The division was disbanded in November 1943 and its components distributed to other units.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 255th Soviet Rifle Division started forming on the 10th July, 1941, at Pavlograd, Odessa Military District, and by 31st of August was assigned to the newly reformed 6th Army, Southwestern Front performing defensive operations in the Donbas. In early 1942 it was then assigned to the 57th Army and destroyed in the Battle of Kharkov. It was recreated and assigned to the 15th Army of the Far Eastern Front where it remained. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#251%E2%80%93260 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

In June 1941, the 256th Infantry Division invaded Russia, where it was almost continuously engaged for the next three years. It fought at Bialystok, Nevel, Velikije Luki, Kalinin, and Rzhev (December 1941-January 1942). In the last ten days of December 1941, it held its line near Moscow against odds of ten to one or even higher odds. A month later it was instrumental in saving the XXIII Corps, which the Soviets had surrounded west of Rzhev. Remaining on the central sector of the Russian Front, it held a defensive sector east of Smolensk and took part in the Rzhev withdrawal, but apparently was not present at the Battle of Kursk . The 256th suffered heavy losses at the Battle of Smolensk in the autumn of 1943 and, as part of the 3rd Panzer Army, was destroyed at Vitebsk by the Soviet summer offensive of 1944. The remnants of the division became Divisiongruppe 256 of Corps Detachment H on July 21. They later ended up in the 280th Grenadier Regiment of the 95th Infantry Division.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

On the order of Stavka, the 256th Rifle Division was one of the first 10 Rifle Divisions created from NKVD cadre in late June 1941. L.P. Beria was made personally responsible for raising these divisions. The division was established in the Moscow Military District, finished formation on 13th July, and was assigned to the 29th Army, the 27th Army in August, and the 30th Army in October, Kalinin Front, where it took part in defensive operations. In 1942 the Division was assigned to the 8th Army, Volkhov Front. The division fought at Smolensk, Moscow and Kursk and finished the war assigned to the 22nd Army. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#251%E2%80%93260 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB David Glantz, Colossus Reborn Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 257th Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 457th, 466th and 477th Infantry Regiments, 257th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the XXXXIX Mountain Corp in Army Group South at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In August 1944 the division was destroyed and in October 1944 formally disbanded. The survivors were used to form the 587th Volksgrenadier Division, also know as the Gross-Görschen Shadow Division. Later the same month the division was renamed the 257th Volksgrenadier Division. The division was taken prisoner by the Americans near Füssen.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

On the order of Stavka, the 257th Rifle Division was one of the first 10 Rifle Divisions created from NKVD cadre in late June 1941. L.P. Beria was made personally responsible for raising these divisions. The division was established near Tula in the Moscow Military District, finished formation on 10th July, and was assigned to the 34th Army. The Division took part in the unsuccessful Staraya Russa counter offensive and was smashed. The commander of the 34th Army Kuzma Kachanov was arrested on the 12th September and executed. The Division started forming for a second time on the 8th November 1941 in the Moscow Military District and on the 25th December was assigned to the 3rd Shock Army, Northwestern Front, and soon after the Kalinin Front. In early 1942, short of equipment and supplies the Division pushed towards, but was unable to take, Velikie Luki, which did not fall until 1943. In April 1943, the Division was renamed the 91st Gurads Rifle Division. In June 1943 the Division was formed for the third time at Krymskaya, based on 9th and 60th Rifle Brigades and the 62nd Naval Rifle Brigade and finished the war assigned to the 4th Shock Army in Courland. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#251%E2%80%93260 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB David Glantz, Colossus Reborn Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 258th Infantry Division crossed into Russia in mid-1941, and fought and at Brest, Bialystok, Bobruisk, Yelnya, and Vyazma-Bryansk as well as in the battles around Moscow. The 258th continued to serve with Army Group Center until late summer 1943, and took part in the defensive battles at Jucknov, Gshatsk and Orel. It was also involved in the Kursk offensive. During the retreat from Kursk and Orel, the division defended 9th Army's supply depot at Kromy against heavy odds, withstood fifteen major Soviet attacks, and frustrated the Russian attempt to seize the depot. Later in the year the Prussian division was transferred to the southern sector of the Eastern Front. It took part in the Mius and Dnieper retreats and was at battle group strength by October 1943. It fought in the Nikopol Bridgehead and was routed in March 1944, during the withdrawal from the lower Dnieper bend, where three of its grenadier battalions were destroyed. That August, it was encircled west of the lower Dnieper and was virtually destroyed at Jassy, Romania, in early September. Those few soldiers who managed to escape were sent to Division Group 387, and the 258th Infantry was disbanded.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 258th Soviet Rifle Division, a Uzbek National Division, started forming on the 10th July, 1941, with resources from the Central Asia Military District. On the 15th August it was assigned to the 50th Army (Commander A Yermakov executed for dereliction of duty in November), fought with some good fortune and distinction at Bryansk, Roslavl and Tula and by January 1942 was redesignated the 12th Guards Rifle Division. The division was recreated for a second time and by the middle of 1942 it was assigned to the 5th Tank Army. By the end of the year it was assigned to the 24th Army, Don Front, and fought at Stalingrad. It ended the war assigned to the 25th Army of the Far Eastern Front. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#251%E2%80%93260 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB D. M. Glantz, Zhukov's Greatest Defeat Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 259th Soviet Rifle Division started forming on the 5th July, 1941 at Serpukhov, with resources from the Moscow Military District. On the 31st of July it was assigned to the 34th Army which was assigned to the Northwestern Front in early August. The Division was active in defending the Leningrad-Moscow rail line near Valdai when the commanding officer, F.N. Shilov, was fatally wounded. The division remained in this general sector until late 1942. It fought in the Ukraine and ended the war assigned to the 34th Rifle Corps, 37th Army in Bulgaria. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_infantry_divisions_of_the_Soviet_Union_1917%E2%80%931957#251%E2%80%93260 Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB A.A. Maslov, Fallen Soviet Generals Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 25th Cavalry Division was a mounted division of the Red Army that served for just over a year in the Great Patriotic War. It was formed in the summer of 1941 and served in the region south and west of Leningrad during the following months against the advance of Army Group North during Operation Barbarossa. It survived a German armored counterattack before being pulled back into the reserves in September. In January 1942, it was assigned to the Mobile Group of 2nd Shock Army to take part in the Lyuban Offensive Operation. This offensive aimed to encircle and destroy the German forces besieging Leningrad; in the event, 2nd Shock was itself encircled and forced to break out as individuals and small groups from May into July. The 25th Cavalry was disbanded, and its survivors were used to help rebuild the badly depleted 19th Guards Rifle Division, while the 25th's commanding officer took over the latter division.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_Cavalry_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 25th Guards Rifle Division was formed in the period from 24 April 1942 to 12 July 1942, pursuant to Directive GShKA N org/2/783669 on 16 April 1942, by converting the 2nd Guards Rifle Brigade, ex 71st Naval Rifle Brigade, station Sonkovo, Kalinin region. 11–12 July 1942 the Division left the place of formation for the Voronezh Front, arrived in the front, and from 22 July 1942 until 4 August 1942 it built the defence line on the eastern bank of the river Bityug. Participated in the battles to establish a bridgehead on the river Don north of the city Korotoyak in August 1942, Ostrogozh-Rossoshanskij, Voronezh-Kastornoye, Kharkov offensive and defensive operations. It took part in the operations to take cities of Budapest and Bratislava.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_Guards_Rifle_Division</url>

Editor Name: 25th Hun. Infantry Brigade;25th Hun. Infantry Division
text: The 25th Hungarian Infantry Brigade was formed in 1939. Its TOE consisted of 9,500 men under a major-general with 2 infantry regiments (each with 3 battalions and a machine gun company), an artillery regiment with 7 batteries and various support troops. In January 1942 the Germans demanded more Hungarian forces for the Eastern Front and most Hungarian infantry brigades were reclassified as 'light divisions'. Their TOE however remained largely unchanged. The brigade was renamed the 25th Light Division. In March of 1943 the division was sent from Hungary to join the Hungarian Occupation Group assigned to security duties in occupied Russia. As part of a general reorganization of the Hungarian Army after Stalingrad the 25th Light Division was merged with other units and renamed the 25th Infantry Division. In January of 1944 the Hungarian First Army to which the division was then subordinate, mobilized to defend Hungary's northern Carpathian frontier against the advancing Red Army. In August 1944 the division was part of a reactivated Hungarian Second Army defending Northern Transylvania from the invading Red Army. The division was disbanded in April 1945.Dr. Nigel Thomas and Lazlo Pal Szabo, The Royal Hungarian Army in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 25th Mechanized Corps was formed in March 1941 at Kharkov in the Kharkov Military District. The corps included the 50th and 55th Tank Divisions, and the 219th Motorized Division. The 50th Tank Division was formed at Kharkov, the 55th at Chuguyev, and the 219th Motorized Division at Akhtyrka. The corps was commanded by Major General Semyon Krivoshein.<cr>The 25th Mechanized Corps was part of the Reserve of the Supreme High Command on 22 June 1941. Between 24 and 29 June it deployed by rail to the Kiev region. The corps was originally to support the 19th Army and was assigned to it on 30 June. The corps was slow in deploying forward from Kharkov. As a result, the 23rd Mechanized Corps supported the 19th Army instead. During the first half of July, it was assigned to support the 21st Army to replace the mechanized corps destroyed in the border battles. Between 3 and 8 July the corps moved to the Novozybkov region. The corps included 163 older model tanks on 1 July (6 BT tanks and 157 T-26 tanks) and was reinforced by 64 T-34 medium tanks by 13 July. On 13 July, the corps was ordered to concentrate the 219th Motorized Division in the Rudnia, Borkhov, and Pribor region, 15 to 25 kilometers to the west of Gomel. The 50th Tank Division was to attack along the Bykhov and Bobruisk axis from its positions. 300 tanks of the corps launched heavy unsuccessful attacks in cooperation with the 67th Rifle Corps against Heinz Guderian's forces south of Bykhov.<cr>On 16 July, the corps was in the Krichev area, according to Western Front commander Semyon Timoshenko. On 18 July, the 50th Tank Division was in the Voshchanka and Aleshnia region, 40 to 50 kilometers wast of Rogachev and 15 to 20 kilometers east of Dovsk, according to Timoshenko's situation report. Its 10-tank detachment and a motorized company had reportedly destroyed 70-80 wheeled vehicles, 10 tanks, and killing up to 500 German soldiers in the Mahsevskaya Sloboda region from 17 July. The 219th Motorized Division was in the Chechersk and Voronovka area. The 55th Tank Division was at Novozybkov. According to Timoshenko's 21 July report, the corps was attacking. The 50th Tank Division was on the southern outskirts of Obidovichi, the 219th Motorized Division was unsuccessfully attempting to capture Maly Propoysk with its motor rifle regiment, and the 55th Tank Division was still at Novozybkov. On 22 July the corps was ordered to capture Propoysk. On 23 July it was fighting for Propoysk. The corps suffered heavy losses in its attacks and regrouped on 24 July. Between 25 and 27 July it resumed the offensive. The corps shifted back to defense on 31 July. On 10 August, the 55th Tank Division became the 8th and 14th Separate Tank Battalions. On 14 August a Stavka directive ordered the corps command and control units along with those of the 20th Rifle Corps to form the Bryansk Front headquarters.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_Mechanized_Corps_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 25th Motorized Division was sent to the Russian Front in June 1941, and served on the central sector for the next three years. It fought in the 2nd Panzer Group's battles at Zhitomir, Uman, Kiev, Bryansk, and Tula (south of Moscow). It spent January 1942 to June 1943 in the Bryansk/Orel sector, took heavy casualties at Kursk in July, and fought at Smolensk in October 1943. Meanwhile, on June 23, 1943, it was redesignated the 25th Panzer Grenadier Division. From November 1943 to June 1944, it held part of 4th Army's sector near Orscha. In the summer of 1944, the 25th Panzer Grenadier suffered heavy losses in the encirclement east of Minsk. The parts of the division which escaped were assigned to the 107th Panzer Brigade.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

At the outbreak of hostilities, the corps was part of 19th Army deployed near Kiev. It comprised the 127th, 134th and 162nd Rifle Divisions. The army was assigned to Western Front and participated in the Battle of Smolensk. At this time, Hero of the Soviet Union Alexander Gorbatov was deputy commander, having just been rehabilitated after a 1936 sentence in the Gulag for 'counter-revolutionary activities'. The corps was dissolved in July 1941. It was briefly reformed in August and served as the basis of 52nd Army in Southwest Front. The corps was reformed once again in February 1943 as part of 69th Army and consisted of 4th and 41st Rifle Divisions and 77th Guards Rifle Division. It participated in the Lvov-Sandomierz Operation and the Carpathian Offensive in 1944 and the Vistula-Oder Offensive and the Berlin Strategic Offensive in 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_Army_Corps_(Soviet_Union) Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 25th Rifle Division was formed in 1918 at the beginning of the Russian Civil War. Shortly after the start of Operation Barbarossa in June 1941 Stavka Order #20466 attached the 25th Rifle Division to the 14th Rifle Corps, 9th Army, Southern Front. It took part in the Siege of Odessa and was evacuated by sea in October 1941 prior to the city's fall. The division arrived in Sevastopol in time to prepare for the defence of the port against the oncoming German offensive. The division was destroyed during the following Siege of Sevastopol in July 1942. The division was subsequently reformed in the Arkhangelsk Military District in 1943. It did not see any further action in the Second World War.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 25th Tank Corps was formed in June 1942 in the Moscow Military District.<cr>The 25th Tank Corps moved to Bryansk Front area at Voronezh in late June and then, on 5 July, was assigned to 5th Tank Army. The 25th was roughly handled in the tank battles around Voronezh, but not caught up in the German advance to the Don and the Volga Rivers. Instead, 25th Tank Corps remained in the Voronezh area until December, when it was shifted south and took part in the 'Malyy Saturn' Operation with 1st Guards Army. By January 1943 the 25th Tank Corps was part of Southwestern Front's Mobile Group with additional supporting units.<cr>Unfortunately, between the continuous advances and fighting from December to February and Manstein's counterattack in late February and March 1943, 25th Tank Corps suffered almost 90% losses and in March 1943, went into STAVKA Reserves to be rebuilt and refitted. In July, the corps went back into action with 11th Guards Army in the Bryansk Front.<cr>The 25th Tank Corps fought only briefly in the summer offensives that started in July-August after Kursk, and by late August was back in reserve in the Moscow Military District. There it remained until October 1943, probably reequipping all the tank brigades with T-34 tanks in 3 tank battalions each. In late October 1943 it was sent to 1st Ukrainian Front, with which it remained for the rest of the war. At that time the corps included additional supporting units.<cr>In the fighting after the liberation of Kiev on the right bank of the Dnepr 25th Tank Corps fought under 13th and 60th Armies west of Kiev. By March 1944 the corps' SU regiments had been changed.<cr>The 25th Tank Corps was part of 1st Cavalry Mechanized Group for the
Lvov-Sandomir Operation in July 1944. In September 1944 the corps received 296th Guards Light Artillery Regiment (24 76mm guns) At the end of 1944, as the Front prepared for the Vistula-Oder Operation, 25th Tank Corps converted 746th Antitank Battalion into the 746th Heavy SU Regiment (ISU-122s).<cr>As a result of the operations in January 1945 that advanced the corps to the Oder River, the 746th was redesignated as 262nd Guards Heavy SU Regiment. This was the last change in organization made to the corps during the war. 25th Tank Corps ended the war in May 1945 near Berlin, after taking part in the Berlin Operation in the first echelon of 1st Ukrainian Front.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 25th Tank Divisio  was formed in February - April 1941 at Gomel in Western Special Military District from 44th Light Tank Brigade as part of 13th Mechanized Corps with:<cr>
49th Tank Regiment
1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Tank Battalions
each Bn = 2 companies of 17 T-26s + 1 HQT-26, 35 tanks per bn
50th Tank Regiment
1st, 2nd, 3rd Tank Battalions, equipped as above
25th Motorized Rifle Regiment
1st, 2nd, 3rd bns
25th Howitzer Regiment
25th Reconnaissance Battalion
25th Motorized Pontoon Battalion
25th Antiaircraft Battalion<cr><cr>This division, along with the rest of 13th Mechanized Corps, was 'completely understrength' on 22 June 1941, according to the Western Front's deputy commander. 25th Tank Division was the best equipped unit in 13th mech, but it only had 247 T-26 tanks, most in dire need of major repairs. The reconnaissance
battalion was missing trucks and motorcycles, and antiaircraft battalion had no equipment or weapons. While the howitzer regiment was fully equipped with guns, it had almost no trucks or tractors to pull them, and the gun crews were all away in training camps when the Germans attacked! The division was directly in front of 2nd Panzer Group's advance south of Minsk, and was officially disbanded on 4 July 1941 - one of the first divisions stricken from the Red Army order of battle, in the war.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

he 260th Infantry Division was formed from reserve units in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave during the general mobilization of the German Army. Its soldiers came from Baden and Württemberg. It contained the 460th, 470th and 480th Infantry Regiments, 260th Artillery Regiment and various support units. In October 1939 it was sent to the Upper Rhine and spent most of the Battle of France in OKH reserve. The division was on occupation duty in France until July of 1941 when it was sent to the Eastern Front.In the summer of 1943 the 470th Grenadier Regiment (most infantry regiments in the German Army by this point were designated grenadier regiments) was disbanded after heavy losses and an additional battery composed of five captured Russian 152mm howitzers joined the artillery regiment. In April 1944 the 470th Grenadier Regiment was reformed and the division now consisted of three regiments with two battalions each plus a divisional fusilier battalion. The division was surrounded and destroyed in the Minsk Offensive and never reformed.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IISamuel W. Mitcham, German Order of Battle Volume I: 1st-290th Infantry Divisions in WWIIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 260th Rifle Division started forming on the 2nd July 1941 at Kalinin and on the 15th August was assigned to the 50th Army, Bryansk Front. The division was trapped in the Bryansk pocket and whilst 1000 men escaped the division was officially disbanded by the 17th November, 1941. The division was raised for the 2nd time at Volokolamsk near Moscow, from the 55th Rifle Brigade, in May 1942. In September it was assigned to the Don Front where the commander was demoted for lack of military success. It fought with some success at Stalingrad. In July 1943 it fought at Bryansk, Gomel and assisted in the capture of Kovel. In 1944 The Division fought in Operation Bagration, in the capture of Warsaw and Berlin and ended the war assigned to the 77th Rifle Corps near Berlin. A distinguished Division , it had been awarded the honorific of 'KOVEL', Order of the Red Banner and Order of Suvorov. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/260th_Rifle_Division Nigel Askey, Operation Barbarossa, Vol IIIB Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 261st Rifle Division began forming on 18 July 1941 at Berdiansk in the Odessa Military District. It was made up from a combination of reservists, militia, and volunteers, and its basic order of battle was as follows: 974th Rifle Regiment 976th Rifle Regiment 978th Rifle Regiment 809th Artillery Regiment The division went into Southern Front in August, first as part of 6th Army, but was reassigned to 12th Army, in the same Front, by September 1. It remained with that Army up to at least August 1942 but then was assigned to the Transcaucasian Front's Black Sea Group of Forces. It then spent much of the later part of World War II, from January 1, 1943,[8] onwards with the small 45th Army of the Transcaucasian Front, which was guarding the Soviet borders with Turkey.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_102nd_Military_Base

The 262nd Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 from Austrian reservists as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 462nd, 482nd and 486th Infantry Regiments, 262nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 262nd Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was stationed in the Saar during the Polish Campaign. The division remained there until after the fall of France in 1940.<>The division was part of the IV Army Corps in Army Group South at the start of Operation Barbarossa. By early 1943 the infantry regiments were reduced from three to two battalions each and the artillery regiment added a Nebelwerfer battery. The division fought in the Battle of Kursk and suffered heavy casualties. In February 1944 the division was disbanded and most elements combined with other units to form 'D' Corps Detachment and the remainder of the division was distributed to other units throughout the Army.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IISamuel W. Mitcham, German Order of Battle Volume I: 1st-290th Infantry Divisions in WWIIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 262nd Rifle Division began forming at Vladimir in the Moscow Military District as the 16th NKVD Mountain Division on 26 June 1941. It used 1,500 NKVD troops as a cadre, and was transferred to the Red Army as the 262nd Rifle Division before 10 July. Without completing its formation, on the night of 19-20 July the division was moved to the Mozhaysk area as part of the Reserve Front's 33rd Army. A week later it was transferred to the Northwestern Front's 34th Army. Later that month, it suffered heavy losses in the Staraya Russa counterattack.<cr><cr>In the second half of October, it moved east to the Kalinin Front's 31st Army, which was preparing for the Soviet winter counteroffensive in the Battle of Moscow. The division fought in the Kalinin Defensive Operation and the Kalinin Offensive during the winter campaign.<cr><cr>In 1943 it became part of the 43rd Army. Until 15 September, the division fought in defensive battles near Demidov, then fought in the Dukhovshchina-Demidov Offensive. The division remained with the Kalinin Front, which became the 1st Baltic Front on 20 October. In October and November, the 262nd fought in the advance on Vitebsk during the Belorussian Strategic Offensive as part of the army's 1st Rifle Corps. It then defended positions on the approaches to Vitebsk, rejoining the 39th Army on 15 December.<cr><cr>The army became part of the 3rd Belorussian Front for Operation Bagration in June 1944, and remained with the front until April 1945. On 23 June 1944, at the start of Operation Bagration, it was part of the army's 84th Rifle Corps. It subsequently advanced into Lithuania during the Vilnius Offensive and the Kaunas Offensive during the summer. On 12 August the 262nd was awarded the Order of Suvorov 2nd class for its actions in the capture of Kaunas. The division fought in the Memel Offensive in October. From January 1945, the division moved into East Prussia, attacking towards Tilsit in the Insterburg-Koenigsberg Offensive. The division spent the last months of the war in the Samland Group of Forces near Konigsberg.<cr><cr>In April, the division and the rest of the 39th Army were withdrawn to the Reserve of the Supreme High Command and moved to the Soviet Far East in May and June in preparation for the Soviet invasion of Manchuria. The 262nd was transported to the Choibalsan area by rail, then marched 400 kilometres (250 mi) to concentration areas south of Tamsagbulag. At the beginning of the invasion on 9 August, the division was part of the 39th Army's 113th Rifle Corps in the Transbaikal Front. The 262nd fought in the Khingan-Mukden Offensive Operation of the invasion.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/262nd_Rifle_Division</url>

The 263rd Infantry Division was formed in August 1939 as part of the 4th Wave. It contained the 463rd, 483rd and 485th Infantry Regiments, 263rd Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the IX Army Corps in Army Group Centre at the start of Operation Barbarossa. In April 1943 the 483rd Grenadier Regiment (most infantry regiments in the German Army by this point were designated grenadier regiments) was disbanded and its two battaltions added to the other two regiments in the division so that each now had three battalions. By this time the division also had two companies of Ost infantry from the 263rd Ost Battalion assigned to it. In May 1944 the 483rd Grenadier Regiment was reformed by taking one battalion from each of the other two regiments so that the division now had three regiments with two battalions each. The division surrendered to the Russians in Courland in May 1945.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 264th Rifle Division began forming on 10 July 1941 at Poltava in the Kharkov Military District. Its basic order of battle included the 1056th, 1058th, and the 1060th Rifle Regiments. The division was barely formed and lacked much of its equipment when it was sent to the front on nine trains at the end of July. By 30 July, it was taking positions defending the line of the Dnieper near Kaniv, south of Kiev. By 5 August, the 264th was part of the Southwestern Front's 26th Army. It was trapped in the Kiev pocket in early September and destroyed almost immediately in the pocket. The 264th was officially disbanded on 19 September.<cr><cr>The second formation of the 264th began forming in February 1942 in the Ural Military District, including the basic order of battle as the first formation. By the time its commander was assigned on 1 May, the division had been relocated to the Moscow Military District. In May, it was assigned to the Moscow Defence Zone for training, and in August the 264th joined the 3rd Tank Army, part of the Reserve of the Supreme High Command behind the Western Front near Moscow. The division was part of the army's mobile group for several front-level offensives in 1942, which occasionally stretched the German defenses but never broke through. Thus, these actions were mostly ignored by Soviet accounts. The division fought in heavy fighting through the fall of 1942 around Rzhev, Sychyovka, and Zhizdra. On 20 October 1942, it was converted into the 48th Guards Rifle Division for its actions.<cr><cr>The division was formed for a third time on 20 July 1943 with the 35th Army in the Far Eastern Front. It included the same rifle regiments as the previous formations, and spent the entire war with the 35th Army. On 8 August 1945, the army was with the 1st Far East Front for the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, which began the next day. While other units of the army engaged in a speedy advance through the Japanese line, the 264th spent the entire campaign systematically reducing Japanese fortifications in and around Hutou in conjunction with the 109th Fortified Region. By the end of the invasion, the 264th was so far behind the rest of the army that it was assigned to the 87th Rifle Corps in the front reserves. For its actions, the division was awarded the honorific 'Ussuri.'<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/264th_Rifle_Division</url>

The 265th Rifle Division began forming on 26 June 1941 in the Moscow Military District as the 17th NKVD Mountain Division. It was one of the fifteen NKVD divisions that began forming on 26 June and was transferred to the Red Army in early July. The 265th, whose major subunits included the 450th, 941st, and 951st Rifle Regiments, the 798th Artillery Regiment, and the 224th Anti-Tank Battalion, remained in the Moscow Military District at least until 10 July, and later that month moved to Leningrad with a 1500-man cadre of NKVD personnel. In early August it joined the 23rd Army, fighting in the Continuation War north of Leningrad on the Karelian Isthmus. On 26 August, its first Red Army commander, Major Ivan Prytkov, was assigned to the division. On 14 October, the division was transferred to the Neva River front, south of the city. In November it became part of the 8th Army, which was part of the Volkhov Front from early 1942. In November 1943, the 265th was withdrawn to the Reserve of the Supreme High Command and from February 1944 was either part of the Leningrad Front or the 3rd Baltic Front until the end of 1944. Between June and July, it was part of the 21st Army's 110th Rifle Corps for the Svir-Petrozavodsk Offensive on the Karelian Isthmus, which eventually forced Finland out of the war. In August the 265th became part of the 3rd Baltic reserves, and in October it was with the 3rd Shock Army's 7th Rifle Corps in the 2nd Baltic Front. Just before the Vistula-Oder Offensive began in January 1945, the division transferred to the 1st Belorussian Front. It fought in the advance through Poland and in the Battle of Berlin in April and May 1945. During the war, the division was awarded the honorific 'Vyborg'.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/265th_Motor_Rifle_Division

The 266th was first formed between 26 June and 2 July 1941 at Kaluga in the Moscow Military District as the 26th NKVD Mountain Division. By 2 July, it was transferred to the Red Army as the 266th Rifle Division. In early August, the 266th joined the 21st Army of the Bryansk Front.  In late August, the 2nd Panzer Group advanced south across the Desna River, breaking through the 21st Army. At this time the division was part of the army's 66th Rifle Corps and suffered heavy losses. It was disbanded on 30 August.<cr><cr>The 467th Rifle Division started forming in the Stalingrad Military District on 14 December 1941. On 22 December the division was redesignated as the 266th Rifle Division at Kuybyshev in the Volga Military District. After it was redesignated, the division was moved a short distance west to the Volga River area near Stalingrad. It remained there, forming and training under the Stalingrad Military District, until April 1942, when it was assigned to the Reserve of the Supreme High Command (RVGK). In late April, the 266th joined the Southwestern Front's 6th Army. On 12 May, when the Kharkov offensive in the Second Battle of Kharkov began, the 266th was an assault unit and had the most success in its initial attacks. As a result, it was farther into the pocket when the German counterattack surrounded the army in the Izyum Pocket in late May. The division never made it out and the pocket was mopped up between 26 and 28 May. The 266th was officially disbanded on 30 May.<cr><cr>The 266th was reformed for a third time on 26 August 1942 in Kuybyshev Oblast, part of the Volga Military District. The 266th remained in the district until October, when it was assigned to the 4th Reserve Army in the Reserve of the Supreme High Command. On 10 November, the division went to the front with the army, which became the 2nd Guards Army and was assigned to the Southwestern Front. Just before it fought in Operation Little Saturn in December, the division transferred to the 3rd Guards Army's 14th Guards Rifle Corps.<cr><cr>In late February 1943, the division was with the 5th Tank Army. By the end of March 1943, it was back with the 3rd Guards Army. After April, the 266th was part of the 32nd Rifle Corps. On 5 September, the division fought in the recapture of Artemovsk during the Donbass Strategic Offensive, and it was later awarded the honorific 'Artemovsk'. In late October, the army became part of the 4th Ukrainian Front. On 13 February 1944, the division was awarded the Order of Suvorov, 2nd class. In late February, it was transferred to the 3rd Ukrainian Front's 6th Army with the 32nd Rifle Corps. The 266th became part of the 46th Army in March and transferred to front reserves in May. In June, it joined the 5th Shock Army. It fought in the Second Jassy–Kishinev Offensive with the army and moved into the RVGK with the army in September.<cr><cr>In late October, the division transferred with the 26th Guards Rifle Corps to the 1st Belorussian Front, where it fought for the rest of the war. In January 1945, during the Vistula–Oder Offensive, the division loaded 30 men into each of its 18 US 2.5 ton trucks, added enough 'collected vehicle' to motorize most of the 1006th Rifle Regiment heavy weapons, and used this improvised motor rifle force to support tank units pursuing retreating German troops across Poland. By this time most of the division artillery had been motorized with half-tracks, including both Lend-Lease US M3A1s and captured German vehicles. The division fought in the Battle of Berlin from April 1945. In the battle, it was with the 5th Shock Army's 26th Guards Rifle Corps, part of the 1st Belorussian Front.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/266th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 267th Infantry Divison fought at Brest-Litovsk, Bialystok, Bobruisk, Yelnya, Vyazma, and north of Moscow. It suffered greatly in the Soviet winter offensive of 1941–42. The division had lost so many horses from the cold, the lack of supplies, and lack of fodder that when it did have to retreat on December 17, 1941, it had to leave all of its artillery behind. It nevertheless remained in the line and fought in the defensive battles of Gshatsk, Juchnov and Spass-Demensk in 1942. It remained in the Spass-Demensk sector until August 1943, when it was sent back to Bryansk in September. From October 1943 to June 1944, it defended Mogilev and fought in all the major battles of Army Group Center until July 1944. At that time it was encircled and smashed near Minsk, along with the bulk of the 4th Army. The remnants of the division were finally destroyed near Memel on August 13. Its last commander, Lieutenant General Otto Drescher, was killed that day. The Horsehead Division was officially declared dissolved shortly afterwards.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The division began forming from reservists on 10 July 1941 at Stary Oskol, part of the Orel Military District. Its basic order of battle included the 844th, the 846th, and the 848th Rifle Regiments, as well as the 845th Artillery Regiment. By mid-August, the 268th had been assigned to the 52nd Army, defending the Volkhov River line near Leningrad, where it remained until early 1942. The division's positions were located in impassable swampy forests, and as a result it held a front of 34 kilometers in October 1941. From January 1942, the division fought in the Lyuban Offensive Operation, initially as part of the 2nd Shock Army Operations Group, attacking across the Volkhov. The Soviet attack achieved a breakthrough, and in February the 267th was transferred to General Korovnikov's Operational Mobile Group of the 59th Army, which was attempting to exploit the breakthrough by advancing into the rear of the German troops besieging Leningrad. A German counterattack in the spring cut off the 2nd Shock Army and the 59th Army, and the division was trapped in the swamps west of Volkhov. It took several months for the German forces to completely clear the pocket, but by 1 June the division had only 2687 men, 964 officers, and 773 non-commissioned officers. After the pocket was eliminated, the 267th was officially disbanded on 30 July 1942.

The division was reformed on 12 September 1942 at Serpukhov, part of the Moscow Military District, with the same basic order of battle as the previous division. In mid-September the 267th was transferred to the Moscow Defence Zone for training, and in late November it was sent to the front as part of the 6th Army of the Voronezh Front. At the end of 1942 the division moved south with the 6th Army to the Southwestern Front, and fought in the Soviet offensive in early 1943 towards Kharkov and the northern Donbass. The 267th remained with the 6th Army until September 1943, and was usually part of the 15th Rifle Corps. In September, the division was withdrawn to the Reserve of the Supreme High Command (RVGK), but returned to the front a month later in the 28th Army of the 4th Ukrainian Front. It was transferred to the 5th Shock Army's 63rd Rifle Corps in November, and in January 1944 was withdrawn to the RVGK with the 63rd Corps.

In February, the corps and the 267th joined the 51st Army, with which they fought in the Crimean Offensive in May 1944. After the recapture of Crimea, the 51st Army became part of the RVGK and moved north to the 1st Baltic Front. By 27 July, the division was fighting at Siauliai during the Siauliai Offensive. On 15 August, the division was fighting off armored counterattacks from the Grossdeutschland Division and the 4th and 12th Panzer Divisions at Auce. From late August to the end of the war, the 267th was part of the army's 1st Guards Rifle Corps. In February 1945, the army transferred to the 2nd Baltic Front, and it spent the last weeks of the war blockading German troops trapped in the Courland Pocket.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/267th_Rifle_Division</url>

The 268th Infantry Division invaded Russia on June 22, 1941, and spent the rest of its career on the Russian Front. Here it fought in the Brest-Litovsk sector, at Bialystok, Smolensk, in the Battle of the Yelnya Bend, at Vyazma, before Moscow, against the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42, in the defensive actions of 1942, and in the Rzhev withdrawal. In the summer of 1943 it suffered such heavy losses in the Battle of Kursk and the associated retreat (including the battles of Bryansk and Mogilev) that it was down to battle group strength by October. It was downgraded to Division Group 268 on November 2, 1943. Simultaneously, it was attached to the 36th Motorized Division.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The division began forming on 26 June 1941 at Mozyr in the Western Front as the 12th NKVD Mountain Division with a cadre of border guards. It was almost immediately redesignated the 268th Rifle Division and transferred to the army, and by 10 July it moved back to Moscow to keep ahead of the German advance. Its basic order of battle included the 942nd, 947th, and the 952nd Rifle Regiments, as well as the 799th Artillery Regiment. In late July, the 268th was moved to the Leningrad Front, where it was assigned to the 8th Army around 1 August. After six weeks the division was transferred to the 55th Army, defending positions along the Neva River, where it remained until September 1942. In January 1943, just before Operation Iskra, which eased the Siege of Leningrad, the division was in front reserves. At the beginning of the offensive on 12 January, the 136th Rifle Division and the 268th, supported by tanks and artillery, captured a bridgehead between Shlisselburg and Gorodok 1 that was approximately 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) wide and 3 kilometres (1.9 mi) deep. In the spring of 1943, the 268th was moved back to the 55th Army, and in May became part of the 67th Army. It absorbed troops from the disbanded 55th Naval Rifle Brigade in September. On 21 January 1944, the division attacks towards the Mga station and captured it. During the Vyborg-Petrozavodsk Offensive north of Leningrad in June and July, the division was part of the 21st Army's 110th Rifle Corps. After the end of the first phase of the offensive, which forced Finland to leave World War II, the 110th Rifle Corps and the division were relocated to the 42nd Army in the Baltics by August. The division spent last two months of the war in the spring of 1945 blockading trapped German forces in the Courland Pocket.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/268th_Rifle_Division

The 269th Infantry Division crossed into Russia with Army Group North on June 22 and played a major role in the XXXX Panzer Corps’ annihilation of the Russian III Armored Corps on the Dubysa. The division was down to 40 percent of its authorized strength by October, but still fought well in the Battle of the Volkhov, southeast of Leningrad, in early 1942. Meanwhile, it disbanded its III/469th, III/489th and II/490th Infantry Battalions.In the winter of 1942-43, the 269th was sent to Norway to rest and refit and remained on occupation duty at Bergen for more than a year and a half. In October 1944, it returned to the European mainland via Denmark and fought in the Vosges Mountains and in the Battle of the Colmar Bridgehead on the Western Front, where it was again reduced to battle group strength. In January 1945, it was transferred to southern Poland. (By now its 490th Grenadier Regiment had been disbanded and the other two regiments had only two battalions each.)
