28th Antiaircraft Battalion<cr><cr>The 28th Tank Division is famous in Soviet Army lore because of its leadership. The division commander. Colonel Chernyakovskii, went on to become the youngest Front commander in the Red Army (he rose from Colonel to Colonel-General in 3 years ! ) , and the commander of 55th Tank Regiment was one of the
first Heroes of the Soviet Union in the war. The division was nearly complete in artillery and personnel, but had no modern tanks and only 230 light tanks, mostly BT-5 and BT-7 types, and a 'handful' of old T-28 medium tanks, on 22 June 1941.<cr>The 28th Motorized Rifle regiment was separated from the rest of the division and went into battle independantly along the Baltic coast. The remainder of the division suffered heavy casualties from German air attacks in the first days of the war, so 125th Tank Regiment, from 202nd Mechanized Division, was placed under 28th Tank's command on 26 June and served with the division from then on. Retreating across the Baltic states, on 14 September the division HQ also took control of 3rd NKVD Motorized Rifle Regiment.<cr>In November 1941 the remnants of the division were reorganized as 241st Rifle Division.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 290th Infantry Division invaded the Soviet Union with the LVI Panzer Corps of Army Group North in June 1941. It was an effective fighting unit. The 290th Infantry spearheaded the initial attack into Russia and played a major role in the capture of Dvinsk. In August it fought in the First Battle of Lake lImen and was surrounded in the Demyansk Pocket in January 1942. The division’s freedom of action was not restored until February 1943. It then fought at Dno, Lake Ladoga, and the Battle of Nevel that winter. By the fall of 1943, the division was down to six grenadier battalions and its tank destroyer and reconnaissance battalions had been consolidated into a single schnelle battalion. The division suffered heavy losses in the Leningrad withdrawal and was isolated in the Memel by October. Its 503rd Grenadier Regiment was disbanded that fall, and it was down to four grenadier battalions and three artillery battalions. It remained in the Courland Pocket, holding off several Soviet attacks, until March 1945, when it boarded ships and was sent to Neutief on the Frische Nehrung in East Prussia. It both inflicted and suffered heavy casualties in the last Soviet attempts to crush the Army of East Prussia. The 290th Infantry Division remained isolated in East Prussia until the end of hostilities and surrendered to the Red Army in May 1945.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The 290th Rifle Division began forming on 12 July 1941 at Kalyazin in the Moscow Military District from reservists. Its basic order of battle included the 878th, 882nd, and the 885th Rifle Regiments, as well as the 827th Artillery Regiment. After only five weeks, the division was assigned to the 50th Army. In late September, the division was encircled in the Bryansk pocket by Operation Typhoon, the German advance on Moscow. The division's remnants broke out from the pocket by 23 October. On 27 November the 827th Artillery Regiment was removed from the division and replaced by the 1420th Artillery Regiment on 22 January 1942. In May, the 290th transferred to the Western Front's 10th Army. During the last four months of 1943, the division was part of the 33rd Army, 49th Army, and the 68th Army, as it advanced from Smolensk to the Mogilev-Orsha line on the Dnieper. At the end of the year, the 290th transferred back to the 10th Army, but in spring 1944 it was moved to the 49th Army. The division fought in Operation Bagration and was awarded the Order of Kutuzov, 2nd class, for recapturing Grodno. By August it began to outrun its supply lines, and received 1200 rear area conscripts and militia from Grodno, and 380 newly drafted civilians from areas it advanced through as replacements. In September, the 290th was transferred to the 3rd Army of the 2nd Belorussian Front, with which it fought in the Vistula-Oder Offensive and the East Pomeranian Offensive in early 1945. At the very end of the war, the 3rd Army was transferred to the 1st Belorussian Front, and became part of the front reserve during the Battle of Berlin. By the end of the war, the division's honorifics were 'Mogilev, Order of the Red Banner, Orders of Suvorov and Kutuzov.'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/290th_Rifle_Division

On June 22-23, the first two days of the invasion, the 291st penetrated forty-four miles in the first thirty-four hours-an astonishing total for a non-motorized infantry division in combat. It soon loosely surrounded Riga and repulsed several desperate attempts by the Soviet garrison to break out of the city. Although casualties were heavy, the division held its line, and contained and eventually helped destroy the Russian garrison. Later that year, it took the major Soviet naval base at Liepaja after a bitter struggle.Remaining with Army Group North, the 291st fought in the Battle of Volkhov (January-March 1942) before being transferred to the Velikie Luki sector of Army Group Center in late 1942. It held a sector of the line here for several months. During the winter of 1942-43, three of its grenadier battalions were disbanded and the remnants were merged together to form a single ski battalion. In October 1943, it joined Army Group South, fought at Kiev, suffered heavy losses in the retreat through the northern Ukraine and, as part of the 1st Panzer Army, again suffered heavy losses in the Kamenets-Podolsky ('Hube Pocket') battles of 1944. (During these battles, the 1st Panzer Army was surrounded but-brilliantly led by General Hube-it formed a 'floating pocket' and broke out, despite the efforts of several Soviet armies to destroy it.)The 291st was rebuilt as a 1944 type division in February 1944, when each of its grenadier regiments was reduced to two battalions. It also absorbed the 1st Reserve Grenadier Regiment of the 141st Reserve Division. Several months later, on September 10, 1944, it also absorbed the 1135th Grenadier Brigade. Although still greatly reduced in numbers, the 291st took part in the retreat across eastern Poland and fought in the Vistula campaign of late 1944. The veteran infantry division was finally smashed on January 27, 1945, when it tried unsuccessfully to block the Soviet advance into Silesia. The following month, the remnants of the Elk Division were placed under the command of a special staff, directed by Colonel Georg Heinlein (commander of the 504th Grenadier Regiment) and were absorbed by the 6th Infantry Division.German Order of Battle Vol II 291st - 999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions and Special Divisions in WWII, Samue; W. Mitcham Jr.

With the inclusion of regular Red Army cadre, the 291st Rifle Division was formed from the barely raised 11th Moscow Militia Division on the 12th of July 1941, at Rybinsk. Barely a month later the Division was engaged in the defense of Leningrad, assigned to the 23rd and then 55th Army until 1943. With the lifting of the siege the Division was assigned to the 67th and then 21st Army, fighting its way across Poland, Germany and into Czechoslovakia. The Division was awarded the Order of the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Kutuzov and the honorific GATCHINA. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/291st_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 292nd Infantry Division crossed the Bug River with Army Group Center in June 1941, it fought at Brest and Bialystok, in the Battle of the Yelnya Bend, at Vyazma, and in the subsequent drive on Moscow. It helped check the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42, took part in the defensive actions of 1942 (including Gshatsk and Vjasma), the Rzhev withdrawal (1943), the Battle of Kursk (where it sustained heavy casualties), and Gomel. It took part in the fighting on the Sozh and the Pripjet (Pripyet) marshes, Pinsk, Ostrow, and Narev, and in theretreat in to Poland. Down to battle group strength, it retreated through Poland and was destroyed in the Heiligenbeil Pocket in East Prussia in March 1945. Its survivors were absorbed by other divisions on the Hela peninsula that same month.German Order of Battle Vol II 291st - 999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions and Special Divisions in WWII, Samue; W. Mitcham Jr.

The 292nd Rifle Division started forming on the 2nd July 1941 from reservists in the Moscow Military District. Only partially formed the Division was rushed north for the defense of Leningrad in August 1941. The Division took part in battles on the Volkhov river and at Tikhvin but suffered such heavy casualties it was disbanded in November 1941. The Division was raised for a second time from a Rifle Brigade in June 1942. In August 1942 it was assigned to the 24th Army but suffered such heavy casualties trying to stop the Axis drive on Stalingrad that it was again disbanded in November 1942. The Division was raised for the third time in July 1943 from reserves of the Transbaikal Front. It spent the remainder of the war in the Soviet Far East and took part in the invasion of Manchuria. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/292nd_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 293rd Infantry Division crossed into Russia on June 22 and fought at Brest-Litovsk, Pinsk, Gomel, Kiev, and Bryansk and against the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42. It occupied a sector near Mzensk (not far from Orel) from February to September 1942, and a zone in the vicinity of Bolchov (also near Orel) until June 1943. It fought in the Battle of Kursk in July and at Bryansk in August, and suffered heavy losses at Kharkov in September. Remaining in the line at Kampfgruppe strength, the 293rd fought at Krementschug and Uman in October and November. The battered division was downgraded to Division Group 293 on November 2, 1943, and was assigned to Corps Detachment A. It was finally destroyed at Jassy, Romania, in August and September 1944.German Order of Battle Vol II 291st - 999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions and Special Divisions in WWII, Samue; W. Mitcham Jr.

The 293rd Soviet Rifle Division had a fortunate history in that it was on the periphery of a number of major military disasters in 1941/42 but escaped the fate of being encircled and destroyed. The Division started forming on the 18th July 1941, at Sumy, from reservists in the Kharkov Military District. The Division was rushed into the defense of Kiev in August 1941 but avoided being trapped in the Kiev pocket and spent the winter in the vicinity of Kursk. In 1942 the Division was involved in fighting around Kharkov, assigned to the 21st Army, and once again avoided being trapped, like some of its fellow divisions. The Division retreated all the way to the Don and was withdrawn into Reserve into the Southern Urals, as it was down to about 1,500 men. In October 1942 the Division was back to near full strength and fought with some distinction at Stalingrad. For this it was renamed the 66th Guards Rifle Division in January 1943. The Division was raised for the second time in July 1943 from reserves of the Transbaikal Front. It spent the remainder of the war in the Soviet Far East and took part in the invasion of Manchuria. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/293rd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 294th Infantry Division crossed into southern Russia in the summer of 1941 and was involved in the drive on Kiev, in the capture of Kharkov and the Donetz, and in the checking of the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42. Remaining with Army Group South, it was used to stabilize the 3rd Romanian Army in the fall of 1942, and suffered heavy casualties when the Romamans collapsed and set up the Stalingrad debacle.The bulk of the 8th Luftwaffe Field Division was attached to the 294th in late 1942 during the retreat from the Volga. Remaining in the line, the 294th Infantry fought on the Mius and at Stalino, and was later encircled at Taganrog in August, and again sustained heavy losses in the ensuing breakout. After this, the veteran division was reorganized. It absorbed the remnants of the 333rd Infantry Division and now included the 513rd and 514th Grenadier Regiments (two battalions each), Divisional Group 333 (with the 679th and 680th Regimental Groups), the 333rd Fusilier Battalion, the 333rd Artillery Regiment, the 294th Artillery Regiment, the combined 294th Tank Destroyer/Reconnaissance Battalion, and the usual divisional supply units. The 294th Infantry Division returned to the front and fought in the Nikopol Bridgehead and at Odessa. It was again surrounded and finally destroyed at Kischinev, Romania, west of the lower Dnestr, on August 26, 1944. The few soldiers that escaped the disaster were on leave or in medical facilities. They were attached to the 333rd Infantry Division, which absorbed them when the 294th Infantry Division was officially disbanded on October 9, 1944.German Order of Battle Vol II 291st - 999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions and Special Divisions in WWII, Samue; W. Mitcham Jr.

The 294th Rifle Division started forming on the 10th July 1941 at Lipetsk, from reservists in the Orel Military District. The Division was given 2 months to complete formation and then moved north for the defense of Leningrad in September 1941. The Division took up positions east of the city in the Volkhov river area. In March 1942 the divisional commander, A.A. Kichkailov, was killed in action and the division suffered heavy casualties. In May 1943 the division was assigned to the 52nd Army with which it remained till the end of the war. The Division fought in the Ukraine, Poland, Germany and Czechoslovakia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/294th_Rifle_Division A.A. Maslov, Fallen Soviet Generals Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 295th Infantry Division was formed in February 1940 as part of the 8th Wave. It contained the 516th, 517th and 518th Infantry Regiments, 295th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the IV Army Corps in Army Group South at the start of Operation Barbarossa. The division was destroyed at Stalingrad in January 1943. In February 1943 it was initially reformed as a Kampfgruppe with a single grenadier regiment with three battalions and an artillery battalion. In March 1943 it was sent to Norway where it served as a static fortress division. Over the next few months it expanded to two regiments with four battalions each. The division was taken prisoner in Norway at wars end by the British.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 295th Rifle Division started forming on the 10th July 1941 at Chuguyev, from reservists in the Kharkov Military District, and by August was defending Kiev. The Division was trapped and destroyed in the Kiev pocket, although one infantry regiment did escape. The Division was formed for a second time near Kursk, in October 1941 and was assigned to the 37th Army of the Southern Front. In June 1942 the division performed defensive operations and retreated into the Caucasus, all the way to the Terek River. With the Axis retreat the division distinguished itself in the pursuit and the recapture of Kherson in late 1943. In 1944 the Division fought in the Ukraine and late that year, assigned to the 32nd Rifle Corps, 5th Shock Army ended the war in Berlin. A highly decorated Division, it was awarded the Order of Lenin, Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov and the honorific KHERSON. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/295th_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 296th Infantry Division was formed in February 1940 as part of the 8th Wave. It contained the 519th, 520th and 521st Infantry Regiments, 296th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the IV Army Corps in Army Group South at the start of Operation Barbarossa. During 1943 the division was reorganized into a Type 44 division with three grenadier regiments of two battalions each, a fusilier battalion, an artillery regiment and various support troops. In June 1944 the division was destroyed in the Bobruisk pocket and it was formally disbanded in August 1944.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 296th Rifle Division was formed in early July 1941 in the Odessa Military District and in August was assigned to the 9th Army of the Southern Front. In March 1942 the Division was assigned to the 37th Army and avoided destruction at Kharkov. The Division was pursued by Axis forces all the way into the Caucasus and by August 1942, had suffered such heavy casualties that it was disbanded. The remnants were used as reinforcements for the 242nd Rifle Division. The Division was formed for a 2nd time in July 1943, in Georgia, and spent the rest of the war on the Turkish or Iranian border. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/296th_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 297th Infantry Division first saw action in Russia with Army Group South in July 1941. It fought at Zhitomir (July), Uman (August), Kiev (September), Kharkov (November), and Rostov (November-December), and opposed the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42. In 1942, it was with the 6th Army in the Battle of Kharkov, in the clearing of the Izyum Pocket, in the drive across the Don, and in the Battle of Voronezh. It was subsequently encircled at Stalingrad with the 6th Army and destroyed there on January 25, 1943. German Order of Battle Vol II 291st - 999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions and Special Divisions in WWII, Samue; W. Mitcham Jr.

The 297th Rifle Division started forming on the 2nd July 1941 at Lubny, from reservists in the Kharkov Military District and later on elements of the Kremenchug Militia Division, and by September was assigned to the defense of Kiev. The Division was lucky to escape the Kiev pocket and in October was assigned to the 21st Army in the Kursk sector. In May 1942 the Division was initially held in reserve during the 2nd Battle of Kharkov but suffered such heavy casualties in defensive operations and the subsequent retreat that it was disbanded in July 1942. The Division was formed for a second time on the 25th July 1943 from the 253rd Rifle Brigade and was assigned to the 33rd Rifle Corps of the Southwestern Front. The Division fought with some distinction, including the siege of Budapest, and ended the war fighting near Vienna, assigned to the 46th Army. A decorated Division, it was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Bogdan Khmelnitsky and the honorifics KIROVOGRAD and SLAVYANSK. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/297th_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 298th Infantry Division was formed in February 1940 as part of the 8th Wave. It contained the 525th, 526th and 527th Infantry Regiments, 298th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was part of the XVII Army Corps in Army Group South at the start of Operation Barbarossa. The division suffered heavy losses serving along the Don River with the Italian Eighth Army during Operation Little Saturn. The survivors were merged with two other divisions to form a new 387th Infantry Division in March 1943.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 298th Rifle Division started forming on the 2nd July 1941, at Kalinin, from reservists in the Moscow Military District and by September was assigned to the 13th Army, Bryansk Front. When the Axis resumed the drive on Moscow, the Division was trapped in the Bryansk pocket and destroyed. The Division was formed for a second time in January 1942, at Barnaul, in the Siberian Mlitary District and was assigned to the 50th Army of the Western Front. As the Axis closed in on Stalingrad the Division was transferred south to the Stalingrad sector where it fought with distinction in the Soviet offensive. The Division was assigned to the 21st Army in mopping up the pocket and in March 1943 was renamed the 80th Guards Rifle Division. The Division was formed for a third time in July 1943, in the Transbaikal Front, and in 1945 was assigned to the 36th Army where it took part in the invasion of Manchuria. For this action it was awarded the honorific of 'KHINGAN'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/298th_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 297th Infantry Division was involved in the initial invasion of southern Russia in June 1941, and was almost continuously engaged after that, fighting at Zhitomir and Kiev, in the Donets, and at Kursk (1941). It held a sector in the vicinity of Livny (east of Orel) from January 1942 to August 1943. That fall it fought in the Battles of Bryansk and Gomel in 1943, and distinguished itself as a good combat division, although three of its infantry battalions had to be disbanded due to heavy casualties. The survivors of these units were transferred to other grenadier battalions within the division.On June 22, 1944, the Russians launched their massive summer offensive with 2.5 million men, and their opening attack struck the 299th Infantry; it collapsed within a few hours. Only remnants escaped, but these (along with men returning from leave or convalescent facilities) were used to form a new 299th Infantry Division. This formation, a mere skelton of the original 299th, was the former Corps Detachment G and included the former Division Groups 57, 299, and 337 (now the 528th, 529th, and 530th Grenadier Regiments, respectively), the 299th Artillery Regiment, and assorted divisional troops. It took part in the Polish campaign of 1944 and in the retreat behind the Vistula, and it continued to fight on the Eastern Front until February 26, 1945, when it was practically destroyed on the Heiligenbeil landfront in northern East Prussia. The remnants of the 299th Infantry Division were officially disbanded on April 4, 1945. Its survivors were used to help form Infantry Division Schlageter (RAD Division Nr. 1).German Order of Battle Vol II 291st - 999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions and Special Divisions in WWII, Samue; W. Mitcham Jr.

The 299th Rifle Division started forming on the 10th July 1941, at Belgorod, from reservists in the Orel Military District and by early September was assigned to the 50th Army, Bryansk Front. When the Axis resumed the drive on Moscow, the Division was fortunate not to be trapped in the Bryansk Front but suffered such heavy casualties it was reduced to 800 men and by mid November was officially disbanded. The Division was formed for a second time in June 1942, at Kovrov, in the Moscow Military District based on an existing Rifle Brigade, and was eventually assigned to the 66th Army of the Stalingrad Front. The Division fought in the Soviet counter offensive, in mopping up the Stalingrad pocket, and in July 1943 was assigned to the 53rd Army, Steppe Front where it fought at Kharkov. In September 1944 the Division was assigned to the 57th Army and fought at Belgrade, Budapest and Lake Balaton. The Division was awarded the honorific of 'KHARKOV'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/299th_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 29th Army was first formed in July 1941 in the Moscow Military District on the basis of 30th Rifle Corps. The 245th, 252nd, 254th and 256th Rifle Divisions, and a number of smaller units made up the Army. It joined the Reserve Front and conducted defensive works at Staraya Russa, Demyansk, Ostashkov, Selizharovo. It was reassigned on July 21, 1941, to the Western Front, took part in the Battle of Smolensk, conducted defensive fights in area to the south of the city of Toropets. On October 17 it joined the Kalinin Front and participated in the defense of Kalinin, and the Kalinin, Rzhev-Vyazma 1942, and Rzhev-Sychyovka offensive operations (the Battles of Rzhev). From the end of August 1942 the army defended occupied boundaries on the left bank of the Volga River. In the beginning of February, 1943 the Army's units were transferred to 5th and 20th Armies, and the headquarters was reorganised as headquarters 1st Tank Army.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Combined_Arms_Army

The 29th Mechanized (Motor Rifle) Division was formed at Omsk as the 4th Rifle Division in September 1920. In November of the same year it became the 29th Rifle Division. It became a motorized division in July 1940. At the start of At the start of Operation Barbarossa the division was deployed with the Western Special Military District. The division was destroyed near Minsk in July of 1941 and formally disbanded in September. The division was reformed from the 7th Moscow People's Militia Division in July 1941 and destroyed at Vyazma in October 1941.On December 5, 1941, the reforming of the 29th Rifle Division began in Akmolinsk, Kazakhstan and its organization was completed on January 16, 1942. The division was reformed on the basis of the short lived 459th Rifle Division. The division was consisted of the 106th, 128th and 299th Rifle Regiments, the 77th Artillery Regiment, the 125th Anti-Tank Battalsion and various other support units. The division was held in reserve until June 1942, when its men were deemed to have received sufficient training. In July 1943 the 29th Rifle Division was ordered to Stalingrad and joined the 64th Army. In August 1942 units of the division first made contact with the Germans. During the Battle of Stalingrad they killed 5,242 and took 13,447 Axis soldiers captive. For its service at Stalingrad the 29th Rifle Division was redesignated the 72nd Guard Rifle Division by Directorate of the General Staff order ?104 on March 1, 1943.The 29th Rifle Division was recreated in 1943 and saw action at Kirovograd. It gained the honorific 'Polotsk' serving with the 6th Guards Army of the Kurland Group in May 1945. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Motor_Rifle_DivisionEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 'Falcon Division', as it was nicknamed, performed in an outstanding manner in all of its battles. Crossing into Russia in 1941, it fought in the Bialystok and Minsk encirclements, in the Dniepr crossings, at Smolensk, Bryansk, Tula (in the Moscow sector), and against the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-42. In 1942, it fought in the 2nd Battle of Kharkov, in the Don crossings, in the drive on the Volga and at Stalingrad, where it was itself surrounded in November 1942, and was destroyed in the southern Stalingrad pocket on January 31, 1943. Even as late as January 12, 1943, when it was in its death throes, the 29th, together with the 3rd Motorized Infantry Division, repulsed ten to twelve Soviet divisions and knocked out 100 tanks, all in a single day.German Order of Battle Vol III - Panzer, Panzer Grenadier and Waffen SS Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The corps was originally designated the 29th Lithuanian Territorial Rifle Corps and consisted of troops of the former Lithuanian National Army. At the outbreak of hostilities in June 1941, it was part of 11th Army and consisted of 179th and 184th Rifle Divisions. It fought around Velikiye Luki in July-August 1941 and launched a successful counterattack against 19th Panzer Division on July 21st that temporarily recaptured the city. The corps was disbanded in September 1941. It was reformed in July 1943 in Kursk as part of 13th Army and participated in the Battle of the Dnieper of 1943, and the Belorussian Offensive of June-August 1944. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Rifle_Corps_(Soviet_Union) Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 29th Rifle Division was officially redesignated as a motorised division on 4 July 1940. With 6th Mechanized Corps, 10th Army, Western Front on 22 June 1941. Poirer and Connor appear to say it was wiped out near Minsk in July 1941. It was formally disbanded on 19 September 1941.It was then recreated from the 7th Moscow People's Militia Division in July 1941, and again wiped out at Vyazma in October 1941.On December 5, 1941, recreation of the 29th Rifle Division began in Akmolinsk, Kazakhstan, and its organization was completed on January 16, 1942. It was reformed on the basis of the very short lived 459th Rifle Division. The division was made up of 106th, 128th, 299th Rifle and 77th Artillery Regiments. Other units included the 125th Anti-Tank, 78th Sapper, 124th Signal, and 29th Medical Battalions, and the 104th Reconnaissance Company. The division was held in reserve until June 1942, when its men were deemed to have received sufficient training. In July 1942 29th Rifle Division was ordered to move to Stalingrad and join the 64th Army. In August 1942 units of the division first met with the Germans. During Battle of Stalingrad they killed 5,242 and took 13,447 captive. On February 2, 1943, the Battle of Stalingrad was finally over. Due to the heroism of the soldiers, the 29th Rifle Division (2nd formation) was redesignated the 72nd Guards Rifle Division by Directorate of the General Staff order No.104 on March 1, 1943.The 29th Rifle Division was recreated in 1943 and saw action at Kirovograd. It gained the honorific 'Polotsk' and the Order of Suvorov, 2nd class. With 6th Guards Army of the Kurland Group (Leningrad Front) May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 29th Tank Corps was formed February 1943 in Moscow Military District as part of STAVKA Reserves.The 29th Tank Corps was immediately (15 March 1943) assigned to 5th Guards Tank Army, which was being reformed after the winter battles. The corps remained under 5th Guards Tank Army until May 1945. By 1 July 1943 the tank army was in Steppe Front behind the Kursk salient.<cr>On the morning of 12 July, in the 'biggest tank battle of the war' at Prokhorovka, 29th Tank Corps was right in the middle of 5th Guards Tank Army's attacking line. The corps lost 60% of its tanks on that day and the next, and spent the last two weeks of July repairing and average of 20 tanks a day to
rebuild the tank brigades. 29th Tank Corps fought in the Battle of Kharkov and the advance to the Dnepr River throughout August-December 1943. In September 1943 1549th Heavy SU Regiment (SU-152s) was added to the corps, and in October 1943 the corps finally received its rocket unit: 11th Guards Mortar Battalion (8 BM-13 launchers) . 38th Armored Car Battalion was removed after the Kursk Battle, and the 1446th SU Regiment re-equipped with SU-85s sometime in late 1943. Also during the continuous reinforcement of the corps to try to cover the casualties, all the tank brigades were completely re-equipped with T-34 tanks in 3 tank battalions of 65 tanks by the end of 1943.<cr>29th Tank Corps also received recognition for its performance in combat. On 10 December 1943 the corps received the honorific title 'Znamenskikh' for liberating Znamensk, and on 8 January 1944 the corps received the Order of the Red Banner for its performance in the Kirovograd Operation. In February, for its exploits during the Korsun-Shevchenkovskii ('Korsun Pocket') Operation, the 1549th Heavy SU Regiment became the 339th Guards Heavy SU Regiment, and then was removed from the corps so it could be sent into reserve and re-equipped. In May 1944 29th Tank Corps and 5th Guards Tank Army finally went into reserve after 9 months of almost continuous combat.<cr>The 29th Tank Corps was committed in the drive into the southern Baltic states in July 1944, and fought in that region for the rest of 1944. In addition to its assigned units, the corps frequently controlled or was directly supported by units from 5th Guards Tank Army and other units.In October 1944, 165th was redesignated as a Light Artillery Regiment (still with 24 76mm guns) and assigned to 29th Tank Corps permanently. When the Soviet offensives started in January 1945, 29th Tank Corps had been built up.<cr>On 14 January 1945, when the corps went over to the offensive, it had 149 tanks and 111 SUs on hand - which meant that the tank brigades were slightly under strength (averaging 50 tanks each out of 65 authorized) but the 4 SU regiments in the corps were almost 1/3 over strength! 29th Tank Corps ended the war in May 1945 in East Prussia, still part of 5th Guards Tank Army.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. The 29th Tank Division was formed in February 1941 at Grodno, Western Special Military District as part of 11th Mechanized Corps. On 22 June 1941 included: 57th Tank Regiment 1st Tank Bn - 3 KV and 24 T-34 tanks 2nd, 3rd Tank Bns - each 32 T-26 tanks 58th Tank Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd Tank Bns - each 32 T-26 tanks29th Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns 29th Motorized Howitzer Regiment - 1 light bn only 29th Reconnaissance Battalion 29th Motorized Pontoon BattalionThe 29th Tank Division was the best division in 11th Mechanized Corps, but on 22 June 1941 it had only 3 KVs, 24 T-34s, and 160 light T-26 tanks, including 19 OT-26 flamethrower tanks. The divisional artillery had no 152mm howitzers, the antiaircraft battalion had no guns at all, and there were 'almost no tractors for (any of) the artillery'. 15% of the tanks on hand were in the repair shops when the war started.Located at Grodno, near the border, 29th Tank Division went into battle on the afternoon of the first day of the war. The division speedily shot up and subsequently destroyed in the Bialystok and Minsk pockets. It was removed from the Soviet order of battle in the first week in July.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 2nd Air Army was formed on May 12, 1942, by an order of the NKO of May 5, 1942, within the Bryansk Front. It participated in defensive battles in the Voronezh sector, and then supported the troops of the Southwestern Front during the Battle of Stalingrad. In collaboration with the 8th, 16th and 17th Air Armies it fought for air superiority over the battlefield. The army participated in the Battle of Kursk , the Battle of the Dnieper, Zhitomir-Berdichev Offensive, the Korsun-Shevchenkovsky Offensive, Rivne-Lutsk, Proskurov-Chernivtsi, Lvov-Sandomierz, Sandomir-Silesian, Lower Silesian Offensive, Upper Silesian Offensive, Battle of Berlin and the Prague Offensive.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Air_Army

The corps was formed in April 1941 and consisted of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Airborne Brigades. In 1941, it fought as a part of the40th Army in Southwestern Front to defend Kiev. It escaped the collapse of the Kiev pocket in August with heavy losses and fought in the vicinity of Sumy in September. The corps was transferred to the Taman peninsula as part of 47th Army in May 1942 and converted to the 32nd Guards Rifle Division. in August. Hero of the Soviet Union Mikhail Tikhonov commanded the corps from July, 1941 until its conversion, and then commanded the division thereafter. The corps was reformed in December 1942 and converted, probably into a Guards Airborne Division in spring 1943.Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 2nd Army was activated on October 20, 1939 with General Maximilian von Weichs in command. First seeing service in France, the army was involved in the invasion of the Balkans, before offensive operations in the Ukraine as part of Operation Barbarossa.In 1942 the 2nd Army covered the northern wing of operation Fall Blau operating in the surroundings of Voronezh and suffered a major defeat during the soviet winter offensive that followed the battle of Stalingrad.In 1945 the army was redisgnated Army East Prussia and was pivotal in the defence of East and West Prussia before finally surrendering on 9 May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Army_(Wehrmacht)

The 2nd Belorussian Front was created in February 1944 as the Soviets pushed the Germans back towards Byelorussia. General Colonel Pavel Kurochkin became its first commander. In hiatus in April 1944, its headquarters was reformed from the army headquarters of the disbanding 10th Army.On 26 June 1944 the Front's forces captured Mogilev in the Mogilev Offensive. On 4 July, 2BF was tasked with mopping up the remains of Army Group Center's 4th Army under the command of General Kurt von Tippelskirch and the remains of the 9th Army in a large pocket southeast of Minsk. On 9 July The 2BF attacks northwest from Vitebsk as part of a major Soviet offensive east of Riga towards Rezekne in order to cut off the German Army Group North. On 29 July Soviets reach the coast cutting Army Group North off in Estonia and Eastern Latvia. On 13 September 2BF captured Lom?a, west of Bialystok. In November 1944 Marshal Konstantim Rokossovsky was appointed commander of 2BF just in time for its last two great offensives of World War II. As part of a massive attack by four Fronts on 14 January 1945 2BF attacked East Prussia (East Prussian Offensive) and later Pomerania (East Pomeranian Offensive).On 9 April 1945 Konigsberg in East Prussia finally fell to the Red Army. This freed up 2BF to move west to the east bank of the Oder river. During the first two weeks of April the Soviets performed their fastest Front redeployment of the war. General Georgy Zhukov concentrated his 1st Belorussian Front (1BF) which had been deployed along the Oder river from Frankfurt in the south to the Baltic, into an area in front of the Seelow Heights. The 2BF moved into the positions being vacated by the 1BF north of the Seelow Heights. While this redeployment was in progress gaps were left in the lines and the remnants of the German 11th Army which had been bottled up in a pocket near Danzig managed to escape across the Oder.In the early hours on 16 April the final offensive of the war to capture Berlin and link up with Western Allied forces on the Elbe started with attacks by 1BF and To the south General Ivan Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front (1UF). On 20 April the 2BF join in the attack. By 25 April 2BF broke out of its bridge head south of Stettin and had by the end of the war captured all of Germany north of Berlin as far west as the front lines of the British 21 Army Group which had advanced over the river Elbe in some places.Wikipedia 2nd Belorussian Front

The corps consisted of 9th, 5th, and 72nd cavalry divisions and 15th Motor Rifle Division. It was part of the 9th Army in the Odessa area in June 1941. It fought in Ukraine in the summer of 1941 and then was withdrawn to STAVKA reserve in the fall. It was reorganized as 1st Guards Cavalry Corps in November 1941. It was reformed in December 1941 from 62nd, 64th and 70th Cavalry Divisions as part of Southern Front. It was destroyed in the Second Battle of Kharkov where it fought as part of 6th Army. The corps was officially disbanded 15 July 1942. Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

Formed 1/19/42 from remnants of 1st Odessa Cavalry Division and Stalingrad Don Kazakh [Kuban] Militia Cavalry Division. Redesignated 15th Cavalry Division on 1/26/42. The 2nd Guards Airborne Division was formed from 7th Airborne Corps on 8 December 1942 in Zvenigorod. The division was fully equipped by January 1943 and concentrated in the area of Ostashkov. As a part of the 1st Shock Army, the division attacked the Demyansk Pocket on 26 February 1943. The division only advance 3 kilometers against the German forces and was replaced with the 250th Rifle Division after several days of heavy fighting. The division was transferred to the area of Slugin village. The division was now to take Lyahnovo village, which controlled a road out of the Demyansk Pocket. The 5th Guards Airborne Regiment crossed the Porus River and cut the road on 7 March. However, German counterattacks pushed the division out of Lyahnovo. The division was transferred to the rear afterwards.

The division then transferred to the 18th Guards Rifle Corps in the area of Kursk. They took positions in the second defensive line of the 13th Army, part of the Central Front. From 5 July to 23 August, the 2nd Guards Airborne fought in the Battle of Kursk. Between 26 August and 30 September, the division, now part of the 60th Army participated in the capture of Pryluky during the Chernigov-Pripyat Operation. On 2 October, the 7th Guards Airborne Regiment crossed the Dnieper, capturing a bridgehead near the village of Medwin in the Chernobyl Raion. On 18 November, it went to the village of Rakovic. It captured Radomyshl on 20 November as part of the 15th Rifle Corps. In January 1944, it fought in the Battle of the Korsun-Cherkassy Pocket. It captured Khmelnytskyi on 25 March during the Proskurov-Chernivtsi Offensive, for which it was given the title 'Proskurov'. On 29 March, it captured the villages of Berezhanka and Andreevka in the Chernivtsi Raion, in conjunction with the 62nd Guards Tank Brigade and the 64th Guards Tank Brigade. Between 13 July and 29 August, it fought in the Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive in Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. As part of the 17th Guards Rifle Corps, it captured the villages of Akreshory and Prokurava on 12 September. With the aid of a Katyusha rocket launcher battery, the division captured the Haarde (mountain) in the Carpathian Mountains on 13 September. On 22 September, the division captured Vorokhta and Yablonitsky Pass. It entered the village of Tatarov on the next day. In October 1944, it fought in the Battle of the Dukla Pass. It captured Mukacheve on 26 October 1944. It captured Uzhhorod on the next day.

The division advanced into Czechoslovakia, capturing Michalovce on 26 November. In conjunction with the 5th Guards Tank Brigade, it captured Kralovsky Chlmec on 27 November. Between December 1944 and January 1945, it crossed the Hornad River and fought south of Kosice. On 25 March 1945, it fought in the Moravska Ostrava Operation and seized a bridgehead on the Oder on 19 April. After advancing across Czechoslovakia, the division was disbanded in late June 1945.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Guards_Airborne_Division</url>

The 2nd Guards Army was formed according to the order of the Staff of the Supreme High Command (Stavka) from October 23, 1942, on the basis of the 1st Reserve Army. Formation and training took place in Tambov, Michurinsk and Morshansk areas. On 1 November 1942 the Combat composition of the Soviet Army lists 1st Reserve Army with the 1st Guards Rifle Corps - 24th Guards, 33rd Guards and 98th rifle divisions [under Guards General-Major I. I. Missan], and the 13th Guards Rifle Corps with the 49th Guards, 3rd Guards and 387th divisions.<cr>By the time of the Battle of Stalingrad, the 2nd Guards Army had become one of the most powerful units in the Red Army. The 2nd Guards Army appeared on the scene after the Soviet Operation Uranus had successfully encircled the German Sixth Army at Stalingrad in November 1942. In December 1942, as preparations started for Operation Saturn, the 2nd Guards Army was ordered by Joseph Stalin to prepare for an attack on Rostov. The assault and capture of Rostov was the ultimate goal of the Red Army for Operation Saturn.<cr>In December 1942, plans for Operation Saturn had to be altered. The German Operation Wintergewitter, led by Field Marshal Erich von Manstein's Army Group Don, made an attack on the Stalingrad Front in an effort to relieve the Sixth Army in Stalingrad. Thus, Operation Saturn was changed to Operation Little Saturn, which was to be a counter-attack that would be launched as soon as Operation Wintergewitter ended. The German forces, spearheaded by Army Group Hoth, made rapid initial advances but was stalled at the Myshkova River. Colonel-General Hermann Hoth's panzer divisions were at a standstill and were suffering heavy casualties, even before the bulk of the 2nd Guards Army had arrived. By this time, Manstein realized that the operation was a failure. The 2nd Guards Army, under General Rodion Malinovsky, had been transferred to the Stalingrad Front to halt the offensive. Stalin had agreed to this decision.<cr>In February 1944, the Army relocated to the area of the Perekop Isthmus. The Crimean Offensive was launched across the Perekop Isthmus on 8 April 1944 by elements of the 2nd Guards Army and 51st Army, under the 4th Ukrainian Front. In cooperation with other troops of the 4th Ukrainian Front and the Black Sea Fleet, Sevastopol was liberated on May 9, 1944. In May and June the 2nd Guards Army was relocated to the area of the cities Dorogobuzh Elnya. On May 20, was moved to the Reserve of the Supreme High Command and on July 8 the unit was a part of the 1st Baltic Front. By that time, it consisted of the 11th and the 13th and 54th Guards Rifle Corps. In this structure, on 5–20 July 1944 took part in the Vilnius Offensive/operation at the end of July, and in the Siauliai offensive reflect enemy counterattacks west and north-west of Siauliai. In October, the 2nd Guards Army participated in the Memel offensive. On December 20 it was reassigned to the 3rd Belorussian Front.<cr>During the East Prussian Offensive in January-April 1945, the army broke through long-term German strategic defenses, eliminated in conjunction with other troops surrounded the front of its group (south-west of Königsberg and Samland group).<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Guards_Army</url>

Formed 11/26/1941 from 9th Cavalry Division as part of I Guards Cavalry Corps, it was part of Southwestern Front reserve. It was awarded the honorific titles 'Krimskaya' and 'In the name of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic'. Fought in the Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive and the Dniepr-Carpathian Offensive in 1944 and in the Battle of Berlin in 1945 as part of 1st Ukrainian Front.
