It fought in the Jassy-Kischinev Offensive in the summer of 1944 and advanced into Romania before being transferred to Poland and fighting in the Vistula-Oder Offensive in early 1945. It fought in theBattle of Berlin and was disbanded postwar in western Ukraine in mid-1946.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/31st_Rifle_DivisionEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 31st Tank Corps was forming at Oboyan at the beginning of July 1943 when it was thrown into action with the rest of 1st Tank Army against 4th Panzer Army's 48th Panzer Corps in the first days of the Battle of Kursk. Both 237th and 242nd Tank Brigades had 1/3 or more of their tank forces made up of Lend Lease M3 Grant tanks - nicknamed by their Russian crews 'a coffin for seven brothers', while the rest of the corps had T-34/76S. Without the usual supporting motorized riflemen, antitank. Guards Mortars, or antiaircraft units, the corps fought the battle of Kursk largely as separate tank brigades reinforcing other units, such as 1st Tank Army's 6th Tank Corps or 3rd Mechanized Corps. After the German drive on Kursk was stopped, 1st Tank Army had a short refitting rest and then went right into the 4th Battle for Kharkov and the advance to the Dnepr River and beyond.<cr>The 31st Tank Corps fought throughout this period while still trying to get organized, and did not receive all its required supporting units until nearly the end of 1943.<cr>The 31st Tank Corps finally finished forming in November 1943, after it had been sent back into STAVKA Reserves and given a chance to rest and refit after five months' of fighting semi-organized.<cr>Like many of the tank corps, 31st Tank Corps had a number of SU Regiments under command, depending on the mission. 1244th SU Regiment, for instance, was only with the corps for a few months, and then temporarily replaced by 400th Guards SU Regiment (SU-85s) in February 1944. By late March 1944 31st Tank Corps was in 1st Ukrainian Front reserves preparing for the spring offensives with only 1548th Heavy SU Regiment left of all the SU units it had controlled that winter. When 1st Ukrainian Front started the Lvov-Sandomir Operation in July 1944, 31st Tank Corps was paired with 6th Guards Cavalry Corps in the 2nd Cavalry-Mechanized Group.<cr>In September 1944, 269th Light Artillery Regiment (24 76mm guns) was added to the corps. At the end of 1944, as 1st Ukrainian Front was building up for the Vistula Oder Offensive in January 1945, 753rd Antitank Battalion was replaced in the corps with the 722nd SU Regiment (SU-76s) .<cr>This was the last organizational change made to 31st Tank Corps during the war. It remained as a separate tank corps in 1st Ukrainian Front, ending the war operating as a Mobile Group for 60th Army.<cr><cr>Soviet Order of Battle World War II Volume II by Charles C. Sharp

The 31st Tank Division was formed February 1941 near Botskyi in Western Special Military District as part of 13th Mechanized Corps with:61st Tank Regiment - 0 tanks 62nd Tank Regiment - 0 tanks 31st Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns 31st Howitzer Regiment 1 light, 1 medium bn 31st Reconnaissance Bn 1 co with 9 tankettes, 2 foot companies 31st Pontoon Battalion 31st Antiaircraft BattalionThe 31st Tank Division was virtually unformed when the Germans attacked on 22 June 1941. The division had only 15 BT tanks and some light amphibious tankettes on hand for training, no antiaircraft guns, and no tractors or trucks for the infantry or the howitzer regiment - which did, at least, have all its guns. Caught by German air attacks, the division was scattered and overrun almost immediately and the rest destroyed in the Bialystok pocket. The division was officially dissolved on 4 July 1941.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 320th Rifle Division was formed in September 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, based on an existing division of militia. This formation was devastated in the Kerch Penisula in May 1942, and officially disbanded before the end of the month. A second division began forming in the Transcaucasus in August, and served for the duration in the southern regions of the Soviet-German front. It distinguished itself in the liberation of Yenakiyevo in March 1943, but also suffered massive losses, including the death of the division's commanding officer, along the Dniestr River in May 1944. A substantially rebuilt division soldiered on through the Balkans, ending the war near Vienna.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/320th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 321st Rifle Division was formed in September 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, based on an existing division of militia. This formation had an extremely short career, coming under devastating attack in the north of the Crimea on the day of its redesignation and being officially disbanded just over a month later. A second division began forming in the Transbaikal in February 1942, and served in the defensive and offensive fighting around Stalingrad, eventually distinguishing itself sufficiently to be redesignated as the 82nd Guards Rifle Division. The world had not seen the last of the 321st, however, as a new division was formed from two existing rifle brigades in the spring of 1944, which gave very creditable service for the duration, completing its combat path in northeastern Germany.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/321st_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 321st Static Division was formed as a garrison division in December 1940 as part of the 13th Wave from elements of the 267th and 295th Infantry Divisions (3 battalions from each division). It consisted of the 588th, 589th and 590th Infantry Regiments, the 321st Artillery Regiment and various support units. In October 1942 the division was converted to a field division and sent to Russia. At this time the grenadier battalions had their infantry gun companies replaced by 150mm Nebelwerfer batteries. The artillery regiment also had a battery of 150mm Nebelwerfers. In November 1943 the division was reduced to the 321st Division Group and most of the divisions elements were used to rebuild the 110th Infantry Division. The remaining elements were dispersed to other units. George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 322nd Rifle Division was a standard Red Army rifle division during World War II. It is most notable for liberating Auschwitz as part of the 60th Army on January 27, 1945, in the course of the Vistula-Oder Offensive. Prior to this the division also distinguished itself during the second liberation of Zhitomir on the last day of 1943. It received further distinctions for its service in western Ukraine and in Poland.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/322nd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 323rd Rifle Division was formed as a standard Red Army rifle division late in the summer of 1941, as part of the massive buildup of new Soviet fighting formations at that time. After a successful but costly start in the Soviet winter counteroffensive in the Tula region the division served on relatively quiet sectors into 1943, after which it joined the offensive push into German-occupied western Russia through the rest of that year, winning a battle honor for the liberation of Bryansk. In the course of the destruction of Army Groups Center in the summer of 1944, the division further distinguished itself in the liberation of Bialystok in July. In 1945 the men and women of the 323rd took part in the Vistula-Oder Offensive through Poland and into Pomerania, and then finally in the Battle of Berlin, ending the war with distinction, but being disbanded soon after.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/323rd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 323rd Static Division was formed as a garrison division in November 1940 as part of the 13th Wave from elements of the 62nd and 73rd Infantry Divisions (6 battalions and 3 battalions respectively). It consisted of the 591st, 592nd and 593rd Infantry Regiments, the 323rd Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was converted into a field division in February 1942. By March 1943 after heavy fighting the division had been reduced to a Kampfgruppe. The division was disbanded in November 1943.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 324th Rifle Division was a standard Soviet infantry division of the Red Army during World War II. It was formed as part of the massive mobilization of August 1941, and first saw action in early December in the counteroffensive west of Moscow. During 1942 and into 1943 it saw limited action on a relatively quiet sector of the front north of Bryansk, before joining a limited offensive in February. During the general offensives of that summer, the division fought in the drive past Smolensk, and made a forced crossing of the upper Dnieper River. The 324th played a limited role in Operation Bagration, but distinguished itself in the fighting in East Prussia in 1945, sufficiently to be awarded the Order of the Red Banner. During the course of the war the men and women of the division served under no fewer than nine commanding officers.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/324th_Rifle_Division

The 325th Rifle Division was formed in September 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, made up of older reservists and young men with no prewar training. As with many other divisions in the 320-330 series it was flung into the fighting west of Moscow in the 10th Army to defend the capital and then to take part in the winter counteroffensive. After a year on a quiet sector the division rejoined the fighting in the late winter of 1943, eventually distinguishing itself sufficiently to be redesignated as the 90th Guards Rifle Division. After disappearing from the Soviet order of battle for more than a year a new division was formed in the spring of 1944, based on a cadre of two distinguished rifle brigades, and gave very creditable service for the duration, completing its combat path in East Prussia.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/325th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 326th Rifle Division was formed as a standard Red Army rifle division late in the summer of 1941, as part of the massive buildup of new Soviet fighting formations in response to the German invasion. Like several other divisions in the 320-330 series, it was not fully trained and equipped when thrown into the Soviet winter counteroffensive, and after taking heavy losses mostly served on relatively quiet sectors into 1943, apart from several weeks of costly and futile fighting during Operation Mars. As the offensive into German-occupied western Russia developed during the autumn of that year the soldiers of the division distinguished themselves in the liberation of Roslavl in September. During 1944 the unit continued its combat path through the Baltic states, and in the following year helped liberate Poland and drive into Germany, ending the war near the Baltic coast in western Pomerania.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/326th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 327th Rifle Division was first formed in September 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, based on a cadre of workers from Voronezh. This formation was assigned to the Volkhov Front near Leningrad, toiling through the so-called 'Rat's War' in the wooded swamps of that region and taking significant casualties in the encirclement of its 2nd Shock Army near Lyuban in early 1942. In January 1943, it helped to lead the partial raising of the German siege of Leningrad in Operation Iskra, distinguishing itself sufficiently to be redesignated as the 64th Guards Rifle Division. Well over a year later a second 327th Rifle Division was formed and was also moved to the Leningrad region where it took part in the offensive that drove Finland from the war, then spent the first months of 1945 clearing German forces from the coasts of the Baltic States and containing the German forces trapped in Courland.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/327th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 327th Static Division was formed as a garrison division for service in Vienna in November 1940 as part of the 13th Wave with cadres from the 183rd, 198th and 297th Infantry Divisions. It consisted of the 595th, 596th and 597th Infantry Regiments, the 327th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was sent to eastern France in the spring of 1941. It spent 1942 at LaRochelle in southwestern France and took part in the occupation of Vichy France in November 1942. The division was converted into a field division in July 1943 and sent to Russia. The division was disbanded in November 1943 and its elements transferred to the 340th and 357th Infantry Divisions and other Army formations.<cr><cr>George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War II<cr>Samuel W. Mitcham, German Order of Battle Volume II: 291st-999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions, and Special Divisions in WWII<cr><cr>Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 328th Infantry Division was formed in December 1941 as part of the 17th Wave. It contained the 547th, 548th and 549th Infantry Regiments, 328th Artillery Regiment and various support units. Shortly therafter the division was assigned to Army Group Centre and fought in the Soviet winter offensive of 1941-1942. Each of the divisions three regiments was assigned to different corps in the Army Group and the 547th Regiment was aborbed by the 83rd Infantry Division. The division was heavily damaged around Subzow in October 1942. In November 1942 elements of the division were transferred to southern France and by the spring of 1943 the remainder of the division joined it there. The division was rebuilt and the 569th Grenadier Regiment was added to replace the 547th Regiment. The division returned to Russia in late summer of 1943 and was largely destroyed in the retreat to the Dnieper. In November 1943 it was designated a divisional group and attached to the 306th Infantry Division. It was aborbed by that division in July 1944 with the divisional group becoming the 569th Grenadier Regiment.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IISamuel W. Mitcham, German Order of Battle Volume II: 291st-999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions, and Special Divisions in WWIIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 328th Rifle Division was formed as a standard Red Army rifle division at Yaroslavl late in the summer of 1941, as part of the massive buildup of new Soviet fighting formations in response to the German invasion. Like several other divisions in the 320-330 series, it was neither fully trained nor equipped when thrown into the Soviet winter winter counteroffensive as part of 10th Army, but did its part in throwing back the forces of Army Groups Center from the southern approaches to Moscow in December and January. Over the course of five months of nearly continual offensive combat the soldiers of the division distinguished themselves sufficiently to be re-designated as the 31st Guards Rifle Division. A few months later a new 328th was formed, this time in the Transcaucasian Military Distric as the German summer offensive of 1942 was producing a crisis in that region. This new division had a slow start, but eventually proved itself in fighting through Ukraine, Belarus and Poland, gaining a battle honor for the liberation of Warsaw, and helping to complete the encirclement of Berlin in April 1945. Despite this record, it was disbanded shortly after the German surrender.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/328th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 329th Infantry Division was formed in December 1941 as part of the 17th Wave. It contained the 551st, 552nd and 553rd Infantry Regiments, 329th Artillery Regiment and various support units although the 552nd and 553rd Regiments had only two battalions instead of three as was typical of a German infantry regiment at this point in the war. The artillery regiment also had only two battalions rather than the standard four battalions. By 1943 the division had the standard TOE of three grenadier regiments of two battalions each and a typical four battalion artillery regiment. The pioneer battalion though had only two companies rather than the typical three and none of the grenadier regiments had infantry gun or Panzerjäger companies. In September 1944 the 553rd Infantry Regiment was disbanded and replaced by the 21st Luftwaffe Regimental Group which became the 42nd Jäger Regiment. On May 8th 1945 the division passed into Russian captivity in Courland.<cr><cr>George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War II<cr><cr>Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 329th Rifle Division was first formed in September 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, at Voronezh. This formation was assigned to the Western Front in mid-December as the Soviet winter winter counteroffensive west of Moscow was developing, but had the misfortune to be cut off and destroyed behind German lines. The division was formed again nearly two years later, this time in 1st Ukrainian Front, and served with distinction with this Front during the final twelve months of the war, winning honors for its roles in the fighting in Poland, Breslau and Berlin before ending the war near Prague.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/329th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 32nd Army was formed on 16 July 1941 in the Moscow Military District near the cities of Naro-Fominsk, Kubinka, and the settlement of Dorokhovo. The army was formed with four divisions of Moscow Militia. The assigned units included the 2nd, 7th, 8th, 13th Moscow Militia divisions. In addition, on 20 July 1941, 18th Moscow People's Militia Divisions was assigned to the Army at positions west of Moscow. The 18th had a strength of 10,000.<cr>On 18 July the army was incorporated into the Moscow line of defense and took up defensive positions in the vicinity of Karacharovo. On 30 July the army was assigned to the Reserve Front. On 1 October, the army included the 2nd Rifle Division, 8th Rifle Division, 29th Rifle Division and the 140th Rifle Division. It also included the 685th Corps Artillery Regiment, 533rd Antitank Artillery Regiment, 877th Antitank Artillery Regiment, 200th Naval Artillery Battalion and the 36th Antiaircraft Artillery Battalion.<cr>On 3 October the army was heavily engaged in a defensive battle against German forces advancing on Vyazma as part of the northern wing of Operation Typhoon. On 5 October the army was reassigned to the Western Front and two days later along with the 16th, 19th, 20th and 24th Armies were encircled by the German 4th and 9th Armies and 3rd and 4th Panzer Groups. The 32nd Army was disbanded on 12 October 1941. Small elements of the army were able to break out of the encirclement and were assigned to the 16th and 19th Armies.<cr>STAVKA ordered the army reformed on 2 March 1942. The reformation was completed on 10 March 1942. The army was formed from the Medvezhegorshaya and Maselskaya Operational Groups of the Karelian Front.<cr>Until the end of May 1944 the 32nd Army defended the frontier in the Medvezhyegorsky District and from 21 July to 9 August the army participated in the Svir-Petrozavodsk Offensive, when part of the army reached the Finish border in the vicinity of Longonvara. When Finland was knocked out of the war on 19 September 1944 the army was relegated to guarding the Finnish border.On 15 November 1944 the 32nd Army was put into the Reserve of the Supreme High Command (Stavka Reserve) and on 21 April 1945 was directly subordinated to the Stavka.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Army_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 32nd Cavalry Division was formed in 1938 in the Kiev Special Military District from the 1st Zaporozhe Cossack Cavalry Division.The division participated in the Invasion of Poland. It was assigned to the Ukrainian Front's Cavalry Group.Assigned to the 9th Rifle Corps in the Crimea the division had been undergoing amphibious training before the war started. On 10 July 1941 the division left for Gomel, leaving its assigned tank regiment behind, and was assigned to the 21st Army. The division commander took command of the one of the first 'Cavalry Groups' of the war. In July and August 1941 the group and the division raided into the rear areas and flanks of the German 2nd Army and 2nd Panzer Group south of Smolensk. During this raid the division conducted a successful saber-swinging cavalry charge when they caught a German rear-echelon unit by surprise and overran it in a mounted attack. In October-November 1941 the group and division operated along the flanks of the German attack towards Tula. In December 1941 the division was assigned to the 5th Cavalry Corps in December 1941 before the Corps was redesignated as the 3rd Guards Cavalry Corps on 26 December 1941. The division remained assigned to the 3rd Guards Cavalry Corps for the remainder of the war. On 10 November 1942 the division absorbed the remnants of the 47th Cavalry Division as replacements. In early 1943 the division was upgraded to the new cavalry standards. The division received the 207th Tank Regiment in June 1943. The division was disbanded in the summer of 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Cavalry_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 32nd Guards Rifle Divison fought at Krasnodar, on the Kuban, and in Crimea prior to fighting in Courland. On 1 June 1942 it was part of 47th Army, North Caucasus Front. The division was with the 2nd Guards Army of the 3rd Belorussian Front in May 1945.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Guards_Motor_Rifle_Division

During the invasion of Russia in 1941, the 32nd Infantry Division fought in the battles of Dvinsk, Kholm, Lake Ilmen, and the Valdai Hills, and was tied down in the battles around Demyansk from January 1942 to February 1943. It was encircled much of this time and had to be resupplied by air. Three of its infantry battalions were disbanded in 1942, due to heavy casualties. The 32nd remained on the northern sector during the defensive battles of 1943 and was briefly transferred to Army Group Center in January 1944, where it fought at Nevel. Hurried back to the northern sector after the Russians broke the siege of Leningrad on January 18, the Lion Division was cited for its excellent conduct in the retreat through the Baltic States. Finally withdrawn into the Courland Pocket, it took part in the desperate battles in western Latvia in the winter of 1944-45, before being evacuated to Germany by sea in early 1945. The division was finally cut off in the Hela peninsula by the final Soviet offensives and surrendered to the Red Army on May 8, 1945.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The corps was in Smolensk as part of 16th Army at the outbreak of hostilities. It consisted of 46th and 152nd Rifle Divisions in July 1941. It was disbanded after the Battle of Smolensk and reformed in August 1943 in Southwestern Front. In January 1944, it consisted of 259th, 266th and 279th Rifle Divisions. At that time, it was assigned to 3rd Guards. In April, 1945, it was part of 5th Shock Army during the Berlin Strategic Offensive. Poirier, Robert and Conner, Albert, The Red Army Order of Battle in the Great Patriotic War, Presidio Press, 1985Entry contributed by Stewart King

The 32nd Rifle Division was formed in 1920 in the Saratov area. In 1934 it joined the Special Red Banner Far Eastern Army, serving the Far Eastern Military District as part of the 39th Rifle Corps. It took part in a number of border skirmishes on the Manchurian border near Lake Khasan. By 1941 it consisted of the 17th, 113th and 322nd Rifle Regiments and the 133rd and 154th Artillery Regiments. When Operation Typhoon, the German attack on Moscow began in late 1941 the division was ordered west and was rapidly transported by train to the Mozhaisk Defense Line. By October 1941 the forward elements had arrived and dug in on the old Borodino battlefield. The best the division could hope for was to delay the German advance long enough to form a new line of defense further east. The Germans attacked with two veteran divisions, the 10th Panzer Division and the 2nd SS Division Das Reich on the 32nd Divisions line of defense. The battle continued for five days until the exhausted Russians fell back further to the east and Mozhaisk fell on the 18th of October. The division stayed on the front lines through November and took part in theBattle of Moscow. For its service in these battles the divsion was given the title 29th Guards Rifle Division.A new 32nd Rifle Division was formed and was back at the front by October 1942. The division was in action until the end of the war and was disbanded in 1946.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 32nd Tank Division was formed from 30th Light Tank Brigade in March-April 1941 in western Kiev Special Military District. On 22 June 1941 included: 63rd Tank Regiment 64th Tank Regiment 32nd Motorized Rifle Regiment 32nd Howitzer Regiment - only 1 light bn 32nd Reconnaissance Battalion 32nd Motorized Pontoon Battalion 32nd Antiaircraft BattalionThe 32nd Tank Division was one of the best-equipped units formed in 1941, and one of the best-equipped tank divisions in the Red Army in June 1941. Unfortunately, most of the modern equipment was only received in April and May 1941, and there was no time to train crews, platoons, or companies on the new KVs and T-34 tanks. In addition, the division had only 50.3% of the officers and 42.9% of NCOs assigned, so that experienced leadership was lacking as well as time to train. Overall the division was missing 60% of its authorized equipment. Most critically, only a fifth of the tractors were on hand to ull the artillery, less than 1/3 of the radios, half the telephones, and 10% or less of repair equipment and spare parts required. All of which made it difficult to control, move, or sustain the division in combat.Nevertheless, the 32nd Tank Division managed to hold together throughout the tank battles in the western Ukraine in June and July. In August 1941 the 4th Mechanized Corps HQ was dissolved and the 32nd Tank Division withdrawn into the reserves, where it was disbanded and the personnel used to form 8th Tank Brigade.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 330th Infantry Division was formed in December 1941 as part of the 17th Wave. It contained the 554th, 555th and 556th Infantry Regiments, 330th Artillery Regiment and various support units although all three infantry regiments had only two battalions instead of three as was typical of a German infantry regiment at this point in the war. The artillery regiment also had only two battalions rather than the standard four battalions. In April 1943 the 556th Regiment was disbanded and its troops absorbed into the two remaining regiments. In November 1943 the division was reduced to the 330th Divisional Group and its elements absorbed by the 342nd and 367th Infantry Divisions.<cr><cr>George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War II<cr><cr>Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 330th Rifle Division was formed as an infantry division of the Red Army late in the summer of 1941, as part of the massive buildup of new Soviet fighting formations at that time. It took part in the defense of Tula in 10th Army soon after reaching the front, and remained in that army for a remarkably long time, until April 1944. It fought in the offensive push into German-occupied western Russia through 1943, then in the destruction of Army Groups Center in the summer of 1944, distinguishing itself in the liberation of Mogilev in June. In 1945 the men and women of the 330th took part in the Vistula-Oder Offensive through Poland and into Pomerania, and then finally in the fighting north of Berlin, ending the war with high distinction, but being disbanded soon after.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/330th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 331st Infantry Division was formed in December 1941 as part of the 17th Wave. It contained the 557th, 558th and 559th Infantry Regiments, 331st Artillery Regiment and various support units although the 558th and 559th Regiments had only two battalions instead of three as was typical of a German infantry regiment at this point in the war. The artillery regiment also had only two battalions rather than the standard four battalions. As part of the German 4th Army in Army Group Centre it suffered terribly in the winter of 1941/42. Records show by February of 1942 the division was a mere skeleton fleshed out with every sort of odd unit that could be scraped together and was operating as five improvised Groups named Dolle, Koch, Ronicke, Weise and Haase. In December 1943 the division was disbanded and became the Wahn Shadow Division. In March 1944 that division was rebuilt and designated the 331st Grenadier Division with the original three regiments containing two grenadier battalions each. The division fought in Normandy and the Falaise pocket where it was destroyed. The survivors were distributed to other units.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

One of the so called 'Siberian' divisions, the 331st Rifle Division began forming on the 27th August, 1941, in the Orel Military District, based on workers and reservists from the Bryansk region. As such the Division was also known as the 331st 'Bryansk Proletarian' Rifle Division and went on to have a distinguished history. In November, when moving up to the front line, elements of the Division marched in the October Revolution Anniversary parade in the Red Square. The Division fought with determination in the defense of Moscow and had some success in the Soviets Winter Offensive. In 1942 the Division was assigned to the Western Front, to which it remained with for the rest of the war, and took part in Operation Mars, with limited success and substantial casualties. In April 1943 the Division was assigned to the 31st Army and fought with the distinction at Smolensk and Roslavl, and later in the year was part of the unsuccessful attempts to take Orsha. In 1944 the Division took part in Operation Bagration and was commended for the liberation of Orsha and Minsk. In 1945 the Division fought its way into East Prussia where its leading elements were isolated for 2 days and support elements suffered casualties from the retreating Germans. The Division was enroute towards Prague when the war ended and it was disbanded in Friedeberg, Silesia, in July 1945. A highly decorated unit, the Division was twice awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov and the honorifics of 'PROLETARIAN', 'BRYANSK' and 'SMOLENSK'. Some of the individual regiments were also awarded the honorific of 'MINSK'. It is perhaps surprising that the Division was not renamed as a Guards Division. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/331st_Rifle_Division Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 332nd Rifle Division began forming on the 8th August, 1941, at Ivanovo, in the Moscow Military District, based on the barely formed Ivanovo Militia division. In November, when moving up to the front line, elements of the Division also marched in the October Revolution Anniversary parade in the Red Square. The Division fought in the defense of Moscow and in January 1942 was assigned to the Northwestern Front where it was assigned to operations attempting to retake Velikiye Luki. In October 1943 the Division, assigned to the 4th Shock Army, participated in offensive operations towards Vitebsk, and in July 1944 was recognised for its part in the liberation of Polotsk. In early August, the divisional commander T.F. Egoshin, was mortally wounded by artillery fire when directing his troops during a German counter attack. In 1945 the division fought at Königsberg and in the Courland. The Division was awarded the Order of Suvorov for the liberation of Riga, and the honorifics of 'IVANOVO' and 'POLOTSK'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/332nd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) A.A. Maslov, Fallen Soviet Generals Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 333rd Rifle Division began slowly forming in August, 1941, at Kamyshin on the Volga, and was held in Reserve till the end of the year, when it then participated in the Soviet winter counter offensive. In May 1942 the Division, assigned to the 9th Army, Southern Front, just avoided disaster at Kharkov, lost a regiment at Izium, and spent the year retreating towards the Don, where it was rebuilt. Assigned to the newly reformed Southwestern Front, the Division fought at Stalingrad with some success. In 1943 the Division fought in the Ukraine, and in 1944 in the 2nd Jassy-Kishinev Offensive and ended the war near Bucharest, assigned to the 37th Army. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov for the liberation of Nikopol, and the honorific of 'SINELNIKOVO'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/333rd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of J. Tomlinson

The 334th Rifle Division began forming in August, 1941, at Kazan, in the Volga Military District, and stayed in Reserve until January 1942 when it was assigned to the 4th Shock Army, Northwestern Front. It took part in offensive operations attempting to retake Velikiye Luki with some success as it formed a battery from captured German artillery. In 1943 the Division participated in offensive operations near Smolensk, and in July 1944 was recognised for its part in the liberation of Vitebsk. The division fought at Riga, along the Baltic, at Königsberg and ended the war in mopping up operations in the Samland Peninsula. The Division was awarded the Order of Suvorov for the capture of Landsberg, and the honorific of 'VITEBSK'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/334th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 335th Rifle Division began forming in September, 1941, at Stalingrad, in the North Caucasus Military District, and when assigned to the 57th Army, Southwestern Front, took part in the Soviet Winter offensive. In May 1942, at the 2nd Battle of Kharkov, the Division was only at 50% strength and had to fight it's way out of encirclement. In July 1942 the bulk of the Division was trapped in the Millerovo pocket, in August the Division was listed as without troops and in November it was disbanded. In May 1944 the Division was raised for a 2nd time, based on the 6th Rifle Brigade, in the Far East, where it remained for the rest of the war. It took no major part in the Soviet invasion of Manchuria. A commander of interest was P.M. Volosatykh, demoted in February 1942 and condemned to 8 years frontline duty as a Regiment Commander. He was able to rehabilitate his career, served again as a Divisional Commander and was awarded the Hero of the Soviet Union. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/335th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 335th Static Division was formed in November 1940 using two battalions from the 197th Infantry Division, three from the 298th Infantry Division and one from the 87th Infantry Division. In the summer of 1941 the division was sent to central France on garrison duty. In October 1942 the division was upgraded to a field division and became the 335th Infantry Division. It contained the 682nd, 683rd and 684th Grenadier Regiments, 335th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was sent to southern Russia in February 1943 and was in action almost continuously the next year and a half. It fought at Kursk , Stalino, the Dnieper Bend battles, Nikopol, the retreat through the Donets and in the Zaporoshje bridehead. The division was destroyed at Kishinev, Romania in August 1944 and on October 9, 1944 was disbanded.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IISamuel W. Mitcham, German Order of Battle Volume II: 291st-999th Infantry Divisions, Named Infantry Divisions, and Special Divisions in WWIIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 336th Rifle Division began forming in August, 1941, at Melekess, in the Volga Military District, and in December was assigned to the 5th Army, Western Front. Committed to the defence of Moscow, the Divisions first combat was a disaster; the Officers lost control of the troops who fled the field of battle in a disorderly manner and as a consequence the Divisional Commander, G.M Shapovalov, took his own life. The Division suffered heavy casualties. In 1942 the Division fought in the Rhzev area as part of Operation Mars, and once again suffered heavy casualties, without success. In 1943 the Division was assigned to operations in the Ukraine and fought with success in the liberation of Zhitomir and assisting later on in the liberation of Rovno and Lutsk. The Division fought its way across the Ukraine and ended the war in Czechoslovakia. At this time the Division was at half strength. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov and the honorific 'ZHITOMIR'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/336th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 336th Static Division was formed in December 1940 as part of the 14th Wave from cadres of the 61st and 256th Infantry Divisions. This Saxon unit consisted of the 685th, 686th and 687th Infantry Regiments, 336th Divisional Fusilier Battalion, 336th Artillery Regiment and various support units. The division was posted to Belgium in May 1941, to Le Havre France in June 1941 and to Brittany in April 1942.In May 1942 the division was sent to Russia and in June 1942 the division was upgraded to a field division becoming the 336th Infantry Division. The division was posted to the Hungarian Second Army near Kharkov. Later the division was part of Army Detachment Hollidt during its unsuccessful attempt to relieve Stalingrad. The division was transferred to the Crimea in November 1943 and was destroyed during the Crimean Offensive in May 1944. A few survivors were evacuated by sea from Sevastopol before the city fell. The survivors were incorporated into the 685th Grenadier Regiment of the 294th Infantry Division.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IISamuel W. The 337th Rifle Division began forming in August, 1941, at Astrakhan, in the North Caucasus Military District, and when assigned to the 57th Army, Southwestern Front, took part in the Soviet winter offensive. In May 1942, at the 2nd Battle of Kharkov, the Division was trapped and destroyed in the Izium pocket. The Divisional Commander I.V. Vasilev was killed in this action. The Division was raised for a 2nd time in August 1942 in the North Caucasus Military District where it fought to stop the Axis drive to the oilfields. In 1943 it was in reserve at the Battle of Kursk and fought with some distinction in the Ukraine, where it was honoured for the liberation of Lubny. In 1944 the Division fought in the First Jassy-Kishinev Offensive, where it suffered heavy casualties, the Second Jassy-Kishinev Offensive, through Hungary and ended the war in Austria, assigned to the 27th Army of the 3rd Ukrainian Front. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov, Order of Bogdan Khmelnitsky and the honorific 'LUBNY'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/337th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 338th Rifle Division began forming in September, 1941, at Penza, in the Volga Military District, and when combat ready was assigned to the 37th Army, Western Front. The Division took part in the Soviet winter offensive but was trapped by German counter offensive operations in February 1942, and along with most of the 33rd Army was destroyed by May. Remnants of the Division, including the Divisional Commander and some staff officers, eventually made it back to Soviet lines. The Division was raised for a 2nd time in June 1942, based on the 18th Rifle Brigade, and was assigned to the Western Front. In 1943 the Division fought in the Rzhev area and in operations that eventually led to the liberation of Smolensk. In early 1944 the Division took part in the unsuccessful liberation of Vitebsk and was reduced to 3,500 men. In Operation Bagration the Division had a secondary, follow up role, fought in the Baltic and Riga, and by the end of the year was attempting to surround Königsberg in East Prussia. The Division ended the war performing mopping up operations in Samland, assigned to the 39th Army. The Division was eventually awarded the Order of the Red Banner and the honorific 'NEMAN'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/338th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 339th Rifle Division began forming in August, 1941, at Rostov, from reservists and local communist party members. Barely formed it was rushed to the front and in November took part in the operations that drove the Germans out of Rostov for the first time. In July 1942, assigned to the 56th Army, the Division unsuccessfully defended Rostov and retreated into the Caucasus where it saw action at Krasnodar and finally Tuapse. With the Axis retreat from the Caucasus the Division fought with distinction in clearing the Taman peninsula and in November 1943 crossed over to the Crimea via Kerch. It was at this time that the Divisional Commander T.S. Kulakov was killed in action during an air raid. When the Crimea had been cleared, in September 1944 the Division moved North and fought its way to the Oder River, ending the war at the Oder Spree canal. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov, and the honorifics 'ROSTOV', 'TAMAN' and 'BRANDENBERG'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/339th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) A.A. Maslov, Fallen Soviet Generals Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 339th Static Division was formed in December 1940 as part of the 14th Wave using three battalions from the 52nd Infantry Division, two from a fortress regiment and one from the 229th Infantry Division. It consisted of the 691st, 692nd and 693rd Infantry Regiments, 339th Artillery Battalion and various support units. The artillery battalion was formed into a three battalion regiment in June 1943. In November 1943 the division was reduced to the 339th Divisional Group and merged with other divisions to form the 'C' Army Detachment. Remnants of the division were sent to Poland where they were used to rebuild the 363rd Infantry Division.<cr><cr>George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War II<cr><cr>Entry courtesy Chris Munson

The 33rd Army was initially formed in the Moscow Military District in July 1941, consisting of the 1st, 5th, 9th, 17th, and 21st Moscow People's Militia divisions, plus artillery and other support units.<cr>With the arrival of the German 2nd Panzer Army to Kashira and its 4th Panzer Group to the Moskva-Volga Canal, the Gemans were poised to assault Moscow. On December 1, the Germans hit the centre of the Soviet front. Two German divisions with 70 tanks broke through in the 33rd Army's sector in the 222nd Rifle Division's area to the north of Naro-Fominsk. On December 2, in the 110th Rifle Division's sector the Wehrmacht went over to the offensive and attacked in the direction of Mogutovo. The 113th Rifle Division together with a regiment from 43rd Army led a counteroffensive on Klotovo and Kamenskoe with the task of hitting the rear of the Germans to relieve the pressure on the 110th Rifle Division. As a result of this counterstroke, the enemy was routed. The Soviets captured 47 tanks and about 50 guns. From the west at Naro Fominsk Germans drovr on to Kubinka along a highway, and then to Golitcin and Aprelevka, threatening rears of 33rd and 5th Soviet Armies. At Akulovo village German forces have met with 32nd Rifle Division and artillery fire. It was the last German attempt to break through to Moscow.<cr>At the Battle of Smolensk (1943), after a day of probing, the goal of which was to determine whether German troops had chosen to withdraw from the first set of trenches. The offensive started on 7 August 1943 at 0630 (with a preliminary bombardment starting at 0440) with a breakthrough towards Roslavl. Three armies (under the control of Soviet Western Front) were committed to this offensive: the 5th Army, the 10th Guards Army and the 33rd Army.<cr>However, the attack quickly encountered heavy opposition and stalled. German troops attempted numerous counterattacks from their well-prepared defense positions, supported by tanks, assault guns, and the fire of heavy guns and mortars. On the first day, the Soviet troops advanced only 4 kilometers, with all available troops (including artillery, communications men and engineers) committed to battle.<cr>From April 1944 the 33rd Army, participated in Operation Bagration to retake Belarus as part of the 2nd Belorussian Front. During the Mogilyov Offensive it successfully crossed the Dniepr and Pronya rivers, and liberated Shklov on June 27, 1944. During the Minsk Offensive the army, in conjunction with the 50th and 49th Armies, participated in the rout of the surrounded Wehrmacht forces to the east of Minsk. At the end of July-August the Army participated in the Kaunas Offensive during which it cleared the approaches to East Prussia. On September 10, it was released from VGK reserve, and joined the 1st Belorussian Front on October 19 in preparation for the Warsaw-Poznan Offensive.<cr>On 1 May 1945 during the Battle of Berlin, the Army consisted of the 16th Rifle Corps (323, 339, 383 RDs), 62nd Rifle Corps (95, 222, 362 RDs), 49th Rifle Division, 115th, 119th Fortified Region, and other support formations and units. After the initial Berlin breakthrough, 33rd Army, alongside other armies of the 1st Belorussian and 1st Ukrainian Fronts helped to rout the surrounded German forces to the east of Berlin. Military operation for 33rd Army concluded on 6 May. <cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Army_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 33rd Guards Rifle Division was formed as an elite infantry division of the Red Army in May, 1942, based on the 2nd formation of the 3rd Airborne Corps, and served in that role until after the end of the WWII. It was the second of a series of ten Guards rifle divisions formed from airborne corps during the spring and summer of 1942. It was briefly assigned to the 47th Army in the North Caucasus Front but was soon moved to the Volga Military District and saw its first action as part of 62nd Army in the fighting on the approaches to Stalingrad. It was withdrawn east of the Volga in September, but returned to the front with the 2nd Guards Army in December, and it remained in this Army until early 1945. After helping to defeat Army Group Don's attempt to relieve the trapped 6th Army at Stalingrad the 33rd Guards joined in the pursuit across the southern Caucasus steppe until reaching the Mius River in early 1943. Through the rest of that year it fought through the southern sector of eastern Ukraine as part of Southern Front (later 4th Ukrainian Fronts) and in the spring of 1944 assisted in the liberation of the Crimea, earning a battle honor in the process. The Crimea was a strategic dead-end, so 2nd Guards Army was moved north to take part in the summer offensive through the Baltic states and to the border with Germany as part of 1st Baltic Front. During the offensive into East Prussia the division and its 13th Guards Rifle Corps was reassigned to 39th and the 43rd 43rd Armies before returning to 2nd Guards Army in April. For its part in the capture of the city-fortress of Königsberg the 33rd Guards would receive the Order of Suvorov.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Guards_Rifle_Division

The corps was assigned to Arkhangelsk Military District in June 1941 and was the basis for forming 43rd Army in July. The corps was reformed as part of 2nd Ukrainian Front in January 1944. At that time, it consisted of 50th and 297th Rifle Divisions. It fought as a part of 27th Army in Moldova in 1944, participating in the Iasi-Kishinev Offensive in August 1944. At that time, it consisted of 93rd Guards Rifle Division and 78th, 202nd, and 206th Rifle Divisions. Transferred to 6th Guards Tank Army, it fought in Hungary for the rest of the war. In October 1944, it consisted of 78th and 337th Rifle Divisions and 1st Rumanian Volunteer Rifle Division. The 33rd Rifle Division was formed in 1922 at Samara and moved to Belarus in the next year. It fought in the Soviet invasion of Poland in September 1939 and in the Occupation of Lithuania in June 1940. After Operation Barbarossa, the division fought in the Baltic Operation and Leningrad Strategic Defensive. In January 1942, it fought in the Tropets-Kholm Offensive. The division participated in the Leningrad-Novgorod Offensive, the Pskov-Ostrov Offensive, the Tartu Offensive and the Riga Offensive. In 1945, the division fought in the East Pomeranian Offensives and the Battle of Berlin.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

Formed in March 1941 at Sokulka in Western Special Military District as part of 11th Mechanized Corps with: 65th Tank Regiment - 1 bn of 2 cos - 20 tanks total 66th Tank Regiment - 1 bn of 2 cos - 20 tanks total 33rd Motorized Rifle Regiment 1st, 2nd, 3rd bns 33rd Motorized Howitzer Regiment 1 122mm bn 1 152mm battery 33rd Reconnaissance Battalion 33rd Motorized Pontoon Battalion 33rd Antiaircraft BattalionThe 33rd Tank Division had only 40 T-26 tanks on hand on 22 June, no antiaircraft guns, and was short almost 90% of the trucks and tractors it was authorized. It was, officially, 'not up to strength' and considered the least ready division in 11th Mechanized Corps. On its first move, on 22 June, it was caught by the Luftwaffe and lost 50% of the equipment it did have. The remnants of the division, effectively no more than a reinforced rifle regiment, was destroyed in the Bialystok pocket in early July.Soviet Order of Battle Volume I by Charles C. Sharp

The 340th Rifle Division began forming in August, 1941, at Balashov, in the Volga Military District. In December it was assigned to the 50th Army, Western Front, near Tula. The Division fought with some success in the Soviet Winter Offensive but by May 1942 it was in reserve recovering from its losses. In July, assigned to the Bryansk Front, it attempted to stop the Axis summer offensive with limited success. In late 1942 the Division was transferred to the Voronezh Front and in February 1943 took part in the liberation of Belgorod, and later on Sumy and Kiev. The division fought across the Ukraine and Poland and finished the war In Slovakia assigned to the 38th Army, 4th Ukrainian Front. The Division was awarded the Order of the Red Banner, Order of Suvorov, Order of Kutuzov and the honorifics 'SUMY' and 'KIEV'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/340th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union) Courtesy of John Tomlinson

The 341st Rifle Division first formed on September 1, 1941 in the North Caucasus Military District at Stalingrad. <cr><cr>
Col. Aleksandr Ilich Shchagin was assigned to command of the division on the day it began forming, and he continued in command throughout the existence of this formation. The division's personnel contained a significant number of non-Russian nationality. In October, while still barely formed, the division was assigned to 57th Army, which was also just in the process of forming-up in the Reserve of the Supreme High Command. In December the division and its Army moved to join Southwestern Front, taking part in the winter counter-offensive which led to the creation of the Izium salient south of Kharkov. By the end of January 1942, the 341st had been transferred to 9th Army in Southern Front, on the southern flank of the salient. It was still holding this position on May 17, as Southwestern Front was attacking northwards from the salient towards Kharkov, when the 14th Panzer Division of 1st Panzer Army smashed through the division's flank, driving its remnants north and west into what became the Izium Pocket. While 9th Army continued to carry the 341st in its order of battle until June 1, in fact it had broken up within 48 hours of the German attack; while Colonel Shchagin and many other personnel managed to escape, the division was effectively disbanded on May 19.<cr><cr>About two years later, almost to the day, a new 341st Rifle Division began forming on May 1, 1944, in the Karelian Front, based on the 77th Naval Rifle Brigade in 19th Army.Col. Ivan Vasilievich Obydenkin commanded the reformed division until mid-October. He was briefly succeeded by Col. A. V. Molokov until Col. Ignatii Alekseevich Moskalev took command on October 28, which he would hold for the duration of the war. The division served directly under 19th Army through September, taking part in the limited fighting that pushed Finnish forces back from Kandalaksha towards Alakurtti. In November the 341st moved even farther north, to the 131st Rifle Corps in 14th Army, which by then was simply a garrison force in northern Finland. In January 1945, the division left the active forces completely, assigned to the Belomorsky Military District on coastal defense duties.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/341st_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 342nd Rifle Division began forming in September 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, in the Saratov oblast. It arrived at the front southwest of Moscow in December, in time to take part in the winter counteroffensive. During most of 1942 and into 1943 the division served in primarily defensive roles in 61st Army along the northern face of the German-held salient around Oryol. Following the Soviet victory at Kursk the 342nd took part in the operation that eliminated that salient, and then in the further offensives that liberated Bryansk and pushed on towards Smolensk and the Dnieper River. During these tactical-level actions the division distinguished itself sufficiently to be re-designated as the 121st Guards Rifle Division, one of the last Guards divisions to be formed before the postwar period. In November 1944, a new 342nd was formed in the Far East, and saw action against Japanese forces in northern Manchuria, assaulting across the Sungach river during the Soviet invasion of that region.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/342nd_Rifle_Division

The 343rd Rifle Division was first formed in late August, 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, at Stavropol, in the Caucasus region. Its first major operation was in the liberation of Rostov in December, 1941. Following this, it was nearly caught up in the debacle near Kharkov in May, 1942, but managed to evade the German spearheads during Operation Blue to join the forces defending the Stalingrad region during the summer and fall. Following the German surrender at Stalingrad, on May 4, 1943, it was re-designated as the 97th Guards Rifle Division. Over a year later, a new 343rd Rifle Division was formed, based on the personnel and equipment of a Fortified Region, just after the start of Operation Bagration, the destruction of Army Groups Center. This new division went on to distinguish itself by helping to liberate the Polish city of Bia?ystok, and ended the war in East Prussia, near Königsberg.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/343rd_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 344th Rifle Division was formed in the Baryshsky and Kuzovatovsky Districts of Ulyanovsk Oblast between August and October 1941 in accordance with an 11 August decree of the State Defense Committee. Its basic order of battle was as follows:

1152nd Rifle Regiment
1154th Rifle Regiment
1156th Rifle Regiment
913th Artillery Regiment
In November 1941, in accordance with Direction number 55 of the Stavka and commander of the 26th Army Reserve op/2999 number from 25 November 1941, the division was loaded onto trains at Cheboksary and shipped to Noginsk, and then to Lyubertsy where it was manned and received weapons.

In December the 344th was assigned to the Moscow Defense Zone as part of the last-ditch defenses of the capital. It first went into combat in January 1942, in the 50th Army of Western Front. It remained in this Army until April 1943, when it was moved to the 49th Army in the same Front. It took part in Operation Suvorov under this command, and on 28 August made probing attacks against the German Gruppe Harpe to prevent the transfer of reserves; by three days later the division had suffered 2,000 casualties, about one-third of its strength. On 25 September it was awarded the battle honor Roslavl in recognition of its part in the liberation of that city. On 29 September the division recaptured Mstsislaw. In April 1944 it was again reassigned, this time to the 62nd Rifle Corps of 33rd Army in 2nd Belorussian Front, and fought under these headquarters during Operation Bagration. It was awarded the Order of the Red Banner on 10 July 1944, for its role in the forcing of the Pronya and Dniepr Rivers and the liberation of the cities of Mogilev, Shklov and Bykhov in the first phase of Operation Bagration. In August it went into the reserves of 1st Baltic Front, and from September 1944 until February 1945 it served in the 19th Rifle Corps of 43rd Army in that Front, along the coast of Lithuania. From at least October 1944, it had attached the 18th SU Battalion of SU-76s in addition to its organic battalion of towed anti-tank guns. During the last months of the war the 344th was part of the force containing the German forces trapped in the Courland Pocket, and it ended the war in the 1st Rifle Corps of the 1st Shock Army in the Kurland Group of Leningrad Front. On 5 April 1945, the 1154th Rifle Regiment was separately awarded the Red Banner for its role in the capture of Memel.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22nd_Motor_Rifle_Division_%22Atamyrat_Niyazov%22</url>

The 344th Static Division was formed in September 1942 from elements of the 327th, 333rd and 335th Infantry Divisions. It consisted of the 854th and 855th Fortress Infantry Regiments, 344th Artillery Regiment and various support units. One battalion of the 854th Fortress Regiment was sent to the Eastern Front in October 1943 and in August 1944 was absorbed by the 292nd Infantry Division. In April 1944 the 624th and 625th Cossack Battalions were absorbed by the division. The division was destroyed in Normandy and the remnants retreated to Belgium and were distributed to other units. The division was reformed in in Aachen in November 1944 from the 91st and Castorf Kampfgruppes, various Landwehr Fortress battalions and miscellaneous other units. It's two infantry regiments were now designated the 1057th and 1058th Grenadier Regiments. The division was then transferred east and was captured by the Russians south of Berlin.George F. Nafziger, The German Order of Battle Infantry in World War IIEntry courtesy Chris Munson

The 346th Rifle Division began forming in late August, 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, in the Volga Military District. It was assigned to the 61st Army while both it and its Army continued to form up before moving to the front lines in December to take part in the winter counteroffensive south of Moscow. In September, 1942, it became part of the 5th Tank Army, and joined the offensive that encircled German 6th Army at Stalingrad during Operation Operaton Uranus. During 1943 and early 1944 it continued to serve in the southern part of the front, taking part in the liberation of Crimea, before being transferred to the Baltic States region, serving in Latvia and Lithuania until February, 1945, when it was once again reassigned, this time to be part of the follow-on forces in the conquest of eastern Germany.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/346th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 347th Rifle Division began forming in mid-September, 1941, as a Red Army rifle division, in the North Caucasus Military District. It was soon assigned to the 58th Army while both it and its Army continued to form up before entering combat in November, as part of the offensive that first liberated Rostov. During the German summer offensive in 1942 the division retreated back into the Caucasus, fighting to defend the routes to the oil fields at Baku, until the German forces began to retreat after their defeat at Stalingrad. During 1943 and early 1944 it continued to serve in the southern part of the front, taking part in the liberation of Crimea, before being transferred to the Baltic States region, serving in Latvia and Lithuania for the duration of the war, compiling a distinguished record of service along the way.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/347th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 348th Rifle Division was first formed in August, 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, at Kuibyshev. It was assigned to 60th Army shortly after forming and took part in the winter counteroffensive in front of Moscow. Until the end of 1942 it was involved in the dismal and costly battles around the Rzhev Salient, until it was shifted to take part in the equally difficult fighting around the Demyansk Salient. Both of these German positions were evacuated in March, 1943, and, after rebuilding, the division returned to the front to take part in the summer offensive along the Smolensk axis. During Operation Bagration the 348th distinguished itself in the liberation of Bobruysk, and received the name of that city as an honorific. Not long after it was also decorated for its role in the liberation of Bialystok. In 1945 it helped to liberate northern Poland during the Vistula-Oder Offensive, before being reassigned to 3rd Belorussian Front in East Prussia. In the last weeks of the war it formed part of the reserves of 1st Belorussian Front during the Berlin.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/348th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 349th Rifle Division formed in September, 1941, as a standard Red Army rifle division, at Astrakhan. It was assigned to the southern sector of the Soviet-German front, and first saw action in January, 1942, during the winter counteroffensive, but was badly damaged during the German spring offensive that formed the Izium Pocket. The remaining men and equipment of the unit managed to retreat into the Caucasus region in the face of the German summer offensive in such a weakened state that German intelligence wrote the division off as destroyed in October. In fact, the cadre of the division survived, and was transferred to the reserves of Transcaucasus Front in that same month, where it slowly replenished as a low-priority unit. By the end of the year the 349th was assigned to 45th Army along the border with Turkey, and it remained on this quiet front for the duration of the war.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/349th_Rifle_Division_(Soviet_Union)

The 34th Army was formed on 16 July 1941 in the Moscow Military District.<cr>On 18 July the army was assigned to the Moscow line of defense occupying positions west of Maloyaroslavets where it was assigned troops. On 25 July the army became part of the backup for Lieutenant General Bagdanov, which on 30 July was designated as the Reserve Front the army headquarters located in Lüübnitsa, Russia (now Estonia). On 6 August the army was reassigned to the Northwestern Front.<cr>The army was tasked to defend the eastern bank of the Lovat River from Kholm to Kulakovo south of the German held city of Staraya Russa. STAVKA Directive 00824 tasked the army to strike the left wing of the German forces defeating and them in the area between Soltsy and Staraya Russa. If successful, the operation could cut off the entire right flank of the Army Group North. According to the order the army was by 15 August to advance more the 25 miles to the line of Snezhka-Chudinovo-Rechnye Kottsy, and by 18 August was to reach the line of Volot-Dolzhino.<cr>By 11 August the army had reached the Polist River along a 24-mile front from Vzglyady to Gojko and launched their offensive. The German X Corps only had small outposts on its flank with the 30th and 129th Infantry Divisions east of Staraya Russa arrayed against the Soviet 11th Army and the 290th Infantry Division on the south side of Staraya Russa guarding the German right flank. After the start of the Soviet Offensive the German forces were moved west of Staraya Russa.<cr>The first echelon, consisting of the 245th, 257th, 262nd Rifle and the 25th Cavalry Divisions, advanced quickly reaching there 18 August goals by 14 August and cutting the railroad between Dno and Staraya Russa.<cr>By the end of September the army's line had stabilized to the north and northeast of Demyansk from Lake Vella to Lychkova and remained in these positions through the end of the year.<cr>At the end of 1942 and in to 1943, the army prepared itself for its role in the Demyansk Offensive.<cr>Prior to the start of the offensive the German successfully withdrew their forces from the Demyansk Pocket and the 34th Army was limited to pursuing rear guard forces. By 28 February the army had arrived at the Lovat River. By the elimination of the pocket the front line had been significantly decreased, and the units of the 34th Army were reassigned to the 11th and 52nd Armies and the headquarters airlifted to the area northeast of Staraya Russa where it took command of some of the forces assigned to the 27th Army.<cr>On 18 March the army, with forces recently reassigned from the 27th attempted to storm Staraya Russa. The army encountered five German divisions along the line of villages Dinner Medvedno, Bryashnaya Gore Sobolev Derevkovo to Porus, the attack was repulsed, restarted on 20 March when it was able to liberate a few small villages moving a little closer to Staraya Russa but unable to liberate the city. The army remained outside Staraya Russa until November 1943 holding the defensive line and attempting to storm the city.<cr>On 20 November 1943 the forces assigned to the army were transferred to 1st Shock Army and the headquarters placed in STAVKA reserve. On 15 January 1944 the headquarters was redesignated 4th Army.<cr><cr><url>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Army_(Soviet_Union)</url>

The 34th Guards Rifle Division was originally formed on 29 August 1942 from the 7th Airborne Corps in the Moscow Military District. It was assigned to the 28th Army, part of the Southern Front. In April 1943, it was transferred to the 5th Shock Army, which later became part of the 4th Ukrainian Front. After participation in retaking Yenkiyevo, it was awarded the battle honour. In January 1944, it became part of the 31st Guards Rifle Corps of the 46th Army. In November 1944 it was finally transferred to the 4th Guards Army, which it was part of for the rest of the war. During Operation Konrad I, the 34th Guards were pushed back by battlegroups from the 6th Panzer Division and 8th Panzer Division.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Guards_Rifle_Division

In 1941 the 34th Infantry Division joined in the invasion of the Soviet Union as part of Army Group Center and was heavily engaged at Minsk, Smolensk, Gomel, and Vyazma; in the Battle of Moscow; and against the Russian winter offensive of 1941-42. The 34th Infantry fought around Juchnow in the defensive battles on the central sector in 1942, took part in the bitter defensive battles for Kharkov in January 1943, fought at Orel in July and August, and distinguished itself in the third battle for Kharkov in August 1943. The following month, its grenadier regiments each lost a battalion due to heavy casualties. The division performed well in the retreat through the northern Ukraine in the spring of 1944, fighting at Cherkassy and Uman, among others.After three years of more or less continuous action on the Eastern Front, however, the division was pretty well burned out by summer and was sent back to Germany.German Order of Battle Vol I 1st - 290th Infantry Divisions in WWII, Samuel W. Mitcham Jr.

The corps was part of 19th Army in STAVKA reserve at the outbreak of hostilities. At that time, it consisted of 129th, 158th and 171st Rifle Divisions. Originally assigned to the defense of Kiev, the corps was transferred to the Smolensk area and assigned to the Western Front. While fighting with the Western Front and it was cut off in the Vyazma Pocket. Survivors of the corps did escape the pocket, but the corps was disbanded in October 1941. The corps was reformed as part of 46th Army in January 1944 and at that time consisted of 195th, 236th and 394th Rifle Divisions. Future Colonel-General and holder of the Order of Lenin Max Reiter was a former commander of this corps, having turned over command just before the outbreak of hostilities. 4th Tank Bn - all light tanks
34th Motorized Rifle Regiment
34th Motorized Howitzer Regiment
34th Reconnaissance Battalion
